News.title: Two children among eight dead in Russian strikes on Ukraine, officials say
News.content:
Eight people, including two children, have died during a Russian missile and drone attack on Ukraine, according to local officials.

President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Wednesday that Russia had been preparing for a "massive attack", urging people to heed air raid alerts.

In the early hours of Thursday, the Ukrainian military reported multiple missile and drone strikes around the country.

The attacks come after Zelensky met US President Donald Trump in Washington DC this week to urge the US to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Two girls, aged 5 and 12, were among the six killed in a village near the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih when a ballistic missile hit a private house, a local official said.

Eight more people were injured, including two children, the official added, noting that the number of casualties could rise.

In Kyiv, one person died and fires broke out in three non-residential buildings overnight, the capital's mayor Vitali Klitschko wrote on Telegram.

The mayor of Poltava also reported a death on Telegram, which came after he said a Nova Poshta postal terminal had been attacked.

Explosions were also heard in Lviv, its mayor Andriy Sadovyi said, reporting that residential buildings had been damaged.

Multiple people were injured with some trapped under a building, he added, saying residents were helping rescuers to clear the rubble.

News.title: Israel building new land barriers in Gaza and displacing families
News.content:
"We've been displaced from place to place, and now we have nowhere left to go," says Umm Mohammed al-Shawish.

She is desperately searching for somewhere to live after Israel moved yellow concrete blocks that mark out where it controls in the Gaza Strip.

Families living in al-Tuffah in northern Gaza woke on Monday to find the blocks had been moved westwards into the centre of Salah al-Din road, a key north-south route through Gaza.

Nearby, an Israeli flag was flying on top of an earth barrier around 3m (10ft) tall.

The al-Shawish family home was destroyed during the war. On Sunday, they had to flee again after the Israeli military called to warn of an attack on a nearby building. Their only shelter was a tent, which was torn apart by the strike.

"We are going to die here," Mohammed al-Shawish said. "Death is better than humiliation. No-one is standing with us."

Under the terms of the US-brokered ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas last October, Israel agreed to withdraw its forces from across Gaza to a designated demarcation - the Yellow Line.

The deal was meant to leave Israel in temporary control of the area behind the Yellow Line - equating to 53% of Gaza's territory. However, the Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu recently said the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) controlled more than 60%. In May, he said publicly that his "directive" was to move to 70%.

Hamas accuses Israel of violating the October ceasefire agreement by moving the Yellow Line westwards. A senior Israeli government official said Israel rejected Hamas's claims outright. The BBC was told: "IDF deployments and security lines are operational measures taken to protect Israeli citizens and prevent Hamas from rebuilding its terror army. Israel will continue to act against any ceasefire violations."

The Israeli military initially marked the Yellow Line with concrete blocks, before moving some markers further into Gaza. But Israel has now constructed a network of barriers, having started soon after the ceasefire. The barriers now stretch more than 42km (26 miles) and cover 85% of Israel's Yellow Line, with the longest section already 13.8km (8.5 miles).

Experts have told the BBC that the earthworks suggest Israel is planning for a long occupation of the strip. In some areas the earth barrier effectively moves the de facto "border" - the Yellow Line - deeper into Gaza, further increasing the deadly no-go zone for Gazans.

One section of the embankment near the al-Mawasi camp is more than 1.5km beyond where the Yellow Line was originally mapped. Another section in Khan Younis is positioned more than 500m over it.

News.title: How serial killer James Desborough preyed on vulnerable homeless men
News.content:
"He's really off his head. He doesn't care... he is kamikaze."

Those were Claudio Aquilino's words during a 999 call the day before he disappeared.

He was frightened and told police he wanted nothing to do with a crime he believed was about to be committed by a man called James Desborough.

About 12 hours later on 18 April 2025, CCTV captured Aquilino with Desborough in a Newquay pub.

It was the last time Aquilino was seen alive.

Police found his burnt remains in a stream months later as they searched woodland owned by Desborough near Sticker, a small village in south Cornwall.

By then another man - Daniel Coleman - had also vanished after last being seen in Desborough's company. His remains were found nearby.

Desborough denied murdering either man, claiming they had died separately in a "series of unfortunate circumstances", but yesterday he was convicted of both of their murders after a seven-week trial at Winchester Crown Court.

He was given a whole life prison sentence with no chance of parole.

On the same day police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that had housed him.

News.title: Uefa to hold emergency meeting over controversial Fifa World Cup plans
News.content:
Uefa will hold an emergency meeting on Thursday afternoon to discuss its response to the controversial World Cup stakeholder plans proposed by Fifa and its president Gianni Infantino.

European football's governing body kept up its offensive over the plans after it was discovered Fifa had sent a letter, seen by the BBC, to all 211 member associations giving them until 19 September to decide if they want to accept the deal, and with it the first $20m (Â£15m) of an initial $40m (Â£30m).

"We have learned of Fifa's deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn," said Uefa. "This says everything you need to know about this plan."

It was Uefa's second statement on the issue. The first claimed Fifa had "crossed a line".

It is not known precisely what will be discussed at the meeting, which will be held virtually.

Many associations, including the Football Association, are furious at only learning through the media of the proposal to sell a 20% stake in Fifa competitions to private finance - led by the Thrive Eternal investment vehicle owned by Joshua Kushner, the brother-in-law of US President Donald Trump's daughter Ivanka.

FA chairwoman Debbie Hewitt was among the Fifa vice-presidents not given advance warning. Uefa's unease has been echoed by the Asian, South American and North and Central American Confederations.

Three of the 2026 World Cup semi-finalists are among Uefa's 55 members. It knows the nuclear option of its members pulling out of the tournament would severely damage the financial viability of the concept.

That is very much viewed as the outer edge of what is possible, particularly as one Uefa member has said it is broadly in agreement with Infantino's proposals.

"We can see the pragmatic benefits for Czech football," said Czech Republic FA president David Trunda.

News.title: Limiting sugar before age two linked to better brain health
News.content:
"They may be onto something," said Rachel Richardson, the methods support unit lead for evidence production and methods directorate at Cochrane, an independent non-profit network that gathers and summarises medical research.

However, she said this "does not represent a smoking gun" linking early sugar intake to dementia.

One big issue is, it is impossible to know how much sugar each of the people in the study were actually eating, merely when they were born relative to sugar rationing.

"This evidence relates to people born in the 1940s and 1950s and so its applicability to young children today is limited - for example, weaning took place earlier and this would have a large impact on the early nutrition of babies and children," said Richardson.

Prof Ian Maidment, professor of clinical pharmacy at Aston University, said: "It is an interesting idea, it helps inform debate, but in my opinion we need more evidence."

He said connecting "something that happened 80 years ago" and projecting that onto health now meant there were "loads" of other factors that could be playing a role.

Dr Sara Rodrigues, from Alzheimer's Research UK, said: "It's important to remember that this was an observational study.

"This means it can identify links between diet and dementia risk, but it cannot prove that eating less sugar directly prevents dementia.

"Eating a healthy, balanced diet is one of the best ways to support your brain health and it's never too late to make positive changes."

News.title: Body of Scottish woman found inside suitcase in Greece
News.content:
The body of a Scottish woman has been found inside a suitcase in an abandoned building in Greece, prompting a multi-agency investigation.

Police Scotland confirmed they are liaising with authorities after the woman was reportedly discovered by a homeless man in the Kypseli district in Athens on 18 July.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, is thought to have travelled to Greece from Cyprus last month, state broadcaster ERT reports. She is believed to have died between five and seven days before she was found.

Greek police told BBC Scotland News the body of a British woman was found and fingerprint data from Interpol matched a woman born in 1988. Investigations are ongoing.

News.title: Interest rates expected to be held again by Bank of England
News.content:
The committee of five women and four men will announce their latest interest rate decision at 12:00 BST, with a hold the widespread expectation.

The Bank rate is the MPC's primary tool for maintaining the rate of rising prices - inflation - at a target of 2%.

The latest official figures show inflation in the UK was 2.6% in the year to June, down slightly on the previous month but still above its 2.3% target.

The inflation rate is likely to go up in July, as millions of households in Scotland, England and Wales feel the impact of a 13% rise in domestic energy prices.

The increase was the result of the impact of the Iran war on wholesale energy prices.

Conflict in the Gulf, and uncertainty over the chances of a lasting truce, hang over the MPC's meeting and decision this month and in the months ahead.

Many analysts expect interest rates to be unchanged in the foreseeable future, with the possibility of the next change being a rise.

"A new government finding its feet, and the situation in the Middle East becoming increasingly uncertain, mean that a hold on [the] base rate decision would be a welcome dose of stability," said Katie Horne, from savings platform Flagstone.

"People have had more than enough uncertainty over the past year, and even a temporary pause eases the pressure a little."

News.title: Inquiry finds MoD Afghan data breach was foreseeable failure
News.content:
The committee also questioned the decision not to provide confidential briefing to parliamentarians, with then-Defence Secretary Grant Shapps pushing back against plans to tell then-shadow defence secretary John Healey of the breach.

Thursday's report also questioned the government's overarching policy to not comment on special forces matters, describing it as "inappropriate" in the context of the breach.

The committee added that special forces involvement "should not prevent Parliament and the public from understanding how administrative failings occurred".

Dhesi said: "Secrecy has been too easily used as a shield against proper accountability in areas far removed from sensitive operations."

The role of UKSF in the resettlement scheme was also questioned by the committee after reports the breach had been due to their involvement in deciding whether to relocate Afghan special forces.

The committee was unable to establish this connection, due to the "neither confirm nor deny" policy of the government, but it did raise concerns over the handling of these cases.

In February 2024, BBC Panorama revealed that British Special Forces had been given a de facto veto over Arap applications from their Afghan counterparts seeking to relocate to safety in the UK.

Afghan special forces served alongside UKSF on some of the conflict's most dangerous missions and are considered among those at the highest risk of reprisal since the Taliban takeover.

Last year, the BBC obtained internal MoD documents - also cited in the report - showing a British Special Forces officer personally rejected 1,585 resettlement applications from Afghans with credible links to special forces in a matter of weeks, in 2023. The UKSF officer did not approve a single application during that period.

The rejections from UKSF left many in fear for their lives and former members of the Afghan special forces told the BBC they were living in hiding.

One said he had been interrogated and beaten by the Taliban before he went on the run, while another said he had escaped first but had heard the Taliban had gone to his home looking for him.

"I'm living in a very bad situation. I am in hiding and mostly my family can't live together and we cannot go out and we cannot work," he said. "I feel I have been left alone in the midst of hell."

The government had to announce a review in 2024 and since then 884 former members of Afghan special forces, who served alongside UKSF, have since had their rejections overturned.

The defence committee report outlined that the "proportion of decisions subsequently overturned demonstrates the seriousness of that failure".

The UK government closed Arap to new applications in 2025, but the report said the government had a "special responsibility" to the Afghan special forces it had wrongly rejected. Many of them had made their applications in 2021, but were still living in fear due to "government delay or error".

The defence secretary currently faces a legal challenge at the Royal Courts of Justice from former Afghan special forces who are unable to escape to the UK.

In a hearing on Wednesday, the court heard one family had "$200 left to survive".

A MoD spokesperson said: "This incident should never have happened and we acknowledge the significant impact it has had on many people.

"Thousands of eligible Afghans have already been safely relocated to the UK, where they can rebuild their lives and we are committed to ensuring that we conclude the Afghan resettlement programme by the end of this Parliament.

"We are learning the lessons from this incident and important reforms are already in place, including improved data protection standards, strengthened case-working processes and better programme governance.

"We welcome the public and parliamentary scrutiny of our actions, so we can learn more and be held to account, and we'll continue to work closely with the committee on this issue."

News.title: Former farmer, aged 99, fulfils wish to lead cow at show one more time
News.content:
A 99-year-old care home resident in south-west Scotland has fulfilled his wish to show a cow at his local agricultural show one more time.

Staff at the Belmont Care Centre in Stranraer put a post on social media about former farmer Jackie Brown's dream in the hope of being able to see it realised.

It came to the attention of the organisers of Stranraer Show who organised for Jackie to come along to the farming event on Wednesday.

He showed one of the Ayrshire cows - just as he had done many times across his pioneering career.

News.title: Burnham says nuclear sub investment will protect UK and boost jobs
News.content:
The Dreadnought-class submarines will replace the UK's four Vanguard-class vessels that have been in operation since 1992, carrying Trident missiles to provide a nuclear deterrent.

Those Vanguard submarines are due to be retired in the 2030s, with the Dreadnoughts entering service at the same time.

The project has taken 20 years to get to this stage and was first announced in 2006 by the then Labour Prime Minister, Tony Blair. A decade later, in 2016, MPs formally approved building the new submarines.

Thursday's announcement of Â£8.4bn marks the start of what has been called the fourth phase of the project.

The spending was already planned, and was included in the Defence Investment Plan, published in the final days of Sir Keir Starmer's government.

The plan sets out Â£63.6bn over the next four years for what is called the Defence Nuclear Enterprise.

The bulk of the money (Â£47bn) will go on keeping the nuclear submarines in operation, continuing with the Dreadnoughts, starting work on what might replace them in 30 years' time, and constructing several other new submarines and upgrading the UK's naval docks and manufacturing facilities.

The prime minister will use his visit to Barrow-in-Furness to stress how defence spending can have economic benefits for the country.

"The submarines produced in Barrow will protect Britain for decades to come, and the 47,000 jobs and apprenticeships will change lives both in this town and in dozens of places like it," he said prior to his visit.

"British money, spent on British workers, British firms and British skills, in the places that were written off for 40 years."

The government says the spending on the UK's nuclear defence currently supports around 47,000 British jobs â and is forecast to rise to 65,000 by 2030, including 22,000 apprenticeships by 2035.

Since becoming prime minister, Burnham has said he wants to reduce the number of young people not in employment, education or training and has announced funding to help those starting apprenticeships.

In a further step, Burnham has said the public procurement process, used to decide how to spend taxpayer cash, will favour companies offering 45-day work placements.

Speaking to the Jimmy's Jobs of the Future podcast,, external he said there would be "more social value weighting in public contracts", with a particular focus on firms offering such placements.

He said the move had been inspired by his time as Greater Manchester mayor, when he oversaw a rise in the number of 45-day placements offered by private firms.

But the announcement offered little detail of the extent of the changes, how they would be implemented and how many firms he expected to roll out the placements as a result.

Liberal Democrat defence spokesperson James MacCleary called for the use of defence bonds to "raise dedicated funding to rebuild capabilities across the whole of the armed forces".

For Reform UK, Danny Kruger dismissed Burnham's announcement as a "rehashed spending plan" that did "nothing to address the crisis in the UK's nuclear programme".

"If the prime minister actually cared about keeping Britain safe and ensuring our armed forces can stand alongside our allies, he would commit to a significant increase in spending and a total overhaul of both procurement and the nuclear enterprise," Kruger said.

Green Party Westminster leader Ellie Chowns questioned the decision to spend billions of pounds on "weapons that must never be used".

"Ministers should not pretend that the best way to create employment is by funnelling ever-increasing sums into the nuclear weapons programme," she said.

News.title: Police to take no further action against Polanski over guillotine re-post
News.content:
The Metropolitan Police has said it will take no further action against Green Party leader Zack Polanski after he re-posted a photo of a man wearing a T-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

In a statement, the force said it did not believe sharing the picture constituted an offence.

A Green Party spokesperson said it was "obvious from the start" that no crime had been committed, and said Reform UK was "using this as a political football for their own cynical purposes" as a distraction.

In response to the Met's decision, a Reform UK spokesman said: "Once again we see that we are living in two-tier Britain."

"Zack Polanski is allowed to get away with inciting murder whilst ordinary people up and down the country get a knock at the door for making a joke online."

The Met said after careful review it had concluded it was unlikely the sharing of the image online would constitute a criminal offence.

It said the post has been shared by about 130 accounts and the police should not treat individuals differently based on their public profile, meaning any investigation would have to consider all those accounts too.

"Given it is unlikely their actions would have ultimately constituted an offence, such an extensive investigation was deemed to do be disproportionate and not a reasonable use of police resources."

While the Met Police said it would not be taking further action over the sharing of the image, it said it had determined that a crime should be recorded in relation to the wearing of the T-shirt and had referred a crime report to Avon and Somerset Police, who cover Bristol where the photo was taken.

Shortly after the Met Police's statement, Avon and Somerset Police said "the threshold for a criminal offence has not been met".

Setting out its decision, the Avon and Somerset Police said: "Particular consideration has been given to the context around the image; its use of song lyrics, and the marketing of the T-shirt as a satirical piece.

"No complaints were received from people at the event at which it was worn and there is no evidence the wearer of the T-shirt intended to threaten any individual, or encourage anyone else to do so."

The force added they it took the safety of elected politicians "extremely seriously" and it would continue to take action "wherever a threat is identified".

News.title: Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
News.content:
In an emotional speech he praised those caring for his father, who has Alzheimer's, and said he wanted to deliver changes to help "my dad and the millions like him".

Speaking to reporters afterwards, he said he wanted to extract more from existing budgets to fund the reforms.

"I think we owe it to the public before we talk about tax rises.. you first have to look the public in the eye and say 'Are we doing everything we can do from within what we've got?'"

For example, he said his announcements on improving pay and training for the social care workforce "will be fully funded".

But he added that fuller reforms "will require difficult decisions" and these "would be put before the country at the right time, and we will hopefully proceed with people's consent".

Burnham said in "an ideal world" he would not want anyone to have to sell their home to pay for care, describing it as a "really awful process".

He added proposals he previously put forward, when he was health secretary in 2009, were intended to stop that, saying: "If everybody on the NHS principle contributed a little, it would mean everybody could protect the majority of what they'd worked for."

He later held talks with Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey and Conservative shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew as part of efforts to get cross-party backing for any changes. Tory leader Kemi Badenoch was unavailable.

The Conservatives have previously urged the prime minister to rule out tax rises or increased borrowing to pay for social care changes.

Speaking to the BBC's Radio 4 PM, Andrew said it had been important to set "red lines" around funding.

He acknowledged finding funding would be a "challenge" but added that there was "a significant amount of money in the system - it's just sometime it is not in the right place".

Burnham did not invite the leaders of Reform UK or the Green Party of England and Wales to the talks. Both parties have expressed disappointment at this.

The PM said there was a feeling at Westminster that social care was "too big a political risk" to deal with, adding he wants to take on the challenge as the "risks of failing to act are too great".

Burnham highlighted the financial impact of care costs on people and spoke of how fixing issues in social care could ease the pressure on the NHS and make savings.

The PM said Baroness Casey's review should consider how to pay for a national care service, adding there needs to a system that becomes "highly integrated" with the NHS.

Burnham said he wants to "immediately" focus on the social care workforce, noting a fair pay agreement is due to come into force from 2028/29 and described it as a "massive building block of a national care service".

News.title: Serial killer given whole life orders for murders of two men as police investigate four more deaths
News.content:
Serial killer James Desborough has been given two whole life prison sentences with no chance of parole - as police revealed they are looking into four unexplained deaths at the homeless shelter that housed him.

Desborough, already serving a minimum of 19 years for the murder of his prison cellmate, was given the whole life tariffs for killing 57-year-old Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, 43, in Cornwall.

Aquilino and Coleman met Desborough at Newquay's Sandy Lodge homeless shelter, where police are now reviewing the unexplained deaths of two other men and two women.

Sentencing, Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini described Desborough, 40, as "a highly dangerous individual who had no regard for the life of those you think are worthless".

Higher humidity, cooler temperatures and a forecast for rain raised hopes of relief Thursday for a parched portion of southwestern France engulfed by wildfires that have charred an area four times the size of Paris in recent weeks.

With moisture moving in from the Atlantic Ocean coast, national weather service Meteo France forecast light rain in the town of Lège-Cap-Ferret, on a peninsula that's been a leading edge of the devastated region.

Local officials reported a “rather calm" night, with a fire that has not grown beyond the 42,000 hectares (about 162 sq. miles) already affected. Fire crews remained at “total mobilization” with 2,200 firefighters and over 20 aircraft.

Humidity that reached 80% overnight was expected to drop by midday, authorities said, though some rainfall was expected along the coast that “could reach the fire zone.”

Temperatures that peaked around 40 Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) a day earlier were set to drop Thursday, topping out at 27 C (80 F) along the coast. An “orange” heat wave alert — the second-highest level after “red” — was lifted shortly before dawn.

The fires in the Bordeaux wine-growing, forested and tourism-heavy region are among the blazes that have swept across pockets of southern Europe in recent weeks, including Spain and Greece.

On Wednesday, authorities said three firefighters had died on the Greek island on Crete, as the wildfire emergency stretched from the Atlantic coast to the eastern Mediterranean.

At the peak of the evacuations, a third of a million people were driven from homes and vacation sites in France and Spain.

Early reactions to Spider-Man: Brand New Day have singled out Sadie Sink as the film’s surprise stand-out, with critics describing the Stranger Things star as “devastating in her role”.

Tom Holland’s latest outing as Spider-Man has also been called his “best performance” in the role.

The fourth standalone Spider-Man film, which premiered at the Dolby Theatre in Hollywood on Monday ahead of its cinema release, sees Holland return as Peter Parker alongside Zendaya, Jacob Batalon, Jon Bernthal, Mark Ruffalo, and Sadie Sink in a mystery role.

Directed by Destin Daniel Cretton, Brand New Day is set four years after Spider-Man: No Way Home and follows Peter Parker as he continues fighting crime alone after Doctor Strange’s memory spell erased him from the lives of MJ, Ned, and the rest of the world, while his spider powers begin evolving beyond his control and a mysterious new villain emerges.

The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey gave the film four stars in her review, and wrote that it is “not only the best of the MCU takes on the character, but it’s also flat out the best Spider-Man film since Sam Raimi’s Spider-Man 2”.

She added that Sink was “excellent”, admitting that she couldn’t say more about her role “without giving the game away”.

open image in gallery The fourth standalone Spider-Man film sees Holland return as Peter Parker alongside Zendaya, Jacob Batalon, Jon Bernthal, Mark Ruffalo, and Sadie Sink in a mystery role ( Sony )

Fandango correspondent Erik Davis described the film as “deeper, more thoughtful and more mature than the previous trilogy”, adding that Cretton had crafted “some of my favorite Spider-Man fight sequences of the Holland era”.

On Sink, he wrote: “And yes, the Sadie Sink mystery absolutely pays off. She’s perfect.”

Brian Davids of The Hollywood Reporter wrote that “Peter Parker is changing, and so is the ‘Spider-Man’ franchise.”

He described Brand New Day as “the most emotional, most mature and most atmospheric instalment in the franchise”, adding that it “will meet your expectations in some places and defy them in others”.

Peter Howell, film critic at the Toronto Star, said the sequel leaves behind “the multiverse tedium” that dominated recent Marvel stories in favour of “a grounded Spider-Man tale that’s back to the grungy city roots of the comic book hero we knew and loved”.

He added that Holland “finally nails the sarcasm, angst and love hassles of Spidey/Peter Parker as Stan Lee first envisioned the character”.

Collider senior host and producer Perri Nemiroff called it “far and away a favourite of the recent MCU instalments”, saying writers Chris McKenna and Erik Sommers built the story around “the importance of work-life balance and community”.

“Can’t believe how emotional the film made me,” she wrote.

Variety senior artisans editor Jazz Tangcay described Brand New Day as “action-packed from start to finish”, adding that this “might be Tom Holland’s best outing as Spiderman to date.”

open image in gallery Critics have described Tom Holland’s latest outing as Spider-Man as his ‘best performance’ in the role ( Sony )

Germain Lussier, senior reporter covering entertainment for Gizmodo and io9, admitted the film had moved him to tears. “It’s a massive movie that balances like 5 different through lines in equal measure, each better than the last. It can feel a little overwhelming but it all comes together so beautifully it works,” he wrote.

New Rockstars’ Erik Voss described Brand New Day as “an emotionally meaty dwelling on loneliness and suppressing what we truly are”. He singled out Sink’s performance, writing that she is “devastating in her role and I can’t wait to see more of her in the MCU.”

MovieWeb host Joseph Deckelmeier was equally enthusiastic, describing it as “easily the best Spider-Man movie yet”. He praised its “incredible action, real emotional stakes, huge surprises”, adding: “Tom Holland and Sadie Sink are incredible in this film.”

Pamela Gores, managing editor of The Direct, also drew attention to Sink’s character, saying it has an “ambitious” and “potentially divisive start”, even as she described Brand New Day as “an emotional triumph” and “a juggernaut of a film that truly feels like a comic book come to life”.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day opens in cinemas on 31 July.

A major incident has been declared on the Suffolk coast as firefighters battle a substantial heathland blaze at Dunwich Heath, near Leiston.

The Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service was mobilised shortly after 5.30pm on Wednesday following reports of a wildfire.

The inferno is currently spreading south-west, posing a threat to St James’ Church, situated off Westleton Road. Authorities confirmed the major incident status was enacted "due to the size and complexity" of the rapidly developing situation.

Dan Davis, a station manager for the service, has issued an urgent plea for the public to steer clear of the area and ensure windows and doors remain shut.

“Crews from Leiston attended the scene and were met with what is a large-scale, wind- driven forestry fire,” he said.

“The incident has subsequently been upgraded to a major incident.

“We currently have approximately 90 firefighters on scene working incredibly hard in arduous conditions to bring this fire under control.”

Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service station manager Dan Davis urged the public to avoid the area if possible and keep windows and doors closed ( Suffolk Fire and Rescue Service )

Mr Davis added: “I’d like to provide reassurance that we are going to remain on scene until we bring this fire under control.”

It comes amid UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) issuing an amber heat-health alert for the East Midlands, the East, South East and London.

The alert remains in place until 9am on Thursday, with the agency previously warning that rising temperatures may increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

Separately, in Scotland, crews said they were making “significant progress” tackling a wildfire in the Cairngorms that broke out two weeks ago.

A number of homes in the remote region were evacuated as plumes of smoke billowed into the sky, and vast swathes of trees, heather and grasslands have been left charred and blackened.

Speaking on the track on Wednesday, Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) deputy assistant chief officer Michael Humphreys told the Press Association that fire crews are making progress in tackling the blaze.

However, he warned the risk of flare-ups remains high.

“It’s been an absolutely devastating fire for wildlife and for the local community who have come out in force to really support us, which we really do appreciate,” he said.

“To control this fire, what we’ve had to put in place is a significant number of fire breaks.”

Warning: the following story contains potential spoilers for Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

A secret part of the new Spider-Man film might have accidentally been spoiled by one of the movie’s musicians.

During a red carpet interview at Monday’s Los Angeles premiere of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, singer Steve Lacy — whose song “oh yeah?” is featured in the film — was asked which character was his favorite in the fourth installment of the superhero franchise.

“Out of all of the characters in the film you’re aware of and, without spoiling anything, who is your favorite? Or who are you most excited to see?” the interviewer asked Lacy, 28, on the carpet.

Lacy took a second to think before responding.

open image in gallery Steve Lacy appeared to reveal a major spoiler about 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' at the Los Angeles premiere of the movie ( Getty )

“You know what? Jean,” Lacy answered. “I like Jean. She’s the villain but there’s a reason to her madness.”

The reporter, who looked stunned, asked him, “Is that a spoiler?” but the “Bad Habit” singer did not respond to the question.

It did not take long for fans to latch on to Steve’s admission and take it as confirmation that franchise newcomer Sadie Sink is playing X-Men’s telekinetic mutant Jean Grey in the movie — and that she will be revealed as a villain.

Speculation over Sink’s role in the fourth Spider-Man film has been rampant after her casting was first reported in March 2025, but her character’s name had been kept under wraps as Marvel did not release any official information about the Stranger Things star’s part in the iconic franchise.

Now, fans are stunned that Lacy appeared to reveal the big secret so casually after years of Sink, 24, holding it in.

“The way Sadie has been dodging spoilers all press tour only for Steve Lacy to drop it like it’s nothing… girl is in the trenches rn,” one person wrote on X. Another added, “Bro just needed one interview to destroy everything.”

open image in gallery Sadie Sink, Jon Bernthal, Tom Holland, Zendaya and Jacob Batalon star in the new Spider-Man movie ( Getty )

Another said that “he can’t be serious,” with one person adding: “It was funny but I'm genuinely dumbfounded by how stupid he is. Slipping up a spoiler happens all the time sure, but if you see the clip of this guy Steve Lacy that is not normal.”

However, some fans are still optimistic that Lacy might have been referring to Lisa Colón-Zayas’s character, who was previously reported to be Captain Jean DeWolff, a NYPD detective.

A representative for Lacy did not immediately return The Independent’s request for comment.

Brand New Day, which comes out July 31, picks up where Spider-Man: No Way Home left off nearly five years ago, with Tom Holland’s Peter Parker dealing with the aftermath of a spell that made the entire world — including his best friends, played by Zendaya and Jacob Batalon — forget his existence.

News.title: AMR chatbot could prevent drug-resistant infections in African hospitals
News.content:
A phone-based chatbot advising medics how to prescribe antibiotics has helped raise the quality of care in African hospitals and should stop bugs developing dangerous resistance, developers say.

Staff at four hospitals across Zambia and Kenya have been using two digital tools in a pilot project to try to address one of the world’s biggest health threats.

Anti-microbial resistance (AMR) is caused by germs evolving so that medicines such as antibiotics designed to kill them no longer work.

The menace is linked to nearly five million deaths each year and makes it increasingly difficult to treat infections. The annual death toll could nearly double in the next 25 years, according to some forecasts.

The rise in AMR is being significantly driven by the misuse and overuse of antimicrobials in human medicine and in agriculture.

Using antibiotics when they are not necessary, using the wrong ones, or getting the dosage wrong, all add to the chances that bugs will develop resistance.

With a shortage of new drugs in the development pipeline, one push to defeat AMR has been to get medics to stick to existing prescription, dosage and treatment advice.

The Antibiotic Stewardship Programme through Innovation, Research, and Education (ASPIRE) is trying to give them guidance using technology they already have in their pockets.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at this year’s Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, following on from her third place at the 2018 Games in Australia.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

News.title: China’s chip breakthrough triggers global tech rout
News.content:
China has achieved a breakthrough in developing technology crucial to the AI boom, overcoming US efforts to limit Beijing’s access to the systems.

China’s chip giant Shanghai Yuliangsheng has started production of deep ultraviolet lithography machines, according to The Information, a tech publication.

These machines, which can reach the size of a double-decker bus, use high-powered lasers to imprint designs on to silicon wafers, which are used to make chips.

Until recently, only Western companies and allies of the US had the capability to produce these machines.

The most advanced versions of the technology have largely been the preserve of companies such as Dutch giant ASML and Japan’s Nikon.

These machines have been cut off from China by US export controls, preventing their production of advanced chips as Washington seeks to slow the development of AI in the country.

Semiconductor stocks plunged on the report. Trading was briefly halted on South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index after it suffered a collapse of nearly 11pc overnight, following a bleak day on Wall Street.

Advanced semiconductors, such as those used in AI chips, rely on minuscule circuits, invisible to the naked eye. They can only be manufactured by directing tiny lasers onto microchip wafers, a process known as ultraviolet lithography.

News.title: Ramsay-Peaty ‘human first, athlete second’ as he settles for second bronze
News.content:
So a pair of bronze medals for the man who once only dealt in gold. Not that Adam Ramsay-Peaty thinks that is necessarily such a bad trade when he also computes the wider price of sporting domination.

“I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it,” Ramsay-Peaty said after his return to international competition continued in his now favoured 50m breaststroke with a second podium place at these Commonwealth Games. “That period of time, where I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human,” he added. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”

Aged 31, and with a baby girl on the way with wife Holly Ramsay, Ramsay-Peaty’s order of priorities might be understandable, but it was still another performance to raise questions over whether he can again climb to the top of a major podium.

Swimming is not kind to the over-30s – Michael Phelps was the first man in 2016 to win an Olympic gold in the pool even at the age Ramsay-Peaty is now – and we still have another two years until the Los Angeles Olympics. It would be the greatest achievement even of the Englishman’s extraordinary career to win his third individual Olympic title.

He trailed from the start here and was almost exactly a second outside his world record – set almost a decade ago – as Australia’s Sam Williamson completed a breaststroke double ahead of South Africa’s Michael Houlie in second. “As you get older, it gets harder,” said Ramsay-Peaty, before adding a crucial caveat, “but I’m enjoying it more…in my head, I’m getting fresher.”

Sports.title: Iconic top-flight club where Pep Guardiola spent a season ceases to exist after being officially liquidated
Sports.content:
A 114 YEAR-OLD Italian club once home to a host of all-time greats is now extinct.

Brescia Calcio once boasted a midfield duo of Pep Guardiola and Ballon d’Or winner Roberto Baggio, but is now officially bankrupt.



Midfield maestro Andrea Pirlo also won his first professional silverware at the north Italian outfit, and hometown boy Mario Balotelli is yet another of the club’s glittering alumni.

But the once legendary side, based at the foot of the Alps, had been staring down the barrel for over a year.



At the end of the 2024/25 season, ex-Leeds United owner Massimo Cellino failed to pay around £1million of debt to the Italian league authorities, alongside months of overdue staff wages worth millions of euros.

The former Serie A founding member was initially docked four points and relegated to the third tier amid the financial turmoil, before being officially expelled from the 2025-26 season altogether.

Cellino hired and fired coaches 24 times across eight ruinous years at Brescia, before eventually plunging the side into insolvency.

A Lombardy court has now put a final nail in the club’s coffin, decreeing its judicial liquidation.

The legal resolution has condemned the former talent hotbed to an ignominious end, despite Brescia receiving over around £3m from boyhood star Sandro Tonali‘s £100million move to Spurs this summer.

Italian football will now have to mourn the loss of a provincial giant.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Despite Brescia’s population only amounting to 201,000, only 11 clubs have played fewer seasons outside the country’s top two tiers.

However, local powerbrokers have taken drastic action to ensure the city is not starved of professional football.

Brescia Colmo’s century of footballing heritage has been resurrected via Union Brescia, founded last year after Mayor Laura Castelletti persuaded a local rival to rebrand and relocate.

The astonishing move materialised after the chairman of FeralpiSalò, an ex-Serie B club based in a neighbouring town, agreed to breathe life into Brescian football and transfer his existing entity to the nearby city.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino breaks silence on plan to sell World Cup – but shameless Fifa REFUSE to take questions from media
Sports.content:
GIANNI INFANTINO has broken his silence after his controversial plans to sell the World Cup threatened to plunge global football into civil war.

The Fifa president’s sensational plan to sell off parts of the World Cup to the highest bidder was revealed on Tuesday and was met with fierce backlash from all directions.



And despite the threats of a boycott from Uefa and major footballing nations, Infantino has doubled-down on his stance – which it is claimed would create a £20billion subsidiary to run the World Cup and other Fifa competitions by offering stakes of up to 20 per cent to external investors.

Infantino, 56, provided an update in a video shared by Fifa on Wednesday, rather than taking questions from the media.



He said: “It’s part of a democratic process, a consultation process and, above all, it is an opportunity but not an obligation, and, as I said, it kicks off the consultation process.”

The Swiss insisted that Fifa’s 211 members would have the final say on the plan.

Critics blasted Fifa for trying to “enrich themselves and their friends”, as football‘s regional bodies including The FA said they had been blindsided by the move.

Even some of Fifa’s eight vice-presidents were left in the dark over the plan, which could raise as much as £7.5bn according to Infantino.

He continued: “FIFA obviously continues to govern football without any external interference.

“And the flagship tournament it organises, like the FIFA World Cup or the FIFA Women’s World Cup, will always remain.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

In a five-page letter to members outlining the merits of the proposal, Infantino said positive responses before the 19 September deadline would see £15m made available as soon as January.

He has insisted the proposal to set up what will be known as Fifa Forward Enterprise will unlock new commercial opportunities and give rise to the next Cape Verdes, one of four nations to make their debuts at the 2026 World Cup following its expansion to 48 teams.

One of the proposed investors has already been identified as Thrive Eternal, conveniently a fund run by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump‘s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, following Infantino’s close ties with the US President before and during the World Cup.

Uefa said the deadline being just 53 days away “says everything you need to know about this plan”.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino’s £7.5billion cash grab leaves football on brink of civil war 60 years on from England’s greatest day
Sports.content:
THE World Cup used to be so simple — and today serves as the perfect reminder of that.

It was exactly 60 years ago that Bobby Moore was lifting the Jules Rimet trophy and being hoisted on the shoulders of his England team-mates.



Those iconic scenes at Wembley came after a tournament that had just 16 teams and lasted only 20 days.

There were no hydration breaks or half-time shows and certainly no private investors looking for a slice of the pie.



The biggest worry was the trophy being stolen — and even that had an innocent ending, thanks to Pickles the dog finding it.

Sadly there is no Pickles this time to save the messy situation, which is rapidly becoming a dog’s dinner.



Football is on the brink of civil war after Gianni Infantino revealed on Tuesday his radical plans to flog off parts of the World Cup.

It essentially involves the creation of a new company, Fifa Forward Enterprise, that would allow them to sell stakes in their commercial and event operations.

Fifa stress those shareholdings would be “minority” and “non-controlling” investments — yet could still raise US$10billion (£7.52bn).

Uefa have warned it “crosses a line” and are expected to hold an emergency meeting on the matter.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Others — such as Asia’s governing body, the AFC — revealed they were “not consulted on the proposal” and were blindsided by Infantino.

The same applies to Concacaf, who represent Central and North America and are “deeply concerned by the lack of due process” that has taken place.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has waded into the debate and the outcry on social media is so great that some are pining for the days of Sepp Blatter.

Imagine saying that when Infantino’s predecessor announced in 2015 that he was finally ending his 17-year reign of corruption as Fifa president?

The nuclear option of some countries boycotting the World Cup has been floated, namely by those at Uefa.



That was their solution back in 2021, when Fifa proposed hosting the World Cup every two years.

It is the obvious move to play as Fifa know the tournament simply does not work without the European heavyweights, especially if you are inviting 64 teams to the party, as is Fifa’s proposal.

At this summer’s 48-team World Cup, six of the eight quarter-finalists were from Europe.

The winners, Spain, were too — and that was also the case in 2018 when France got their hands on the trophy.

Infantino’s big plan to sell stakes in the World Cup is around the commercial money that can be made.



But that is simply a non-starter if the Uefa teams refuse to be a part of this wild new landscape.

The fear is, though, that it is harder to predict a united front coming from those that oppose this outlandish scheme.

Cash is king — and there is a lot of it on the table for those that give Infantino’s proposals the green light.

The Fifa president has written to all 211 of the governing body’s member associations, who will vote on the matter.

In the letter, Infantino outlined the extra £30million they could receive by giving the thumbs-up to his plans.



Part of that comes in the shape of a £15m lump sum, which member associations would have access to.

The idea would be that it is spent on things like stadiums and training centres, with the money’s use audited.

Countries would then get access to a further £15m over the following three years through their member association funding.

The upcoming cycle from 2027-30 was budgeted at £6m per member association — but Fifa say that would rise to £15m if Infantino’s proposals are voted through.

Clearly, some countries would welcome a cash boost like that and there has been praise for the plans as well as opposition.



The Czech Republic FA’s president, David Trunda, has given them his backing and will not be alone.

And then there is the elephant in the room — Russia.

Infantino revealed earlier this year that Fifa would look into reintegrating them into international football after they were banned in 2022 following their invasion of Ukraine.

That could lead to further splits between European countries, with Russia having political influence over at least half a dozen Fifa member associations.

Ultimately, it is the vote of those members that will decide if Infantino gets his wish.



The controversial Swiss requires majority support from them and also backing from the Fifa Council, which consists of 37 members.

And whether people like it or not, history has shown us that Infantino usually gets his way.

The fiasco around USA star Folarin Balogun’s suspension reprieve at the World Cup this summer showed that and made a mockery of the game.

There were concerns afterwards about Donald Trump’s influence, as the US President got his way by simply picking up the phone.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Fifa had already cosied up to Trump by awarding him their inaugural ‘Peace Prize’ after he was snubbed for the Nobel version.



The question now is, does anyone have a trump card to stop Infantino?

Sports.title: Chelsea’s Instagram raided by thousands of Kazakhstan fans after ‘trialist’ scores seven minutes into pre-season clash

The 17-year-old “trialist” scored just seven minutes into Chelsea‘s pre-season clash against Western Sydney Wanderers on Tuesday.



Kazakh football fans have shown their support for Satpayev as the Blues shared footage of his goal against the Wanderers on social media.

Sports.title: Newcastle star close to tears as he’s forced off just 21 minutes into second game back from SIX-MONTH injury lay-off
Sports.content:
INJURY-JINXED Newcastle star Fabian Schar’s return to action after a six-month lay-off ended in agony.

The Swiss centre-half hobbled off early as his comeback turned into a nightmare, with the Toon slumping to an alarming 4-1 pre-season defeat at Bristol City.



A dejected Schar headed straight to the dressing room on 21 minutes for treatment after collapsing in a heap with what looked like a muscle injury on the half-way line.

It was cruel on Schar, 34, who has been battling his way back to fitness after being sidelined with an ankle injury and then a foot infection.



He had been relishing his ninth campaign with the Geordies after signing a new one-year contract extension last month.

And the sight of him trudging off was a blow for Toon boss Eddie Howe whose preparations for the new campaign have gone from bad to worse.



He has already lost the services of Kieran Trippier, Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali with Bruno Guimaraes’ future also looking uncertain amid Arsenal interest.

Howe desperately needs reinforcements before the Prem season starts judging by their abject Ashton Gate show.

For shambolic Newcastle looked utterly leaderless after Schar, who was crocked in a 4-3 win over Leeds at St James Park way back in January, limped off.

Ex-Sunderland forward Sam Greenwood rubbed salt into the wounds six minutes after Schar’s unfortunate exit with a stunning free-kick for the Robins.



BEST FREE BETS AND BETTING SIGN UP OFFERS

And then City’s new striker Lorent Tolaj brushed Sven Botman aside before beating the Tynesiders’ new French keeper Ewen Jaouen.

Max Bird piled on the agony after half-time when he broke clear before driving past Jaouen as Newcastle’s leaden defence was prised apart.

Toon skipper Harvey Barnes gave the travelling fans something to shout about on 78 minutes with a cool finish.
