Abe, Scanlon, Milos Kerkez and Trey Nyoni were replaced at half-time by Ngumoha, Kieran Morrison, Kostas Tsimikas and Curtis Jones respectively. Elliott was presented with a sight of the Wrexham goal by Koumas minutes after the restart but his first-time shot from 20 yards was well saved by Ward. The Wales international also denied Szoboszlai from distance but this was a Liverpool performance – and pre-season friendly – that failed to ignite.

Wrexham substitute Nathan Broadhead almost succeeded with a powerful drive from 25 yards that was pushed away by Mamardashvili. Brunt and Kieffer Moore both had good late chances to equalise but miscued from close range.

Sports.title: WSL brings back Sunday evening kick-offs after indifferent viewing figures
Sports.content:
The Women’s Super League will bring back Sunday evening kick-offs this season as part of an overhaul of its broadcast strategy after indifferent viewing figures last season.

The Guardian has learned that the WSL will offer six different TV slots to broadcasters after releasing its fixtures for the 2026-27 campaign later on Thursday in a significant change from last season, when the majority of televised games took place on Saturday and Sunday lunchtimes.

Sky Sports, which has the live rights for 163 of the WSL’s 182 games, retains the Saturday 12.45pm slot and noon on Sundays, but has also been given new regular kick-off times of 7pm on Friday and 6pm on Sunday.

The BBC will broadcast 19 matches live at 12.30pm on Saturdays and 2.30pm on Sundays.

The WSL’s new strategy is to spread games across the weekend after scheduling most fixtures at noon on Sundays last season, with multiple televised matches kicking off at the same time in a move that diluted the audience.

The change this season follows a lengthy consultation with broadcasters, clubs and fans, with the WSL seeking a schedule that maximises its TV audience and matchday attendances.

The Sunday evening kick-off was dropped last season after negative feedback from clubs and fans, as attendances were generally poor, but it was popular with broadcasters and was Sky’s best performing slot in 2024-25 with an average audience of 144,000.

In an attempt to balance these competing interests, the Sunday evening game will mostly be brought forward 45 minutes to 6pm – with some changes likely to avoid clashes with the 4.30pm Premier League games – while the WSL will attempt to schedule derbies for that slot and Friday evenings where possible.

The Guardian revealed last December that the WSL was considering further changes to its kick-off times this season after concern from Sky in particular at some of their viewing figures for lunchtime games.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

An average audience of 59,000 watched Sky’s live coverage of Arsenal’s home win over Liverpool that month, even fewer than the 71,000 people who watched Arsenal v Chelsea on Sky in the same noon kick-off slot the previous month.

As well as struggling to attract a casual audience the decision to schedule up to four of the six weekly matches at the same time proved unpopular with the most committed WSL fans, who were unable to watch multiple matches live.

Sky are paying the vast majority of the joint £65m broadcast deal with the BBC, who are believed to contribute around £8m in rights fees, so have a significant say but the WSL has consulted widely.

Sports.title: Fifa opens disciplinary proceedings against Argentina over Falklands banner and final chaos
Sports.content:
Fifa has opened disciplinary ­proceedings against Argentina over the Falkland Islands banner ­displayed after their World Cup semi‑final win against England in Atlanta.

As Argentina celebrated ­reaching the final with their dramatic 2-1 ­victory, several players held a sign ­proclaiming “Las Malvinas son ­Argentinas” – the ­Malvinas are Argentinian – in ­reference to the ­British overseas territory in the south Atlantic.

The dispute over the islands, which have been ruled by Britain since 1833, is long running and led to a 74-day conflict in 1982, during which more than 900 people – 649 Argentinians and 255 Britons – lost their lives.

Fifa’s disciplinary code ­prohibits “using a sports event for ­demonstrations of a non-sporting nature” and the banner prompted political debate on both sides of the ­Atlantic. A spokesperson for the then UK prime minister, Keir Starmer, said: “The World Cup might not be ours, but the Falkland Islands ­definitely are.” Andrew Giuliani, the head of the White House Fifa taskforce, defended Argentina’s players, saying the US believed in free speech.

The incident was not the first time an Argentina team had expressed such sentiments. In 2014, Fifa fined Argentina £20,000 for a far larger banner held ‌up by players before a friendly with Slovenia in La Plata.

Fifa’s full World Cup charge sheet against the Argentinian Football Association also includes ­“discriminatory chants and gestures, late kick-offs, failure to comply with match and security protocols, the display of inappropriate messages by the team and spectators and the throwing of objects by spectators in relation to several matches”.

0:18 Ugly scenes as Argentina lose World Cup final – video

Several players are also under investigation in relation to the ­chaotic scenes that followed ­Argentina’s 1-0 extra-time defeat by Spain in the final. As Spain attempted to celebrate, ­altercations broke out across the pitch at New York New Jersey Stadium.

The Argentina midfielder Leandro Paredes, who was seen wrestling Spain’s Eric García to the ground, faces three counts of assault under the Fifa disciplinary code, while the defender Nahuel Molina faces two counts of assault (one completed and one attempted) and one count of unsporting behaviour.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The assistant coach, Roberto Ayala, faces one count of assault, and Thiago Almada, an unused substitute in the final, one count of unsporting behaviour. Spain’s Gavi also faces an unsporting behaviour charge.

“In accordance with the Fifa ­disciplinary code, the respondents have now been provided with the opportunity to present their position, following which a decision will be issued by the Fifa disciplinary committee in due course,” said Fifa.

Sports.title: ‘I’m very sorry’: Mancini apologises after being reappointed as Italy head coach
Sports.content:
Roberto Mancini issued an apology in his first public comments after being reappointed as the Italy head coach, three years after he abandoned the same job for a lucrative contract with Saudi Arabia.

“I’m very sorry,” Mancini said. “It was like losing the woman of your life. And it means you did something that shouldn’t have been done. So I’m sorry, very sorry also for everything that happened over these last three years … I’m going to try to bring the national team back where it belongs.”

Italy failed for a third straight time to qualify for the World Cup, prompting the resignations of Gabriele Gravina as federation president and Gennaro Gattuso as head coach in April, shortly after the playoff defeat to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 61-year-old Mancini led the Azzurri to the European Championship title in 2021 but resigned as Italy coach in August 2023, taking over Saudi Arabia’s national team two weeks later. “It was completely my fault,” Mancini said, referring to a lack of communication with Gravina.

Mancini’s first match back in charge will be against Belgium in the Nations League on 25 September at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome. He was asked about what type of reception fans might give him. “I realise some people will be against me,” Mancini said. “I’m hoping the squad plays well enough that maybe people will forgive me.”

Mancini was fourth-choice option for the Italy job after Carlo Ancelotti and Pep Guardiola turned it down and Andrea Pirlo was dropped as a candidate amid political concerns over a sponsorship deal with a Russian betting firm.

Sports.title: Manchester City leading opposition to Premier League’s £1.5bn EFL proposal
Sports.content:
Manchester City are leading the opposition to the Premier League’s plans to offer £1.5bn to the English Football League in a landmark financial settlement which will be discussed at a meeting of the 20 clubs on Thursday.

The Premier League wants to put its proposed offer, which would be spread over 10 years, to a vote in the hope of getting the matter resolved before the start of the season, but City are understood to have come up with a counterproposal amid concerns about how the package will be funded.

A number of City’s misgivings are shared by other members of the so-called big six, who will be asked to pay more than other Premier League clubs towards the New Deal for Football, but it is unclear how many of them are prepared to back their rivals.

City remain short of allies within the top flight as they wait for the much-anticipated judgment of an independent tribunal after being charged with 115 breaches of financial fair play rules, despite settling a long-running legal dispute with the Premier League over its associated party transaction rules last year.

Quick Guide How do I 

The Guardian has learned that City irritated several clubs by submitting a series of late amendments to proposed rule changes before the Premier League’s annual general meeting in June, which were defeated by 19 votes to one.

City and other big clubs are understood to be unhappy with the Premier League’s proposal to fund the financial redistribution package by increasing the levy on transfer fees from 4% to 6%, which would leave the bigger spending clubs with a large bill. The Premier League will only ballot clubs on Thursday if it is confident of getting the 14 votes required for the proposal to pass, with sources describing executives as cautiously optimistic despite facing some opposition.

At an average of £150m a year, the Premier League’s proposed contribution has not altered significantly since a similar offer of £750m over five years was put forward in September 2023, although it has doubled the length of the deal.

If approved by the clubs and accepted by the EFL an initial payment of £100m would be made this season, with larger contributions to be made in subsequent years until the 2035-36 season.

It is unclear whether the EFL would accept the Premier League’s first offer however, with its chair, Rick Parry, believed to be holding out for a bigger deal.

If approved the EFL would allocate 80% of the New Deal to the Championship clubs, 12% to League One and 8% to League Two.

City and the Premier League declined to comment.

Sports.title: Defence promises to be a central issue for Carrick and Manchester United
Sports.content:
Manchester United’s central defender quintet of Leny Yoro, Ayden Heaven, Harry Maguire, Matthijs De Ligt and Lisandro Martínez: an ideal blend of youthful zest and experienced winners or a unit that may prove vulnerable and injury-prone across the long months of the campaign?

In Yoro, Heaven, Maguire, De Ligt, and Martínez, Michael Carrick can talk of high potential and seasoned operators who will patrol the manager’s backline safely. Except it would be understandable if the 44-year-old privately has any concerns about the five defenders, as a unit, especially as there is no plan to strengthen the position unless one (or more) departs.

Carrick is after all entering a debut full season as manager and will be leading United on four fronts for a first time: in the Premier League, FA Cup, Carabao Cup and, after two years, the Champions League.

When taking temporary charge last January, following the sacking of Ruben Amorim, Carrick had only 17 league matches to negotiate, as United were out of all other competitions. The job he executed impressed. Carrick wiped away the angst and chaos left behind by Amorim. He lifted United from seventh with 32 points, nine behind Aston Villa in third place, where the team finished by the end of the season.

The coming term, though, is the acid test that may expose a callowness at elite level that totals only 20 games piloting United, including the three of his previous temporary incumbency. So being difficult to beat is a fundamental requirement. In those 17 matches last year, United lost only twice - the 2-1 reverses to Newcastle and Leeds - and conceded 18 times.

Yet closer scrutiny of the five whose task is to secure the rearguard’s middle - the fullbacks Noussair Mazraoui, Diogo Dalot and Luke Shaw can operate there, too - throws up uncomfortable questions regarding a zone that requires surety and confidence, as a vital foundation for the side’s success.

Yoro, 20, and Heaven, 19, are young and yet to progress beyond the potential stage of their nascent careers. For each the answer to how soon they should mature into cast-iron performers has to be now.

Yoro, with 66 appearances since joining in July 2024 from Lille for £52m, is the more senior but has been lightweight, at times, and prone to the occasional error. After two seasons, needing time to bed in can no longer be mitigation, so the hope is Yoro’s 6ft 3in frame, serious turn of pace, and calm style will elevate his game.

Heaven, who signed in February 2025 from Arsenal for a nominal fee, made 11 league starts last season and is blessed with technique, recovery speed, and a more physical 6ft 2inch build. He says: “I’m young and I’ve got to be patient, especially in my position. You don’t see a lot of 19-year-olds playing week in, week out. I know it’s nothing personal. I’m waiting for my opportunity.”

Maguire is at the opposite end of the career spectrum. A player who at 33 possesses guile and a defend-first ethos yet is one-paced and may soon creak. Left at home by Thomas Tuchel for England’s World Cup campaign, the former United captain offers leadership.

Under Carrick, Maguire would expect to enter the season as first-choice, alongside Martínez. Except the 28-year-old, who is in his prime, remains plagued by injury, being forced off before halftime of Argentina’s 1-0 World Cup final loss to Spain with a muscle problem, so his fitness for the season-opener at Hull is in the balance.

After a starring role in United’s 2-1 defeat of Manchester City in the 2024 FA Cup final, Pep Guardiola called him “a top-five centre-back in the world”. But however good “The Butcher” is, Carrick cannot rely on him if availability is a struggle.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

De Ligt’s physical robustness may be an even greater concern for the manager. The 26-year-old has not featured since the 2-1 win at Crystal Palace on 30 November due to a back injury that was finally operated on in May.

Speaking after the procedure, he said: “Since November I have done everything, pushing myself in every session and exploring every option, to get back to doing what I love, playing football.” The aim is for De Ligt, who boasts league-winners medals from the Netherlands (with Ajax), Italy (Juventus) and Germany (Bayern Munich), to be back early in the season.

Yet the uncertainty regarding De Ligt, Maguire, Martínez, Yoro and Heaven is mirrored by the club’s so far unconvincing summer window, particularly compared with their rivals.

City, with Elliot Anderson for £116m and possibly also Ayyoub Bouaddi for £85m, Chelsea (Morgan Rogers, £117m), and Tottenham (Sandro Tonali, £100m with add-ons, Mateus Fernandes, £85m) have all splurged big, while Arsenal target Bruno Guimarães (circa £70-80m) and Vinícius Júnior (£140-50m). United’s major signings compass the triggering of a £35m release-clause for Aston Villa’s Youri Tielemans, a 29-year-old with 13 years in his legs and who they faced no competition for, plus the £48m plus £2m Andrey Santos, a 22-year-old with 11 league starts last season for Chelsea.

There are still five weeks of the market left so the picture may have changed significantly by 1 September. But at the moment, making a case for a fit-for-purpose defence - as with the squad - is difficult.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Gianni Infantino’s big World Cup sale and Fifa’s race to the bottom line
Sports.content:
FIFA UNITES THE WORLD

We begin Football Daily’s 29 July 2026 edition with a trip back to 26 February 2016. Gianni Infantino has been elected as the new Fifa president on a promise to clean up a disgraced organisation. “A good day for football,” says the FA director, David Gill. “A good day for the sport,” concurs the American Fifa executive committee member, Sunil Gulati. “Who’s that bald loser on the news?” says an unnamed Republican candidate.

Infantino’s message is simple. “Fifa has gone through sad times, moments of crisis. But those times are over. We enter now a new era. We’ll restore the image of Fifa and make sure you will be happy with what we do.” Infantino, whose pitch included a boast that he had vastly increased Uefa’s revenues, promised to address Fifa’s $550m (£414m) financial black hole. “It’s your money, not the money of the Fifa president,” he said. “The money of Fifa has to be used to develop football … I’m a candidate of the whole world and football. We have to build bridges, not walls.”

We’re tempted to leave it at that, as we’re quietly confident you get the message, but editorial norms dictate we should talk about the news that Fifa is seeking private investment in the World Cup and the rest of its competitions. Big Website has done an explainer and everything. The proposed investment is in excess of £7.5bn and, according to a Fifa statement, would be used to expand the net worth of Infantino and Joshua Kushn – we beg your pardon, we completely misread that. We forgot to meditate, pray and chill this morning, so our focus isn’t as good as it could be. The Fifa statement says the money will be used to “expand football development funding”. Fifa’s money does not belong to its president – Infantino said it himself in 2016.

Look, we all know football is about the bottom line. Money doesn’t just talk; it never shuts up. In that context, it’s some achievement for Infantino and friends to come up with an idea so egregious that almost everyone in football has responded with: “Bit much, mate.” Uefa, Concacaf and the FA are among those who have strongly criticised the proposals. Uefa’s 55 members are to hold an emergency meeting, with a potential World Cup boycott on the table. Just 10 days ago, Ferran Torres scored the winning goal in the Geopolitics World Cup final, a moment of pure euphoria that would be worth gazillions if only you could bottle it. But you can’t. At its best, football revives the child in all of us. Whatever the linguists tell you, there’s no infant in Infantino.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Football belongs to no individual and to no ‌institution. It belongs to the people. If Fifa were transferred into a profit-oriented ⁠corporate structure, it ​would lose ​its soul” – former Fifa president and man of the people Sepp Blatter weighs in on plans to sell off the World Cup.

“I note that, despite the fact that the GWC is over, Football Daily is still arriving in my inbox in the early afternoon. As someone used to it screeching in late like a Djed Spence sliding tackle, I find this disconcerting. Also, the realisation that it isn’t home time yet is almost as disappointing as the contents of the email” – Richard O’Hagan [normal service has resumed, for today at least – Football Daily Ed].

“I think Readng/Readino (yesterday’s full email edition) should turn their grammatical errors into a rebranding opportunity that adds a little continental pizazz. Athletic Readino, Real Readino, Dynamo Readng, Sporting Readino. It’d see people flocking to this bustling, cosmopolitan destination town. Possibly” – Martin Clifford.

“Cancel Football. Too much info” – Peter Craswell.
