Frequently Asked Questions

What is the S&P IPSA?

It is Chile’s main stock index, tracking the 30 most traded and valuable companies on the Santiago Exchange. Think of it as Chile’s equivalent of the S&P 500.

Why does copper matter so much for Chile?

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, and the metal accounts for a large share of exports, government revenue and corporate profits — so copper prices often dictate the mood in Santiago.

What does ‘USD/CLP 933.63 +0.29%’ mean?

It means one US dollar now buys 933.63 Chilean pesos, which is 0.29 per cent more pesos than the day before. A higher number means the peso has weakened.

Who are SQM and Falabella?

SQM is a Chilean mining company and one of the world’s biggest producers of lithium and fertilisers. Falabella is a retail giant that runs department stores, home-improvement shops and a bank across Latin America.

Today’s Focus It is a morning shaped far more by local data than by the overnight tape, which was a quiet drift lower. The Bank of Japan left policy untouched, Europe opened mixed, and US futures are barely changed — leaving Latin Americans free to focus on an unusually busy calendar inside the region. The biggest cluster sits in Santiago. Chile publishes retail sales, industrial production, manufacturing output, and the unemployment rate all at once. Consensus expects a slight improvement in retail but deep year-on-year contractions in mining-heavy industrial production — numbers that will test the IPSA’s recent composure after it managed a small gain in Wednesday’s session. Mexico gets its preliminary second-quarter GDP reading at midday — the first broad snapshot of whether Latin America’s second-largest economy is really running at the 1.3–1.5% annual pace that analysts expect after a near-flat first quarter. That number will steer the peso, which has been remarkably calm against the dollar. Then there is Brazil’s budget. The National Treasury releases the primary surplus, nominal balance and gross-debt-to-GDP ratio at 11:30 BRT. A miss on the nominal deficit — consensus sees minus 133.2 billion reais — would test a market already dealing with an Ibovespa that has dropped more than 12% from its 52-week high and an inflation rate that is running above the target band. What matters today. Chile’s retail and copper data, Mexico’s GDP, and Brazil’s fiscal print will dominate — three local stories that can override the cautious global mood in real time.

01 The overnight tape in one read

The Bank of Japan left its key overnight rate at 1%, exactly as expected, and signalled in its quarterly outlook that it intends to proceed with great caution — not a tightening, yet not a pivot either. That left the yen comfortably stable and did nothing to disturb the funding-currency dynamics that underpin large carry positions in high-yielding Latin American currencies such as the Mexican peso and the Brazilian real.

Europe’s early trade was unenthusiastic, with the DAX and CAC 40 edging fractionally lower as investors weighed some softer German employment numbers. The mood was not a rout, simply a holding pattern ahead of a cascade of US data due tomorrow — including the Employment Cost Index and the Chicago PMI — that will shape the final session of the month.

US futures are pointing to a flat or slightly red open after the S&P 500 gave back 1.52% on Wednesday, wiping out Tuesday’s bounce and closing at 7,316. The prior-session selling was broad: technology and energy led the way down, and Brent crude continued to retreat overnight as demand concerns resurfaced, which directly threatens the revenue picture for Latin America’s oil exporters such as Petrobras in Brazil and Ecopetrol in Colombia.

The dollar was little moved against most Latin American counterparts in electronic trade overnight. No local currency broke its recent range, though the Colombian peso softened marginally ahead of the business-confidence print this afternoon — a setup that leaves local traders waiting for their own catalysts rather than importing conviction from New York or Tokyo.

Assessment — Data-heavy, risk-light MEDIUM The evidence points to a cautious open across Latin America because the dominant external cue — a soft Wall Street close and steady oil slide — pulls the same way as domestic uncertainty. Brazil’s budget figures could easily disappoint given the election-year spending pressures that the central bank itself flagged in June. Chile’s production data will almost certainly show metal output still in contraction territory, though the retail sales print offers a possible upside surprise. Mexico’s GDP is the wildcard: a beat would give the peso a bid and lift the IPC from its 7% discount to its 52-week high, while a miss may reinforce the view that the economy is losing momentum. The variable to watch is the nominal budget balance in Brasília — a number worse than minus 133 billion reais could turn caution into a proper risk-off local session.

02 The board before the open

The board after Wednesday’s close sets a cautious scene. The S&P 500’s 1.52% drop to 7,316 was mirrored almost exactly by the Ibovespa, which settled at 173,885 — a mechanical correlation that leaves B3 with little independent momentum unless local news forces a break. The IPC in Mexico fell a chunky 1.23% to 66,476, deepening its discount to the 52-week high above 71,600 and suggesting that foreign participants are trimming exposure into the GDP print.

Chile’s IPSA was the sole green spot, adding 0.52% to finish at 10,936, though turnover was modest and the move owed more to a handful of defensive names than to any macro conviction. Brent crude continued to leak lower, which will weigh on the heavily energy-weighted Colombian and Brazilian boards when trading resumes — particularly on names such as Ecopetrol and Petrobras that topped the volume list on B3 yesterday precisely because traders were repositioning.

03 What the data shows — Petrobras dominates a defensive session

The B3 volume league was led by Petrobras — the state-controlled oil producer — whose preferred shares (PETR4) rose 1.9% on R$1.319 billion in turnover, the heaviest on the exchange. That is noteworthy because Brent was not rallying; rather, the trade looked like a flight to a liquid, dollar-revenue name inside a weak index, the kind of positioning that often precedes a cautious open.

The pain was concentrated on the losers’ side. Steelmaker CSN (CSNA3) collapsed 7.8% on only R$105 million in volume, suggesting a fragile book. Santander Brasil (SANB11) shed 7.4% in heavier R$378 million trade, and water utility Sabesp (SBSP3) plunged 5.9% on R$805 million — the third-highest turnover on the day — pointing to genuine institutional selling rather than a noise move. These are not names that reverse on a dime, so the damage will carry into the open.

04 Brazil and the currencies

The Brazilian real barely budged on Wednesday, with the USD/BRL pair edging 0.07% lower to 5.1174 in thin, wait-and-see trade. That steadiness is striking given the Ibovespa’s 1.5% slide, and it suggests the FX market is reserving judgment for today’s fiscal numbers — the primary budget surplus, the nominal balance, and crucially the gross-debt-to-GDP ratio, which is expected to edge up to 81.5% from 81.1%.

A debt print above consensus would sharpen the narrative that election-year spending is fraying the fiscal anchor, exactly the risk flagged by the central bank’s Copom minutes in June when it delivered the third 25-basis-point cut to 14.25%. The Selic is still deeply in restrictive territory — inflation is running at 4.7% against a 3% target — but the easing cycle is clearly on a short leash, and any fiscal stumble today could reinforce market bets that the cutting window slams shut as early as August.

The Mexican peso was the epitome of calm overnight, with USD/MXN virtually unchanged at 17.44. It is trading well inside its 52-week range and awaits the GDP release at midday, where a strong quarterly print — above the 1.5% annualised consensus — could give the currency a fresh leg lower toward the 17.20 area. The IPC, down 1.23% on Wednesday, would catch a strong bid in that scenario.

Further south, the Chilean peso weakened marginally overnight, in line with the broader move in the Colombian peso, as copper prices slipped and traders squared positions before Santiago’s data barrage. The USD/ARS — the official rate — actually firmed a touch, with the peso gaining 0.28% to 1,496, though the implicit demand from the parallel market tells a different story about underlying confidence.

05 The regional setup

Index Country Change Ibovespa Brazil −1.52% IPC Mexico −1.23% Merval Argentina −0.71% COLCAP Colombia +0.15% IPSA Chile +0.52%

The regional board after Wednesday tells a story of selective resilience. The Ibovespa and the IPC fell in lockstep with the S&P 500 — down 1.52% and 1.23% respectively — confirming that broad foreign sentiment remains the dominant driver for the two heaviest exchanges. The Merval in Buenos Aires dipped a more modest 0.71%, cushioned by the peculiar Argentine dynamic where local investors treat equities as a haven from a persistently weak peso, not as a play on global growth.

Colombia’s COLCAP managed a barely-there gain of 0.15% to 2,305, with few expectations of drama before today’s cement production and jobless figures. The standout, again, was Chile’s IPSA, which added 0.52% against the regional grain. That gains significance because it happened on the eve of the economic data dump that will set the tone for Santiago’s session — the market has not yet priced in any major disappointment, making it vulnerable to a negative surprise in retail or manufacturing.

06 The technical picture

The Ibovespa’s close at 173,885 leaves it sitting 12.5% below its 52-week high of 198,657, a deep correction that is testing patience. The index has not managed a single session higher in this short run — one straight day down — and is now closer to its 52-week low of 132,129 than anyone in São Paulo would like. A break below 173,500 today on poor fiscal news would open the door to 170,000 with little visible support.

Mexico’s IPC at 66,476 is in a similar bind, 7.2% below its 52-week peak of 71,601 and grinding along a descending trendline. The GDP print at midday is the obvious catalyst: a beat could trigger the short-squeeze that carries the index back toward 68,000, while a miss may accelerate the drift toward the year’s lows near 60,774.

The S&P 500’s configuration matters enormously here because the correlation between US and Latin American equities is running high. Wednesday’s drop to 7,316 took the index to 3.9% below its 52-week high of 7,610, and the absence of a futures bounce overnight implies that Latin American boards will have to find their own footing — or simply follow the path of least resistance lower.

07 What to watch

Brazil’s nominal budget balance at 11:30 BRT: A figure worse than the R$133.2 billion consensus deficit would test the real and drag rate-sensitive B3 names such as utilities and banks lower.

A figure worse than the R$133.2 billion consensus deficit would test the real and drag rate-sensitive B3 names such as utilities and banks lower. Chile’s quadruple data release at 13:00 UTC: Retail sales, industrial output, manufacturing and the jobless rate hit simultaneously — a clean test of whether the IPSA’s recent outperformance is built on real demand or just local positioning.

Retail sales, industrial output, manufacturing and the jobless rate hit simultaneously — a clean test of whether the IPSA’s recent outperformance is built on real demand or just local positioning. Mexico’s preliminary Q2 GDP at midday: A print above the 1.5% annualised consensus would give the peso a bid and could reverse the IPC’s recent drift; anything softer would reinforce the view that Mexico’s economy is stalling.

A print above the 1.5% annualised consensus would give the peso a bid and could reverse the IPC’s recent drift; anything softer would reinforce the view that Mexico’s economy is stalling. The Bank of Japan’s outlook report fallout: The BoJ’s cautious tone keeps the yen from strengthening abruptly, preserving the low-volatility funding environment that Latin America’s high carry currencies — the real and the peso — rely on.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the Ibovespa fall so sharply on Wednesday?

It moved almost tick-for-tick with the S&P 500, which dropped 1.52% on broad selling. The Ibovespa closed at 173,885 with heavy losses concentrated in rate-sensitive names such as Santander Brasil and Sabesp.

What is the Selic and why does it matter?

The Selic is Brazil’s benchmark overnight interest rate — think of it as the country’s base cost of money. At 14.25% after three recent cuts, it is still deeply restrictive and heavily influences borrowing costs for companies and consumers across B3.

Is the Mexican peso a carry trade?

Yes. With the Bank of Japan holding at 1%, investors can borrow cheaply in yen and invest in higher-yielding pesos. A stable or gently falling USD/MXN rate signals that carry traders remain comfortable, which underpins demand for Mexican assets.

What is the COLCAP and why did it barely move?

The COLCAP is Colombia’s main stock benchmark. It added just 0.15% to 2,305 because Colombia’s central bank held rates steady at 12% and the market was waiting for today’s local data — cement output and unemployment — rather than chasing global sentiment.

Why does Chile’s data matter so much today?

Santiago publishes four key economic indicators at once: retail sales, industrial production, manufacturing output, and the unemployment rate. Taken together, they give the clearest snapshot of whether the Chilean consumer and its mining sector are recovering — which sets the direction for the IPSA index and the peso.

Dollar-pegged stablecoins continue to eclipse volatile assets in everyday commerce, with Argentine shops and remittance senders using them to dodge currency controls. El Salvador, holding part of its reserves in Bitcoin, watches the US$62,000–64,000 band as a fiscal benchmark. Brazil’s work on a digital real and the region’s cautious central banks—mindful of the Fed’s higher-for-longer stance—are pushing companies and households further into stablecoins. Cross-border pilots using XRP and Bitcoin rails are shaving remittance fees and cutting settlement from days to minutes, a structural shift that foreign investors track as a proxy for how quickly traditional finance may adopt blockchain settlement. 01 The session in one read

Bitcoin settled at US$63,908, a fractional gain of 0.06%, in a session where institutional traders cut position sizes and waited for clearer signals from the US Federal Reserve. The proxy price held within a narrow intraday band, signalling a market that is neither panicking nor chasing a rally.

Ethereum fell 0.60% to US$1,909, giving back a slice of recent gains as developers and investors looked ahead to the next upgrade phase for the smart-contract network. Solana eased 0.14% to US$73.60, while XRP edged up 0.46% to US$1.0729, rounding out a mixed day for the major crypto proxies.

Assessment — Steady Bitcoin props up real-world use HIGH The US$63,908 Bitcoin print tells a story of consolidation, not capitulation. With the Federal Reserve keeping rates elevated, speculative flows into crypto have thinned, but the price has not broken lower, which signals that a base of structural demand—much of it from Latin American users hedging local currencies—is providing a cushion. Ethereum’s dip to US$1,909 and Solana’s drift to US$73.60 reflect a rotation, not a rout, as traders wait for the next catalyst. XRP’s rise to US$1.0729 suggests that payment-focused tokens are being priced independently of the broader market mood. The variable to watch is whether Bitcoin can hold above US$62,000 if US real yields push higher still, because a break below that threshold would test the thesis that Latin American adoption is a genuine price floor.

Across the board, moves were small, underscoring a market where professional desks are running lighter books. 03 What moved it

A hawkish Federal Reserve kept real yields elevated, reducing the appeal of assets that offer no income stream, which compressed Bitcoin’s range and pushed the proxy to a near-flat US$63,908. Institutional desks trimmed risk, waiting to see whether the central bank signals a pause or another hike.

Ethereum’s 0.60% slide to US$1,909 reflected profit-taking after a run of gains, with traders rotating capital into faster chains rather than adding fresh exposure to the network that anchors most stablecoin and DeFi applications. XRP’s 0.46% rise to US$1.0729 came as payments-focused tokens caught a bid, driven by reassessments of their role in cross-border settlement.

04 The Latin American read

Brazil’s central bank has advanced its digital real project, a state-backed currency designed to coexist with private crypto rails, which foreign investors are tracking because it will shape how fintechs such as Nubank integrate Bitcoin and Ethereum into local payments. Argentina’s persistent inflation and a weak peso have deepened everyday use of dollar-linked stablecoins such as Tether and USD Coin, with local exchanges reporting heavy retail inflows whenever the parallel dollar rate widens against the official rate.

El Salvador continues to promote Bitcoin-based payment apps alongside the US dollar, and a Bitcoin proxy anchored at US$63,908 helps frame the country’s fiscal exposure given its government-held reserves. In remittance corridors stretching from the United States into Guatemala and Mexico, senders increasingly buy Bitcoin or stablecoins, transmit them over a blockchain and let recipients cash out locally, cutting fees and shrinking settlement times from days to minutes.

05 The names to watch

Brazilian neobanks such as Nubank and brokerages like XP now offer crypto access to millions of retail clients, typically via Bitcoin and Ethereum trackers, turning crypto into a mainstream alternative asset for middle-class savers. In Argentina, merchants are adopting QR-based payment systems that let customers pay in stablecoins while shops convert to pesos or keep proceeds in digital dollars, creating a de facto dollarisation of day-to-day commerce.

XRP’s design for fast, low-cost transfers has made it a testbed for remittance pilots in the region, even as its regulatory status remains under discussion, which investors track because it affects the viability of enterprise payment projects. Stablecoins also play a growing role in corporate treasury management for tech and export firms in Brazil and Argentina, where companies park working capital in these instruments to reduce exposure to domestic currency swings.

06 The outlook

Bitcoin’s ability to hold near US$63,908 without breaking lower, despite elevated US real yields, suggests that structural demand from Latin American users is providing a cushion. The next catalyst for the region will be any shift in Federal Reserve language, which could either release pent-up speculative flows or drive another rotation into dollar-backed stablecoins as a hedge.

A hawkish Federal Reserve kept real yields elevated, reducing the appeal of non-yielding assets and prompting institutional desks to run smaller positions.

Many stablecoin protocols and dollar-savings apps run on Ethereum, so price softness can cool new retail inflows without disrupting existing usage.

Merchants accept dollar-linked tokens via QR payments, letting customers pay in digital dollars while shops bypass the weak peso and traditional banking rails.

XRP is designed for fast, low-cost cross-border transfers and is being tested in payment pilots that could shave fees and cut settlement times for Latin American corridors.

03 What moved it

The primary driver was a softer US dollar and lower real yields, dynamics that cut the opportunity cost of holding non-interest-bearing metal. Global gold near US$4,063.72 per troy ounce had earlier reflected a 2.0% intraday gain directly tied to this easing in financial conditions.

A brief dip to about US$4,132.28 per troy ounce on July 7, down 0.78%, had shown how sticky US rate expectations can temporarily interrupt a rally, yet safe-haven flows quickly resumed. Standard spot market explanations describe the silver price as the rate for immediate delivery, and recent intraday swings exceeding 1% have been associated with shifts in US inflation data and Federal Reserve guidance on future rate cuts.

Silver’s blistering run—leaving it up nearly 65% year-on-year—is often attributed to investors using the metal as a higher-beta play on gold and as a hedge against currency weakening in emerging markets. When geopolitical risk or recession worries climb, investors rotate from equities and high-yield credit into physically backed instruments priced off the spot market to store value outside the banking system.

04 The Latin American read

Mexico, the world’s top silver producer, sells into a global market where the silver spot price per ounce is the reference for immediate delivery contracts that price and hedge export flows. A 1.69% daily gain in a silver-tracking fund therefore feeds directly through to the revenue assumptions of Mexican mining operators.

Peru ranks among the largest silver- and gold-producing countries, with its mining firms benchmarking long-term supply contracts against these same international spot prices. Daily gains in both metals directly influence the revenue outlook for local exporters and royalty receipts for the Peruvian government.

Latin American miners in both nations frequently employ hedging strategies built on the global spot markets, meaning that a 1–2% daily move in these benchmarks can materially alter the value of hedged output and the mark-to-market on derivatives sitting on their balance sheets.

05 The names to watch

Investors tracking the LatAm mining story should monitor the largest Mexican silver producers, whose export revenues are priced against the very spot benchmarks that advanced today. Peruvian diversified miners with significant gold and silver by-product streams likewise see their forward sales agreements revalued with each daily settlement.

The broader trend of investors favouring exchange-traded funds that track bullion rather than mining shares was reinforced by the session, as physically backed instruments saw inflows during periods of US dollar weakness. Foreign investors can buy more ounces per unit of local currency when the dollar eases, amplifying the appeal of the metal as a safe store of value during policy transitions.

06 The outlook

The path for gold and silver continues to run through the Federal Reserve and the dollar. The short-lived pullback on July 7, when gold fell to about US$4,132.28 per troy ounce on expectations of stickier US rates, showed how sensitive the complex remains to any hint that rate cuts will be delayed. For Latin America’s producers, the key is whether silver can consolidate above the US$58 level through the next US inflation print—a failure to hold would unwind the leveraged premium that has made current spot prices so profitable for Mexican and Peruvian export books.

07 What to watch

US dollar index and real yields: A further softening of the dollar or drop in inflation-adjusted yields would cut the opportunity cost of holding gold and silver further, directly raising the contract value of Latin American output.

Why did gold and silver rise today?

A softer US dollar and lower real yields reduced the cost of holding non-interest-bearing metals, while safe-haven demand from geopolitical and recession concerns pushed investors into physically backed bullion instruments.

How does this affect Mexico?

Mexico is the world’s top silver producer and its miners sell into a global market where the international spot price is the reference for pricing and hedging export contracts, so today’s 1.69% gain in a silver-tracking fund directly lifts local revenue expectations.

What is Peru’s exposure to these moves?

Peru ranks among the largest gold and silver producers, with mining firms benchmarking long-term supply agreements against international spot prices, meaning daily gains feed into exporter revenues and government royalty receipts.

Why is silver moving more than gold?

Silver is often treated as a higher-beta play on gold, magnifying the precious-metals rally; it was recently up nearly 65% year-on-year, attracting investors who use it as a leveraged bet on gold and a hedge against emerging-market currency weakness.

01 Rude awakening after record highs

A hard overnight sell-off shattered the calm on Wall Street, with the S&P 500 plunging 1.52% to 7,316.15 and the VIX rocketing 13.45% to 20.66, yanking traders from record territory into full-scale risk management. The Dow fared even worse, down 2.19% to 51,594.14, a clear rotation out of cyclical value names that are most exposed to the IMF’s fresh global growth downgrade to 3.0%.

The robust US picture—GDP revised up to 2.1%—was utterly overshadowed by the global macro mosaic showing headline inflation reversing course to 4.7% and stalling the disinflation that markets had priced, which in turn capped a more meaningful bond rally. With the yield curve still signalling caution despite the equities rout, investors weren’t just taking profits on expensive Big Tech (Nasdaq fell 1.74% to 24,442.94) but were actively repricing the probability that rates remain higher for longer across developed and emerging markets.

For Brazil, this is the worst of both worlds: a VIX spike that shuts down crowded carry trades and fresh global growth fears that hit demand for the commodity exports which backstop the real. Today’s IGP-M inflation print at a deeply negative -1.09% and unemployment expected to edge down to 5.4% will be read entirely through the external lens, as traders calculate whether the BCB can risk faster Selic cuts to revive the domestic economy while the dollar hesitates but the world suddenly looks jittery.

02 Caught between local cool-down and global heat

The Federal Reserve finds itself trapped between a dome of benign local data and a wall of global inflationary fire. The overnight move in the dollar, which slumped 0.53% on the DXY to 100.88, might normally signal markets betting on a dovish pivot, but the simultaneous yield decline on the 10-year to 4.683% was far too timid to endorse that view—it smacked much more of a panicked flight-to-safety than a fundamental re-pricing of Fed hawkishness.

The upcoming US employment cost index and Chicago PMI data on Thursday now loom extra large, given that June payrolls of 57,000 and a 4.2% unemployment rate suggest the labour market is cooling but has hardly collapsed. A hot wage print would validate the IMF’s thesis of sticky global inflation near 4.7% and push rate-cut expectations further into the future, locking the Fed Funds rate in restrictive territory just as the AI-fueled capex cycle needs lower capital costs to keep its momentum.

For Copom and regional central banks, a Fed forced to stay hawkish while the world slows is a direct threat to the real’s stability. The 0.53% dollar weakness is unlikely to hold if panic intensifies, and any sign that the US is importing inflation again will quickly reverse those flows, punishing the Brazilian curve and potentially diluting the impact of positive domestic surprises like the government’s primary budget reading due today.

03 A slower, more fractured world takes centre stage

The market’s tantrum is a belated recognition that the global economy is entering a phase of slower, deeply uneven expansion, where the 3.0% headline for 2026 masks a chasm between a 2.1% US and a 0.9% Eurozone. This world tilts toward blocs that can generate their own energy and AI-led capital spending, an advantage for the US, while punishing regions dependent on stable trade and cheap energy—a scenario that makes Europe’s recession risk and China’s fragile 50.0 PMI forecast much more consequential for sentiment.

For Latin America, the fragmentation is a double-edged sword: the energy transition and AI supply chains mentioned by the IMF as bright spots offer a long-term tailwind for lithium, copper and Brazilian agribusiness, but the immediate shock of weaker global trade—projected at just 2.9%—hits commodity prices and volumes with a lag. That is precisely why the overnight session cared as much about Mexico’s GDP estimate (a sharp quarterly rebound to 1.3%) as it did about Chile’s copper production figures, processing each data point as a proxy for how individual LatAm economies are navigating a sputtering global trade engine.

The shift from a synchronised post-pandemic boom to a selective, high-cost expansion also means that foreign portfolio flows will become more discriminatory, punishing high-beta markets that lack fiscal discipline. Brazil’s upcoming net debt-to-GDP and nominal budget balance figures, set for release today, now carry extra freight: a messy fiscal showing into the teeth of a risk-off shock would strip away the buffer that the deeply negative wholesale inflation might otherwise give Brasília, exposing the real to a much sharper repricing than overnight’s modest 0.53% dollar dip implies.

What to watch today and this week

Friday (Jul 31): US PCE inflation and personal spending, key global PMIs including China NBS Manufacturing (est 50.0), Bank of Japan rate decision and quarterly outlook, plus LatAm central bank decisions and data from Chile and Colombia.

Next week: A heavy run of global CPI updates from the US, Eurozone and select EMs, scrutinised to see if the IMF’s 4.7% global inflation warning is materialising, plus sustained Fed speaker analysis.

A heavy run of global CPI updates from the US, Eurozone and select EMs, scrutinised to see if the IMF’s 4.7% global inflation warning is materialising, plus sustained Fed speaker analysis. Ongoing: The VIX spike to 20.66 signals a structural re-risking; the contagion into EM FX and rates, particularly the carry-driven real and Mexican peso, is the immediate macro focus alongside fallout from the Middle East energy shock.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did stocks drop so sharply overnight?

The IMF’s July 2026 update formalised fears of stalled global disinflation and slower 3.0% growth, triggering a harsh repricing of expensive equities and sending the VIX soaring 13.45%.

What does the IMF’s 3.0% global growth forecast mean for Brazil?

It signals thinner global trade (2.9% growth) and less commodity demand, making Brazil’s budget and debt-to-GDP data today crucial for maintaining investor confidence in the real.

Is the US economy still the global engine?

Yes, Q1 GDP was revised up to 2.1% annualised, but this strength allows the Fed to stay restrictive, which paradoxically tightens financial conditions for the rest of the world.

How can US inflation fall while global inflation re-accelerates?

Falling US gasoline prices have created a temporary domestic cushion, but global war-related energy shocks and sticky services price rises are driving the IMF’s projection for a sharp rise to 4.7% global inflation.

Will the real weaken further?

It depends on the global mood. If today’s Brazilian fiscal numbers disappoint into a VIX 20+ environment and a cautious Fed, the real faces a steeper devaluation, but a soft dollar and strong IGP-M deflation could partially offset it.

Any twitch in Chinese industrial data arrives first in the futures-tracking fund, while mining equity holders price in costs, taxes and local risk premia that the metal itself does not carry. The energy transition provides the long-term floor under copper expectations. Power grids, electric vehicles and renewable-generation kit all require dense copper wiring, keeping demand forecasts elevated even when short-term manufacturing numbers wobble. Chile and Peru, the top two producing nations, sit at the centre of that narrative, making Latin America the indispensable geography for global copper supply. What matters today. Southern Copper’s 1.95% fall to US$175.47 and Freeport-McMoRan’s 2.68% slide to US$59.99 look like leverage to a broader equity rethink after the sector had priced in much of the higher-metals story. 03 What moved it

Southern Copper’s second-quarter results arrived with headline numbers that would normally support the share price: US$4,289.0 million in net sales and net income of US$1,670.0 million, or US$2.01 per share. Management directly attributed the strong showing to higher metals prices and improved margins, effectively confirming that the copper price environment is working in the miner’s favour.

The sell-off therefore reads as classic profit-taking. Investors had already bid up the shares on expectations that earnings would be solid, and the actual numbers, however impressive, triggered a ‘sell the news’ reaction that also pulled Freeport-McMoRan lower.

04 The Latin American read

As the world’s top copper producer, Chile anchors the supply side of every price conversation, while Peru sits at number two. Southern Copper operates flagship assets in both countries, making its share price a temperature check on Latin American mining sentiment.

When Southern Copper’s stock dips 1.95% to US$175.47 despite reporting US$1,670.0 million in quarterly net income, it is a signal that global investors are not just trading the metal but also weighing local policy stability, tax regimes and permitting pipelines across the Andes.

05 The names to watch

CPER remains the simplest vessel for anyone wanting exposure to copper futures without picking a single miner. Its US$38.35 close and the quiet 0.05% uptick suggest that macro funds are still allocated to the energy-transition theme.

Southern Copper, at US$175.47, and Freeport-McMoRan, at US$59.99, are the operational heavyweights that convert geology into earnings. Both have lagged the futures tracker this session, reminding outsiders that owning the miner means owning a business with costs, community relations and country risk, not just a leverage play on the red metal.

06 The outlook

Copper’s medium-term case rests on two sturdy pillars that Thursday’s price action did not disturb. China, the dominant industrial buyer, continues to shape the futures curve tracked by CPER, while the global build-out of renewable grids and electric vehicles underwrites demand far beyond any single business cycle.

Southern Copper’s US$1,670.0 million quarterly profit proves that miners are already converting those drivers into cash, so the immediate question is whether equity valuations have run ahead of even this favourable backdrop. The next catalyst will likely be a Chinese industrial data point that either validates the futures market’s calm or forces a rapid repricing across the entire copper board.

Why did copper miner stocks fall when the copper fund rose?

The copper-tracking CPER fund reflects futures prices and inched up 0.05% to US$38.35, but Southern Copper and Freeport-McMoRan shares fell because equity investors took profits after strong Q2 earnings from Southern Copper, which reported US$1,670.0 million in net income.

What is CPER and what does it track?

CPER is an exchange-traded fund that tracks copper futures, meaning it moves with traders’ expectations for copper prices rather than the spot physical price of the metal itself.

How did Southern Copper perform in its latest quarter?

Southern Copper reported Q2 2026 net sales of US$4,289.0 million, net income of US$1,670.0 million, and earnings per share of US$2.01, driven by higher metals prices and improved margins.

Why does China matter so much for copper?

China is the world’s largest consumer of refined copper, so changes in its industrial demand quickly feed into copper futures prices and the assets linked to them, including CPER and major miner shares.

The local market found its anchor in crude oil, which steadied after recent declines, offering a lifeline to an index where energy names carry significant weight. Even with the dip, the peso sits far below its 52-week high of 3,864 — meaning it has strengthened nearly 17% from its weakest point, a notable show of force for a currency often at the mercy of global risk appetite. Volumes on the BVC — the Colombian stock exchange — were remarkably light, with meaningful trading in only a single domestic name. That caution is no mystery: the Banco de la República, Colombia’s central bank, meets on Thursday to decide on interest rates, with markets leaning toward a cut from the current 12% level. A rate reduction could lower borrowing costs and support local equities, but it would also narrow the yield advantage that has helped power the peso’s rally. What matters today. The COLCAP’s marginal rise on near-zero liquidity underscores a market holding its breath ahead of a central bank rate decision that could cut borrowing costs from 12%.

01 The session in one read

Wednesday’s trading in Bogotá was less a sprint and more a collective holding of breath. Colombia’s benchmark COLCAP index inched up 0.15% to close at 2,304.68, a whisper of a gain in a session where many global markets were awash in red ink. The S&P 500 finished 1.52% lower, a drop that would normally ripple hard through emerging markets, but Colombian equities found a fragile calm in steadying oil prices.

The Colombian peso slipped 0.21% to 3,211 per US dollar, a modest wobble that did little to reshape the currency’s bullish longer-term picture. At that level, it remains nearly 17% stronger than its 52-week low of 3,864, a rally built on sturdy exports and a high interest rate that attracts foreign capital in search of yield. Yet turnover on the local bourse was negligible: the only domestic stock showing meaningful volume was one ticker with barely any turnover to speak of.

Behind the quiet lies a big event. On Thursday, the Banco de la República board gathers to decide on its benchmark interest rate, currently at 12%. With inflation easing — consumer prices have been drifting lower — and economic growth in need of a spark, many analysts expect a cut. That has kept both equity buyers and currency traders in a wait-and-see posture, tempering any impulse to make bold bets.

The outside world offered little direction. Crude oil, the macro anchor for Colombia’s trade balance and a bellwether for state-controlled oil giant Ecopetrol, steadied near recent levels, lending support but not conviction. In that vacuum, the COLCAP floated gently upward, a market in suspended animation awaiting its next catalyst.

Assessment — Calm surface, depth of uncertainty beneath MEDIUM The session’s tiny 0.15% gain masks a market running on fumes. With almost no domestic stock volume beyond a single name, the COLCAP’s move reflects positioning inertia rather than conviction. The peso’s mild 0.21% dip against a stable oil backdrop suggests traders are reluctant to push it much weaker while the currency’s long-term trend remains upward. The variable to watch is Thursday’s rate decision: a cut would likely lift local equity valuations but could test the peso’s remarkable 17% recovery from its 52-week high, setting up a delicate balancing act for the central bank.

The index’s modest 0.15% rise came from a small number of stocks rather than a broad-based advance. The USD/COP pair, at 3,211, is hugging the lower end of its 52-week range between 3,190 and 3,864 — a range that underscores how far the currency has strengthened without yet breaching the psychologically significant 3,200 floor.

That it did not says something about local conditions: investors are anchored to the rate decision on Thursday rather than to global gyrations, at least for now.

03 Why it moved — oil stabilises and the rate decision looms

Oil is Colombia’s macro heartbeat. The country is a significant crude exporter, and the government’s fiscal health — as well as the share price of Ecopetrol, the most heavily weighted stock in the COLCAP — rises and falls with the barrel. On Wednesday, international crude benchmarks steadied after a run of declines, giving the local market just enough of a reason to tilt marginally positive even as global equities sold off.

The peso’s 0.21% dip to 3,211 tells a more nuanced story. The currency has enjoyed a powerful run, up almost 17% from its weakest 52-week print, thanks to tight monetary policy and a relatively resilient flow of export dollars. A mild pullback in a quiet session, particularly with the US dollar steady against most majors, is not a cause for alarm. It looks more like a small position adjustment ahead of a news-heavy stretch.

That stretch starts in earnest on Thursday, when the Banco de la República reveals its interest rate decision. The benchmark rate has been parked at 12% — a level designed to choke off the inflation that ran into double digits in 2023 and 2024. Now, with price pressures cooling, policymakers are under pressure to ease. A cut, for instance to 11.75% or 11.5%, would lower the return on Colombian fixed-income assets, potentially making the peso slightly less attractive while simultaneously boosting equities by reducing corporate borrowing costs.

The single-name trading volumes hint at the broader mood: no one wants to be the first to commit. The entire session had the feel of a dress rehearsal, with the real performance scheduled for the moment the central bank statement hits screens on Thursday.

04 The day’s movers

Should the central bank cut rates on Thursday, the COLCAP may find a fresh catalyst to test higher levels, while the peso could see the 3,190 level probed from above. Alternatively, if the bank holds at 12%, the peso’s yield advantage remains intact, potentially keeping USD/COP near current levels or even pushing it slightly lower. What is the COLCAP?

A stabilisation in crude oil prices — Colombia’s key export — helped insulate local equities from the US sell-off, while ultra-thin trading amplified small moves.

03 What moved it

Chile’s regulatory backdrop remains the most powerful driver for the two big producers. The government continues to pursue a national lithium strategy that favours public-private joint ventures over full nationalisation, yet periodic announcements on royalty rates and production quotas inject volatility into SQM and Albemarle models.

Argentina’s policy environment adds a second layer. Provinces such as Jujuy and Catamarca are advancing projects with Asian and European partners, but repeated adjustments to export taxes and capital controls make single-name Argentine-exposed developers riskier. That pushes incremental lithium allocations toward the LIT ETF and toward Chile-focused names already trading in New York.

Bolivia’s Salar de Uyuni stays in the narrative background. With commercial extraction still far behind Chile and Argentina, news from La Paz moves sentiment rather than earnings forecasts, nudging short-term flows into the LIT ETF basket when headlines promise progress.

04 The Latin American read

For Latin America, lithium is becoming a fiscal and foreign-exchange anchor. Chile’s Atacama brine exports generate dollar inflows that support the peso and state revenues, making regulatory decisions on lithium a macroeconomic as well as a sectoral event.

Argentina’s provinces see lithium as a development lever, yet the gap between project announcements and output means equities reprice sharply with each change in capital or trade rules. Foreign investors tend to manage this by owning Albemarle or the LIT ETF instead of smaller home-market developers.

Bolivia’s vast resource remains a long-term option for the region. Until La Paz finalises technology partnerships and a stable investment framework, the main listed impact will be episodic lifts in the LIT ETF driven by Uyuni headlines rather than earnings upgrades.

05 The names to watch

Albemarle at US$113.88 is the bellwether for institutional lithium exposure. Long-term supply agreements with cell makers and auto original-equipment manufacturers tie its earnings outlook to global EV sales projections, which analysts still describe as growing across China, Europe and the United States.

SQM at US$67.55 is the higher-beta bet on the same theme. Its fortunes hinge on the Salar de Atacama, where state-set quotas and royalty discussions can compress margins or expand them at short notice, making the stock a vehicle for investors with strong views on Chile’s policy direction.

06 The outlook

Battery-chemistry trends continue to anchor medium-term demand because most mainstream electric vehicles rely on lithium-ion technology, even as research into sodium-ion and solid-state alternatives advances. Producers with low-cost brine operations in the Lithium Triangle are better positioned to hold margins if new supply or technology shifts eventually pressure prices. For now, the daily equity moves suggest a market that is selectively bullish on Chilean brine while keeping one hand on the diversified ETF safety valve.

07 What to watch

Chile quota and royalty updates: Any change to Atacama brine production quotas or royalty tiers will reprice SQM and Albemarle swiftly, because they directly alter the cash-flow models for the world’s lowest-cost lithium region.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did the LIT ETF fall while lithium producers rose?

The LIT ETF holds a blend of miners, refiners and battery-tech companies across many geographies, so its small 0.33% dip reflects broad profit-taking, while SQM and Albemarle rose on specific appetite for Chilean brine assets.

What is the Lithium Triangle?

The Lithium Triangle spans high-altitude salt flats in Chile, Argentina and Bolivia that contain some of the world’s largest lithium brine deposits, forming the backbone of global low-cost lithium supply for electric-vehicle batteries.

Why does Chile policy matter so much for lithium equities?

Chile’s Atacama Desert hosts the world’s most productive brine operations, and government decisions on royalties, quotas and joint ventures directly influence production costs and revenues for SQM and Albemarle, the two top listed producers with assets there.

How do foreign investors access the Lithium Triangle story?

New York-listed SQM and Albemarle shares, plus the Global X Lithium & Battery Tech ETF, let foreign investors gain exposure without directly trading local stocks in Santiago or Buenos Aires.

World.title: Costa Rica Wins Its First Surfing Gold Medal in Regional Games History
World.content:
Costa Rican surfer Rachel Agüero Cabezas won the women’s shortboard title at the Central American and Caribbean Games in the Dominican Republic tpday, delivering Costa Rica its first gold medal in surfing in the history of the regional competition.

The 20-year-old beat Barbados’ Chelsea Tuach 10.50 points to 7.33 in the final at Playa Encuentro in Cabarete, on the northern coast of Puerto Plata province. Agüero’s score came from two waves graded 5.83 and 4.67, while Tuach posted a 5.00 and a 2.33. According to the National Olympic Committee, Agüero took control of the heat from the opening minutes and never surrendered the lead. Tuach needed a wave scored at 5.51 or better to overturn the result and never found one.

Agüero reached the final by eliminating the surfer most observers had installed as the favorite. In the fourth round she defeated Nicaragua’s Candelaria Resano, an Olympian and world championship medalist, by 12.57 points to 11.33. She had opened the competition on the first day of the event with 11.16 points, built on waves of 7.33 and 3.83, to win her heat ahead of Puerto Rico’s Havanna Cabrero and Colombia’s Margarita Conde. That 7.33 stood as the highest-scoring women’s wave of the opening day.

The result caps a season that has established Agüero as the leading woman in Costa Rican competitive surfing. She arrived in the Dominican Republic as the two-time national Open champion, having sealed her second consecutive title only weeks earlier at the closing round of the Banco LAFISE national circuit at Playa Hermosa de Jacó, the beach where she lives and trains.

In March she won the Denga Santa Teresa Pro at Playa Carmen. She has also been competing on World Surf League regional events, the tier where surfers accumulate the results and ranking points that open the door to the sport’s professional circuits. Costa Rica had never won a surfing gold medal at these Games before Wednesday. The country’s only previous podium finishes in the sport came at San Salvador 2023, when Lía Díaz and Anthony Flores each took bronze in longboard.

Sam Reidy added another on Tuesday, beating the Dominican Republic’s Gian Marco Oliva 14.50 to 11.60 in the men’s shortboard bronze heat, a result the Costa Rican Surf Federation described as the first shortboard medal at the Games. Flores finished fourth in the men’s longboard event this year after losing his bronze heat to Mexico’s Heriberto Torres.

The surfing competition ran from July 25 until today at Playa Encuentro, a break that has become one of the Caribbean’s most reliable competitive venues, and drew 71 surfers from 12 countries across shortboard, longboard and stand-up paddle surf. Agüero’s medal was Costa Rica’s third gold of Santo Domingo 2026. The first two came in taekwondo, through Jaycee Bassett and Neshy Lindo.

This edition of the Games is the 25th and marks a century since the first was held in Mexico City in 1926. Organizers programmed 40 sports, more than the Los Angeles 2028 Olympic schedule, and more than 6,200 athletes from 37 countries and territories are competing over 16 days.

Costa Rican surfing has been producing this kind of result with increasing regularity. Díaz became the first surfer from Costa Rica or anywhere in Central America to qualify for the World Surf League’s Longboard Tour, a circuit that opened its season at Huntington Beach in California this month.

Leilani McGonagle won a place on the 2026-27 Challenger Series, the qualifying tier immediately below the elite Championship Tour. Bodyboarder Dulce Agüero reached a podium at Pipeline in Hawaii in March. The national federation has said its planning is now oriented around the qualifying events for the 2028 Olympics, where surfing will again be on the program.

For Agüero, the initial reward is a regional title at 20 and a clear line of sight to the next stage. The Pan American Games in Lima in 2027 come first, and the Olympic qualifying calendar follows behind it.

World.title: Ride-app protest could slow your drive across the Valle Central this morning
World.content:
If you have a flight out of Juan Santamaría today, a shuttle booked to the airport, or a drive between Cartago and San José, leave earlier than you planned. Ride-app drivers have called a protest for 9 a.m. today, and the roads they say they will use are the ones that carry nearly everyone.

Organizers say the convoy will roll along Ruta 1 in Alajuela, through Ochomogo, past Sabanilla and onto Circunvalación, finishing at Casa Presidencial in Zapote. Those details come from the drivers themselves. As of first light Wednesday, the Policía de Tránsito had not published an advisory confirming the route, so treat that list as the plan rather than the result. Plans like this one shift, shrink or start late.

What the drivers have called is a tortuguismo, a go-slow. Nobody blocks anything. The convoy simply travels in a pack at a crawl, and every vehicle behind it travels at the same speed. That distinction is the whole story for you. A closure gets you a detour, an officer waving you around, and a police post you can see from a distance. A go-slow gets you none of that. There is no sign, no announcement, and no way to tell you are in it until you already are. Once you are boxed in on a divided highway, your only real option is to wait.

Ruta 1 is the reason this matters to travelers. It is the corridor between San José and Juan Santamaría, so anything that slows it slows every airport transfer, every hotel shuttle and every rental car heading for a return desk. Ochomogo sits on the climb between Cartago and San José and is the pinch point for that whole side of the valley. Circunvalación is the ring road that absorbs traffic coming off Ruta 27 and feeds it around the capital toward Zapote. Between them, those three points decide whether the Valle Central moves.

If you are flying out this morning and have not left yet, go now. Whatever cushion you would normally give yourself, add an hour on top of it. That sounds excessive on a normal Wednesday, and on a normal Wednesday it would be. The problem with a go-slow is that the delay is not proportional to the protest.

A few dozen vehicles moving at 20 kilometers per hour (about 12 miles per hour) for half an hour can leave a line that takes two hours to drain, because the road behind them keeps filling at normal speed while the front of it empties at a crawl. You do not lose the time the protest lasts. You lose the time it takes the backlog to clear.

Check in online before you leave, and if you have a bag to drop, know your airline’s cutoff rather than guessing at it. If you are running late, call the airline from the road rather than waiting until you reach the counter. Missing a bag cutoff by ten minutes is a different problem than missing a flight, and airlines can sometimes do something about the first if they hear from you early.

If you are already on Ruta 1 and traffic ahead of you dies, stay in the lane you are in. Weaving between lanes to get past a convoy does not work, and on that stretch it puts you alongside heavy trucks that cannot stop quickly. Do not try to overtake the group. If you have not yet committed to the highway, Ruta 3, the old road through Heredia and Alajuela, runs roughly parallel and gives you a way to reach the airport without joining the line. It is slower on a good day and it will be crowded today, but a slow road that is moving beats a fast road that is not.

Coming from Cartago, the alternative to Florencio del Castillo is the old road, and this week that carries a complication of its own. The Romería is already underway. Tránsito started its operation on July 25 with about 150 officers on that corridor and reinforces it between July 31 and August 2, and pilgrims are walking the shoulder in numbers. The old road is an option this morning, but drive it expecting people on foot rather than a clear run.

If you are not traveling and have nothing that cannot move, the simplest answer is to not drive between roughly 9 a.m. and midday. Reschedule the Zapote appointment. Take the errand in the afternoon. Every vehicle that stays home is one that is not in the line in front of somebody trying to catch a plane.

Behind all of this is a bill that has been moving through the Legislative Assembly for years. Expediente 23.736 would regulate transport offered through platforms such as Uber and DiDi, requiring drivers to register with the CCSS and Hacienda, pay an annual permit, and meet insurance and background requirements. The Comisión de Gobierno y Administración finished working through 282 mociones de fondo on Tuesday and approved nine of them, sending the revised text back to the plenary. That vote is what put drivers on the road this morning.

The drivers want two things added before it passes. They want a ceiling on the commission platforms take from each fare, and they want guaranteed benefits and due process when a company deactivates an account. Drivers made both demands at the Assembly earlier this month, saying they had not been heard during the drafting.

Aprimotec, an association representing platform drivers, asked the Assembly and the Executive on July 20 to stop the bill’s advance altogether, arguing the text was written around the traditional taxi sector and would push drivers out of the work rather than formalize it. The taxi sector sees it differently. Canatrans, Fenacotaxi, the Foro Nacional de Taxistas and other transport groups have publicly backed the bill, framing it as legal certainty and fair competition.

Neither side is likely to settle it this morning. What will be settled by lunchtime is whether you made your flight.

World.title: ‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?
World.content:
‘BAD FREAK’ CHARGED ON STEAMY WEDNESDAY; ‘WAR RIOR’ ON THE RUN – WHO WON THE FIGHT?

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A viral Facebook fight between two Belize City women known on social media as “Bad Freak” and “War Rior” has resulted in a disorderly conduct charge, with one woman fined and the other still being sought by police.

Twenty-two-year-old Britney Nichole Daly, also known as “Bad Freak,” appeared in Court #3 at the Belize City Magistrates’ Court on Wednesday, July 29, where she pleaded guilty to disorderly conduct.

The charge arose from a public fight on Freedom Street on Tuesday, July 28, involving Daly and Shala Smith, also known as “War Rior.” Video of the altercation quickly circulated on social media.

Police reportedly arrived after the fight had ended and those involved had already dispersed. Authorities later used footage from the Police Fusion Centre’s surveillance cameras to identify the women, leading to Daly’s detention.

Daly, a musician who resides at #22 Freedom Street, was fined $150 plus $5 in court costs. She has until September 30, 2026, to pay the total, or she will face one month in prison.

Outside the courthouse, Daly was asked what prompted the fight.

“To prove a point,” she replied before entering a waiting taxi.

Police say Smith remains at large and is being sought for the same charge of disorderly conduct.

World.title: Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub
World.content:
Man charged and fined $1,000 for molesting wild jaguar cub

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The case of the wild jaguar cub handled in the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve has reached its legal conclusion. The Belize Forest Department has announced that Ruben Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act in connection with the incident, and has paid a fine of BZ$1,000, approximately US$500.

According to the department’s official statement issued from Belmopan on July 29, 2026, Stoll was charged under the Wildlife Protection Act, Chapter 220 of the Laws of Belize, in connection with the incident involving the handling and molestation of a wild jaguar cub within the reserve.

Following the incident, the department stated, Stoll voluntarily returned to Belize and surrendered himself to the authorities, indicating he had been outside the country. He was subsequently charged and paid the fine.

The department paired the announcement with an unambiguous message to the public. Wildlife, it stressed, is not to be treated as pets, photo props, or tourist attractions, and approaching, touching, handling, or otherwise disturbing wild animals can place both people and wildlife at serious risk.

The legal foundation is broad by design. The jaguar is one of Belize’s protected species, and the Wildlife Protection Act defines “to hunt” as “to kill, take, or molest by any method and includes attempting to kill, take, or molest by any method any species of wildlife,” prohibiting the hunting of protected wildlife, obviously immature wildlife, and any female accompanied by its young. A cub, in other words, is covered several times over.

“No one is above the laws of Belize,” the department declared, reminding Belizeans and visitors alike that while the country welcomes the world to enjoy its extraordinary biodiversity, everyone bears responsibility to respect its wildlife, protected areas, and laws.

The resolution will nonetheless leave some Belizeans weighing the arithmetic: a thousand dollars for the molestation of a protected jaguar cub, the national animal’s most vulnerable form, is a figure the public conversation may judge against the offence. The penalty applied is the penalty the law provides, and any change to it belongs to lawmakers.

The department’s closing guidance is the piece worth carrying forward, for every trail, reserve, and encounter: observe wildlife from a safe distance. Admire it. Photograph it. But never touch it, harass it, or interfere with it.

World.title: Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan
World.content:
Minister of Economic Transformation and delegation meet Belizean students in Taiwan

By Zoila Palma: Today, Osmond Martinez, Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, and his delegation met with Belizean students in Taiwan.

The students shared their experiences and perspectives on their studies, culture, and life in Taiwan.

Minister Martinez emphasized that studying in Taiwan contributes to Belize’s human capital development by exposing students to advanced training and real-world innovation in areas where the country needs deeper expertise, particularly information technology, international relations, public health, and border security.

Minister Martinez and his delegation are visiting Taiwan from July 27 to 31, 2026.

World.title: Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance
World.content:
Institute for Social and Cultural Research discuss safeguarding living traditions of Deer Dance

By Zoila Palma: On July 24, 2026, the Institute for Social and Cultural Research (ISCR-NICH) and cultural advocates from the communities of Armenia, Maya Mopan, and Valley of Peace met to discuss the ongoing efforts to safeguard the living traditions of the Deer Dance.

Led by ISCR Director Rolando Cocom, the engagement provided an opportunity for community practitioners to share their knowledge, reaffirm the importance of honouring cultural traditions and community protocols, and identify meaningful pathways for continued collaboration in safeguarding this cherished heritage.

Looking ahead, ISCR will extend consultations to Deer Dance practitioners from communities in southern Belize. Through continued dialogue and mutual respect, we aim to strengthen partnerships with community practitioners, ensuring that safeguarding efforts remain community-led, respecting traditions, and sustainable for future generations.

ISCR extended appreciation to Francis Fonseca, Minister of Culture; Albert Vaughan, NICH President; and the Ministry of Indigenous Affairs for their continued commitment and encouragement in safeguarding and promoting the enduring traditions of our Belizean people.

World.title: New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize
World.content:
New cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers begins service in Belize

By Zoila Palma: A new cohort of 23 Peace Corps volunteers has officially begun their service in Belize following an oath ceremony led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Rhonda Slusher.

The ceremony was attended by Dr. Nadine Rogers, members of the Peace Corps community and government representatives, formally welcoming the volunteers into the Peace Corps’ more than six-decade partnership with Belize.

The volunteers will serve in the Youth Development and Primary Education sectors, supporting locally led initiatives aimed at strengthening youth development and education.

Their assignments will include work with the Youth Empowered by Sports (YES) project, as well as literacy programs and other classroom-based initiatives, while living and working alongside Belizean communities.

As the Peace Corps marks 65 years of global service, the new volunteers will continue a longstanding legacy of partnership, cultural exchange and community-driven development.

World.title: Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum
World.content:
Protected Areas Conservation trust convenes conservation forum

By Zoila Palma: The Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT) recently convened conservation partners for its “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum—a collaborative event designed to strengthen partnerships, celebrate achievements, and chart the future of conservation investment under the Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0.

Hosted in Belize City on July 23 and in Dangriga Town on July 24, the two days of sessions brought together protected area co-managers to exchange experiences, address shared challenges, and maximize the impact of conservation initiatives across Belize.

The “Connect. Reflect. Advance.” forum represented PACT’s commitment to fostering collaboration, transparency, and continuous learning among its partners. By creating space for open dialogue and collective problem-solving, the forum enhanced the effectiveness of ongoing investments while reinforcing a shared commitment to protecting Belize’s rich natural heritage.

PACT says that as it continues rolling out its Conservation Investment Strategy 2.0, the insights and commitments generated during these sessions will help shape future funding streams and strengthen partnerships that deliver meaningful environmental, social, and economic benefits for Belize.

World.title: International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response
World.content:
International News: Fauci invokes 5th amendment during heated Senate Hearing on COVID-19 response

By Zoila Palma: Today, Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment and declined to answer questions from senators during a Republican-led Senate committee hearing examining his handling of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Fauci was subpoenaed by Sen. Rand Paul of Kentucky, who has spent years accusing the retired infectious disease expert of misleading Congress and the public—allegations Fauci has rejected, ABC reports.

During the hearing, Fauci repeatedly responded to questions by saying, “On the advice of counsel, I respectfully decline to answer based upon my rights under the Fifth Amendment.” The constitutional protection allows witnesses to decline to provide testimony that could potentially incriminate them and does not, by itself, amount to an admission of guilt.

Paul pressed Fauci on issues including federal funding for research in China, virus mutations and the origins of COVID-19, arguing that Fauci had helped fund dangerous research and later misled the public. Fauci, however, said he believed the hearing was intended to elicit statements that could support Paul’s repeated calls for his prosecution.

The hearing also highlighted the deep partisan divide over the pandemic and its origins.

The confrontation came as Fauci’s decision to remain silent limited direct exchanges with Paul but gave the senator greater opportunity to present his accusations without detailed responses from the witness.

World.title: Support for students
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade Senator Kamina Johnson Smith (right) confabs with Minister of Culture, Gender, Entertainment and Sport Olivia Grange at the post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday, where Johnson Smith updated the nation on the situation with Jamaican medical students in Cuba.Garfield Robinson

THE Government of Jamaica has pledged continued support for the roughly 270 Jamaican students still studying in crisis-hit Cuba, with Foreign Affairs Minister Senator Kamina Johnson Smith reaffirming the Government’s commitment to the students’

welfare.

Johnson Smith told a post-Cabinet press briefing at Jamaica House Wednesday that her ministry has been closely monitoring the students who remain in Cuba, 40 of whom are sponsored by Cuban scholarships, which are supported by the Government of Jamaica, further noting that one private student has formally advised of his return home.

Meanwhile, she noted that more than 65 students, including five on government scholarships, have completed their medical studies for the 2025-2026 academic year.

“Three others have indicated that they are in the process of continuing their studies elsewhere through academic transfer, and we have to caveat these numbers because we understand anecdotally that others have returned, but they have not formally notified us,” Johnson Smith said.

“And this is understandable, they are there privately, and on their own steam, but just to say that we have the information…and we also have a line of communication that allows for them to not only indicate their return, but to request assistance if they so need,” said the minister.

Johnson Smith noted that those students who remain are offered pathways to repatriation should they express a desire to return.

“This is because our concern remains for their safety, well-being, and academic continuity. We know that prolonged power cuts and reduced public transportation causes challenges for their way of life, and the Government has communicated our preparedness to assist with one-way return tickets should they wish to return but have a difficulty with affordability,” she said.

“We continue to engage the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Finance, and the Ministry of Health, as well as medical tertiary institutions on what, if anything, can be done for those who may wish to return and continue their studies here,” she added.

Many of the Cuban medical students have seen classes suspended or moved online with limited connectivity, as Cuba faces an ongoing energy crisis, worsened by a United States blockade on fuel shipments.

The island’s fuel shortages have been triggering frequent, lengthy, and unpredictable electricity interruptions, affecting not only education but also access to food, medical supplies, and transportation.

Back in February, Johnson Smith said some students had been reaching out and advised that their institutions either closed for a period, in one case for four weeks; and others said that classes had been suspended in favour of virtual studies, which saw challenges with Internet and electricity.

To maintain direct contact, Johnson Smith noted the ministry created a WhatsApp group, at that time linking roughly 320 students with officials in Kingston and the Jamaican Embassy in Havana, a move that allowed the Government to register many privately funded students who were previously outside formal channels.

In the meantime, Johnson Smith said Wednesday that the Government has reaffirmed its commitment to Cuba by contributing US$100,000 through the Caribbean Community (Caricom) as a humanitarian relief effort.

She said Jamaica joined Caricom heads of Government in continuing to express deep concern over the worsening humanitarian situation in Cuba and reaffirmed its commitment to a coordinated regional response to provide humanitarian assistance to the Cuban people.

“While speaking as long-standing friends of both the United States and Cuba, Caricom underscored in our joint single statement that civilian needs must remain the highest priority. We welcomed recent rounds of discussions between the governments and continue to advocate for constructive dialogue as the most effective path to relieve hardship on the people of Cuba,” said Johnson Smith.

The minister added that many Cuban medical professionals who had left the island following an abrupt end to the long-standing health technical cooperation arrangement in March 2026 have since returned to Jamaica and are continuing work under new arrangements with the health and wellness ministry. Johnson Smith added that those who chose to remain are still being accommodated as they continue to work under individual contracts.

“We all continue to value the significant contribution that Cuban medical professionals have made to our health sector over many years, and following the conclusion of the technical cooperation programme, you’d recall that a number of Cuban medical professionals chose to remain in Jamaica and continue to work under personal contracts,” she said.
