Railway infrastructure also requires restoration. However, he said the closed border remains the main obstacle to resuming rail services.

At the beginning of 2026, Armenian media reported that the Armenian-Turkish border would open on 1 February to third-country nationals and holders of diplomatic passports. Armenia’s and Turkey’s special envoys for normalisation, Ruben Rubinyan and Serdar Kilic, reached that agreement in July 2022. The Margara border crossing on the Armenian side has stood ready to receive travellers since December 2023. Despite those agreements, however, Turkey has kept the border closed.

Even so, the two countries periodically announce positive steps. For example, from 1 January 2026, Armenia and Turkey simplified visa procedures for holders of diplomatic, special and service passports. They can now obtain a free electronic visa (e-visa) for short-term trips of up to 20 days.

Background

Since 2008, Armenia’s railway network has operated under a concession held by the South Caucasus Railway company, a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The concession agreement runs for 30 years, with an option to extend it by another 10 years if both sides agree.

Armenian experts say freight traffic on the country’s railways has halved since 2008. Some routes have ceased operating, while the mandatory investment commitments have never materialised.

Despite this, Yerevan asked Moscow to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

Rebuilding these lines would reconnect Armenia with the borders of Azerbaijan and Turkey. This is strategically important for Yerevan, which seeks to fully unblock regional transport links.

Russia has neither acted on Armenia’s request nor indicated a willingness to do so. At the same time, Moscow has said it does not intend to give up its railway concession.

Meanwhile, the Armenian government is considering revoking Russia’s concession and taking control of the railway network itself. It has also left open the possibility of transferring the concession to a third party.

At the beginning of July, Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan announced that Armenia had begun preparatory work to restore the Gyumri–Akhurik and Yerask railway sections.

“We will carry out this work ourselves. As for the remaining sections, we will continue working-level discussions, including with our Russian partners,” he said.

Turkey restores Akyaka–Gyumri railway

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Dictator wants to be liked by everyone. Those who don’t like him must be neutralised’
World.content:
Transparency International Georgia researcher Zviad Koridze believes that Georgia’s current system of governance is built on fostering civil confrontation and deepening divisions within society. In his view, authoritarian regimes rely on social polarisation and the portrayal of people with different opinions as enemies in order to maintain power.

Koridze said that Georgian society still retains the capacity to resist, and that, ultimately, it is civic engagement that will serve as the main force pushing back against these processes.

On 26 July, MMA (mixed martial arts) fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, together with several supporters, announced the creation of a civic movement that will “respond immediately” to issues involving ancestors, religion, history and other subjects that the group considers offensive. According to Kartvelishvili, the movement will be “highly active, well-organised and constructive”, and any “patriotic Georgian” will be able to join. Members of the group also said they were prepared to take responsibility for their actions, including serving prison sentences if necessary.

Zviad Koridze: “the system of governance that has taken hold in Georgia — Bidzina Ivanishvili’s dictatorship — regards civil confrontation as its natural state, just like any other dictatorship. Without it, those in power cannot consolidate their rule. They cannot persuade citizens that their continued grip on power and authoritarian governance serve the public interest. To do that, they need civil confrontation.

“All dictatorships are structured and develop in exactly this way. They need to identify groups and segments of society whose views differ from those of the autocrat. Then another social group must emerge to confront and suppress them. That is the language of civil confrontation.”

“When parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili says that we do not need to join the European Union because we should have the right to make our own decisions, that is clearly not his independent position but Bidzina Ivanishvili’s. Papuashvili’s role is to voice that position and to support the creation of precisely these kinds of vigilante groups. He is expected to welcome their emergence. He sees this as a form of sovereign governance, and that is exactly why he does not want Georgia to join the European Union.

“How can a writer be liked by everyone? Is there a single writer who is universally admired? How can anyone even make such a claim? Or say that a public figure must be liked by everyone? Only a dictator wants that. He wants everyone to like him. And anyone who does not must be neutralised, driven out, persecuted and beaten. That is why he creates groups like these.

“These restrictions are designed to instil a climate of irrational fear, discouraging people from thinking independently, protesting and speaking out. The current situation is exactly the one Bidzina Ivanishvili wants most, and he is using every mechanism at his disposal to maintain it. The only force capable of dismantling these mechanisms is society itself — a society with a firm stance. I do not believe society is silent. I am convinced that our society will resist.”

Civil confrontation in Georgia

World.title: Neptune's moon system is bizarre. JWST data helps explain why
World.content:
Neptune has a very strange moon system.

The farthest planet from the Sun in our Solar System has 16 known moons, named after figures from Greek mythology, and five rings.

Its largest moon, Triton, is the seventh largest moon in our Solar System.

Named after the Greek god of the sea, Triton makes up more than 99 per cent of the mass of Neptune's satellites.

And, unlike any other moon of its size in the Solar System, Triton orbits in retrograde: the opposite direction to Neptune's orbit.

The other 15 moons are tiny.

None of the other giant planets in our Solar System, Jupiter, Saturn and Uranus, have a moon system this unbalanced.

A new study, published in the journal Science Advances, has helped to explain why this might be the case.

Pointing the James Webb Space Telescope at Neptune

Triton's odd retrograde orbit has led researchers in the past to theorise that the moon originally came from the Kuiper Belt, a ring of asteroids beyond Neptune.

As Triton wandered in towards Neptune it was "captured" by the planet's gravity.

In the process, the cosmic gate-crasher may have destroyed Neptune's original moon system, if it had one, according to Ryleigh Davis, a planetary scientist at the University of California San Diego, and lead author on the paper.

"We don't actually know whether Neptune ever had such a system, and the small inner moons and rings are one of the best places to look for clues," Dr Davis said.

"The problem is that these moons are tiny, faint, and so close to Neptune that the planet's light overwhelms them."

Neptune is named after the Roman god of the sea, and its biggest moon, Triton, is named after Neptune's Greek equivalent, while the smaller moons are lesser Greek sea gods. (Supplied: NASA/ Space Telescope Science Institute)

To look for hints of Neptune's original moon system, the researchers used the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

They analysed light signals coming from three of Neptune's inner moons, Larissa, Galatea, and Proteus, as well as its inner rings, to see what minerals they contained.

Dr Davis said the JWST was sensitive enough to look closely at these moons for the first time.

Moon minerals hint at a destructive origin

The researchers found signals from a type of clay, called a phyllosilicate, on two of the moons (Larissa and Galatea), as well as in the rings.

"That was not on our list of things we expected to find," Dr Davis said.

That's because these clay minerals can't form in cold environments: they need liquid water.

"We spent a lot of time convincing ourselves it was real before we let ourselves get excited," Dr Davis said.

The only place around Neptune that can get warm enough for liquid water is the centre of a large object.

"The moons we're looking at, Larissa and Galatea, are far too small and cold for that chemistry to have ever occurred in place," Dr Davis said.

"So the clay had to come from somewhere else: the deep interior of a much larger ancient world.

"The most natural explanation is that Neptune once had a system of large moons, similar to what Uranus has today, that were shattered when Triton was captured billions of years ago."

Neptune's closest neighbour, Uranus, has 28 known moons, five of which are large like Triton.

Neptune's brightness makes it difficult to study its inner moons and rings. (Supplied: NASA/ Space Telescope Science Institute)

The researchers believe Neptune's remaining rings and moons are mostly the innards of those ancient moons.

Helen Maynard-Casely, a planetary scientist at the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation, who wasn't involved in the research, said the findings supported a generally accepted theory for Triton's origin.

"Triton turned up and caused havoc," Dr Maynard-Casely said.

"This gives another piece to the story of how Neptune's moons came to be how they are."

Mysterious mineral spotted

The team also found signals from a mineral they couldn't identify on all three of the moons and the rings.

Dr Maynard-Casely said this was exciting, because it could potentially be a previously unknown material.

"This just highlights, again, how much we don't know," Dr Maynard-Casely said.

The hunt for 'Planet Nine' Eight years after announcing evidence for a potential ninth planet, scientists are somehow still looking for it. So what will it take to find it?

Dr Davis said that figuring out the identity of this material could help researchers learn more about Neptune's original moons, like how large they were.

"I am hopeful we may eventually get a dedicated Neptune mission," Dr Davis said.

The only space probe that has visited Neptune so far was Voyager 2, in 1989. No space agencies have concrete plans to return.

Dr Maynard-Casely said a probe would yield better information.

"Every planetary scientist worth their sodium chloride wants a Uranus-Neptune mission."

World.title: Devices are growing more expensive. Will China's memory chips help?
World.content:
A company carrying China's hopes of securing its own artificial intelligence memory chip supply could help ease overseas data centre-driven shortages that are pushing up the cost of everyday devices.

CXMT has become mainland China's most valuable company at more than $US500 billion ($717 billion) in a stock market debut on Monday that the manufacturer hopes will let it ramp up production.

Memory prices for consumer devices have soared as manufacturers focus on supplying more advanced chips for the AI industry's data centre boom.

The shortage of chips for everyday devices has been nicknamed "RAMageddon".

CXMT is China's leading manufacturer of memory chips. (AFP: Pedro Pardo)

"Shortages in … memory have become more difficult to resolve quickly," said Ellie Wang, an analyst at tech industry intelligence firm TrendForce.

" This is also why more consumer electronics companies are considering CXMT as an additional supplier. "

Tech companies including Dell, HP and Apple have reportedly been testing CXMT memory chips as they look for other sources of supply.

"The appeal for CXMT chips is price," said Sue Keay, director of the University of New South Wales's AI Institute.

It could give Apple leverage over the dominant suppliers Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron, and help it hedge against further shortage-driven price rises, experts say.

However, they warn that if CXMT eases the strain in supply it would not necessarily make consumer devices nor memory chips cheaper.

Why is CXMT so important to China?

The AI boom needs memory chips, called Dynamic Random Access Memory (DRAM), for models such as ChatGPT and Claude to store information and perform their calculations.

But the race to build data centres is straining supply of memory, and the United States has imposed export controls against China buying advanced chips as the countries compete in developing the technology.

CXMT, or ChangXin Memory Technologies, was a "key pillar" of China's ambition to build a self-sufficient chip industry, Dr Keay said.

"CXMT will allow China to reduce dependency on Korea and the US," she said.

Since starting 10 years ago, and with backing from state-owned shareholders, it has emerged as the world's fourth-largest producer of DRAM chips with about 8 per cent market share.

That is behind South Korean companies Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, which account for 36 per cent and 29 per cent, and US firm Micron (24 per cent), according to Counterpoint Research.

How South Korea plans to cash in its AI chips South Korea is doubling down on its bid to lead in AI, unveiling plans last month to spend hundreds of billions on developing its chip manufacturing.

CXMT's customers include Chinese smartphone, PC and server manufacturers.

In 2024 it met only 20 per cent of domestic chip demand but aimed to supply more than two-thirds of the local market in the future, said MS Hwang, research director at Counterpoint Research.

The company's stock market debut has been described as a test of whether China can build a competitive domestic chip producer in a sector largely dominated by foreign firms.

Its shares boomed more than 500 per cent on Monday as it surpassed the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC) as mainland China's most valuable listed company.

What does it mean for China's AI race?

CXMT made its stock market debut as it was transitioning away from being a purely domestic player, according to Mr Hwang.

While CXMT is competitive in making mainstream memory chips used in consumer devices, it lags in the advanced High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) chips that are another important component in AI data centres.

CXMT hopes to catch up in the production of HBM chips. (Reuters: Carlos Barria)

The company is seen as China's best shot at developing its own cutting-edge HBM chips to power Chinese AI models, Brookings Institution expert Kyle Chan told the Associated Press news agency.

Mr Hwang said the company aimed to leapfrog competitors by adopting next-generation technologies that would create more powerful advanced memory chips.

"Although CXMT currently lags in HBM, it is positioned to start catching up by late 2026," he told the ABC.

"CXMT's next strategic road map includes supplying HBM within China starting in 2027."

Will it end shortages and high prices?

Dr Keay said as Samsung, SK Hynix and Micron focused on producing HBM to feed the AI data centre boom, CXMT would help meet the supply gap in chips for consumer devices — if it continued to focus on conventional memory.

American tech firms HP and Dell have shown interest in CXMT's DRAM chips, while the Financial Times has reported Apple has begun testing them for devices sold in China and is lobbying the US government for clearance to buy them.

Western tech companies have been testing CXMT's chips. (AFP: Pedro Pardo)

However, there was a political complication as the Pentagon had added CXMT to a list of companies with alleged links to the Chinese military, said Dr Keay.

"So any deal carries real geopolitical risk for Apple," she said.

The ABC approached CXMT and Apple for comment.

Mr Hwang said it was a "highly plausible scenario" that CXMT's market debut and plans would lead to cheaper technology in Australia and other Western countries.

China unveils its plan to dominate tech and AI future China unveils its five-year plan for tech dominance, pumping bill flying cars, brain-chip implants and, of course, humanoid robots.

"This new fourth major player has made a powerful [stock market] debut," he said.

"As competition intensifies around capacity expansion, CXMT's market presence will serve as a critical driver for lowering global memory prices in the future."

However, other experts said that even if CXMT ramped up production, and Apple and other international brands adopted its chips, it would not mean cheaper consumer electronics in Australia any time soon.

"CXMT is unlikely to flood the market with cheap chips because its output is largely pre-committed, mostly to Chinese customers," Dr Keay said.

"It looks like Apple's first potential use of CXMT chips would be focused on devices for the Chinese market."

Apple is reportedly testing CXMT's memory chips as it looks for other sources of supply. (Reuters: Mike Segar)

Ms Wang, from TrendForce, said CXMT's initial public offering would help it expand production capacity and invest in technology.

"However, new memory capacity typically takes at least a year to translate into meaningful supply, so it is unlikely to provide immediate relief from the current shortage," she said.

"Over the medium to long term, CXMT's capacity expansion could increase the supply of mainstream and consumer DRAM while making the global memory supply base more diversified.

"This should help improve the supply-demand balance and limit excessive price increases, although it may not necessarily lead to an outright decline in memory prices."

ABC with wires

World.title: Liberal MP Andrew Hastie takes stand in WAtoday defamation trial
World.content:
Federal Liberal MP Andrew Hastie has taken the stand in a defamation trial brought against him by a Perth property developer to defend his role in allegedly distributing a covert recording at the centre of the case.

WA businessman Greg Poland is suing national media organisation Fairfax — which has since been absorbed by Nine — and two of its former journalists, over two digital articles published under the WAtoday masthead in 2019.

Property developer Greg Poland, as pictured on his LinkedIn page. (LinkedIn: Greg Poland)

Mr Poland is also suing Mr Hastie, two of his staffers, and former WA Liberal leader Zak Kirkup for their alleged role in sharing a secret recording that formed the basis of the articles.

That toxic soil from the new Perth airport link? The government doesn't know what to do with it A giant pile of soil contaminated with toxic fire-fighting chemicals is sitting in Forrestfield while the State Government figures out how to deal with it.

The reporting alleged Mr Poland planned to dump millions of tonnes of "toxic" soil taken from the construction of Perth's airport rail tunnel at a property south of Perth on behalf of the WA government while the developer was in a senior position on the board of a government authority.

The article relied on a covertly recorded meeting between Mr Poland and sand miner Aaron Grainger at the Subiaco Hotel in 2019.

In the 46-minute recording played to the court, Mr Poland can be heard boasting about his access to Transport Minister Rita Saffioti and suggesting to Mr Grainger he should propose a land swap deal with the government to take the soil.

The secretly recorded meeting occurred at Subiaco Hotel. (ABC News: Cy Millington)

Mr Poland tells Mr Grainger he had been asked by Ms Saffioti to find a solution to the soil issue and was "talking about getting rid of a political headache for the government".

"If we can pull this off, anything you want, Rita will be your friend," Mr Poland is heard saying to Mr Grainger on the recording.

Greg Poland (right) and his lawyer Martin Bennett (left) outside court in Perth. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

Mr Poland said the articles made an imputation that he is corrupt and engages in secret deals between the state government and private businesspeople without due process — claims he vehemently denies.

Hastie denies wrongdoing

Earlier in the week, the court heard how Mr Grainger emailed the audio recording to Mr Hastie's office.

Mr Grainger testified that Mr Hastie told him he wouldn't disclose or share the audio recording with anyone.

He told the court he recorded the meeting without Mr Poland's knowledge because he thought he was being "set up".

Taking the stand in the Supreme Court on Thursday, Mr Hastie said he shared the audio file of the meeting to former WAtoday journalist Nathan Hondros on WhatsApp.

Nathan Hondros is a former WAtoday journalist. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

But he denied he did anything wrong by doing so.

Mr Hastie said he did not accept that he told Mr Grainger he wouldn't share the recording.

He said it was possible he shared it with Mr Kirkup, who at the time was the local Liberal MP, and later went on to become the leader of the WA Liberal Party.

Mr Hastie says he sent the audio file to the journalist. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

"I don't recall sending it to Mr Kirkup, but I don't deny that I probably did," Mr Hastie said.

Concern over 'dumping ground'

Mr Hastie recounted the day he first met Mr Grainger when they spoke about the recording.

He said Mr Grainger told him he was approached by the Peel Development Commission, of which Mr Poland was the then-deputy director, to assist them with "solving a problem".

At the time, Mr Hondros was working for WAtoday, one of the state's daily online news publications. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Mr Hastie told the court he was curious based on what Mr Grainger had told him about the encounter.

"I felt it was significant for the state government," Mr Hastie told the court.

" My concern was that the state government was going to use the Peel region as a dumping ground. "

When Mr Hastie was questioned on why he shared the recording with Mr Hondros, he said it was because he thought he was a "good" journalist.

WA's Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti, and former Labor ministers Alannah McTiernan and Dave Kelly are also expected to give evidence.

World.title: Finger pointed at social media amid racism 'public health emergency'
World.content:
Indigenous leaders have warned online racism is damaging young generations and called on all social media users and publishers to take responsibility for hurtful comments.

It comes as the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners called racism a "public health emergency" at the Cairns hearing of the federal government's Joint Standing Committee on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs inquiry into racism, hate, and violence directed at First Nations people.

Merissa Nona, from Cairns Indigenous social organisation Deadly Inspiring Youth Doing Good (DIYDG), said racism was causing future leaders to take their lives and that averse social media comments were playing a part.

"We're seeing really strong community members getting hit from all corners and then taking their life as a result of external pressures," she told the ABC.

"I've got a few more years in building up resilience and understanding where those comments are coming from. But I know hurt people go on to hurt people."

Call for more regulation

Ms Nona's colleague, Stacee Kethcell, said social media was an important tool for sharing First Nations culture with the world, but the fear of racist reactions played a significant role in their publishing decisions.

"NAIDOC is one week that we have to share with everybody and to celebrate us, and we still cop it," Ms Ketchell said.

"It's an attack on their identity, who they are as people, and they've been judged because someone has a belief or an attitude towards our people."

She said more accountability and regulation was needed.

Stacee Ketchell, Merissa Nona, and Georgiana Thomas-Peddell from DIYDG address the Federal Government's racism inquiry. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

When asked by the inquiry about Meta's submission that it was unaware of any First Nations people being employed as content moderators, she responded that the company's approach to dealing with racism was not enough.

"It needs to be informed by people who have … experienced racism," Ms Ketchell said.

"Racism is constant. It causes young people to doubt themselves and their self-worth."

Nicole Huxley warns racist social media comments could cause a lot of damage to her community's young people. (ABC News: Conor Byrne)

The fight for 'a better world'

Nicole Huxley, an elder in the tiny remote community of Jumbun, 130km south of Cairns, told the enquiry the full extent of the damage caused by social media was unknown.

"I can only imagine how somebody younger than me, who's learning about themselves, is feeling as they read something that is written about them without people knowing them," she said.

"We should not have our children seeing racism because we don't raise our children with racism."

Ms Huxley said a recent social media video of children dancing during NAIDOC Week celebrations in Charters Towers attracted hateful commentary.

"It's so hard to be able to get our children to be able to participate in the wider society and be proud of their culture, let alone trying to do it in the middle of the street and then have people be very racist against what they were doing," she said.

"We're a human race and, if we raise our children without racism, we're going to have a better world."

She called on the community, as well as publishers and government agencies, to take responsibility for racist comments.

"With the current climate of racism in this country, I think it needs to be put on a higher agenda in a lot of the service providers when they're posting on social media about Indigenous affairs," she said.

Ms Huxley said she continued to invest much of her time fighting against racists online.

"I'll never win that fight because you can never change someone's mindset unless they really want it to be changed," she said.

"It drains all of your goodness."

The inquiry travels to the Torres Strait tomorrow, before visiting Hobart and Melbourne next month.

World.title: FIFA's controversial bid to sell the World Cup to a Trump associate
World.content:
Gianni Infantino's $US20 billion ($28.7 billion) proposal to sell stakes in FIFA's events and competitions arm to corporate investors has drawn condemnation from football's international organising confederations.

On Tuesday the FIFA president announced a bid to form a commercial subsidiary called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) that would grant private buyers control over competitions including the World Cup and Club World Cup.

Amid immediate opposition from global football's most influential confederation, the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA), Mr Infantino also set out a one-off $US20 million ($28.7m) funding boost for FIFA member nations who vote to approve the FFE bid.

The commercialisation, frequency and scale of the FIFA World Cup and other tournaments will be determined by investors if the deal is approved. (Reuters: Mark J Rebilas)

The announcements are the latest in a string of controversial decisions made by Mr Infantino without consulting football's major stakeholders.

So, is it going to work and — if so — how? Here's what you should know.

Firstly, what is the FIFA Forward Enterprise?

FIFA, a non-profit organisation, described the FFE as "a new FIFA-owned and controlled subsidiary consolidating FIFA’s commercial and event operations".

FIFA investment scheme deadline FIFA boss Gianni Infantino tells member federations they have until September 19 to decide on his controversial private investor scheme with Joshua Kushner.

The governing body said it would retain control of the subsidiary and authority over football governance, competitions, match calendars and regulatory decisions.

Mr Infantino said FIFA's hope was that the FFE could generate enough commercial revenue to raise $US20 million in additional funding by 2030 for the further development of "infrastructure, coaching, national teams, competitions, grassroots football and the women’s game" in member nations worldwide.

"Parts of [football] have turned [its] popularity into remarkable commercial value – and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game," Mr Infantino said in a statement.

" Our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world. "

FIFA also highlighted how much money each of its 211 members could receive in the "FIFA Fast-Forward Program" initiative the FFE would financially bolster.

Instead of the currently-promised $US8 million ($11.5m) to be distributed during the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, the FFE would generate $US20 million, then $US22 million ($31.6m) and $US24 million ($34.5m) in the following cycles, FIFA said.

If the FFE is approved, members could choose to take part in any additional financial opportunities created under the leadership of the subsidiaries' investors.

If it is rejected, members would only get a previously-promised $US10 million ($14.3m).

Who are the private investors?

The effort is being bankrolled by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.

An investment firm owned by Joshua Kushner has been named by FIFA as a frontrunner to bankroll the FFE bid. (Reuters: Brendan McDermid)

Mr Infantino said the bidding process would encourage "a pool of diverse international investors", although FIFA named Mr Kushner's Thrive Capital investment firm as the frontrunner.

On its website, Thrive says it "builds and invests in internet, software, and technology-enabled companies".

FIFA also said Greg Maffei, the CEO of Bann Ventures which develops healthcare, hotel, commercial and residential spaces, would become "a key commercial adviser" in the FFE's creation.

Mr Maffei is the former president of Liberty Media, which acquired Formula One in 2017.

How have confederations reacted?

UEFA was the first governing organisation to openly condemn Mr Infantino's proposal.

"It is not FIFA's to sell," it said in a statement.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially.

" None of us are the owners of football. "

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) — which includes Australia and Middle Eastern nations as members — said it was not consulted about the proposal.

FIFA boss reveals $US20b plan to sell World Cup FIFA president Gianni Infantino earns more criticism after unveiling a brazen plan to "unleash the commercial potential" of the World Cup.

The Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) said it was "deeply concerned by the lack of due process" surrounding the proposal, while the Confederation of African Football said it would host a meeting of members in the coming week to discuss the bid.

Football Australia only confirmed on Thursday that it had received notice from FIFA detailing the proposal.

"As this is the first time we have been made aware of the initiative, we are now working to understand the proposal in full," a statement said.

"We have requested further information from FIFA to properly assess the strategic, commercial, and governance implications of such a significant step."

What happens next?

Mr Infantino has set FIFA's members a deadline of September 19 for a decision to be made on the FFE.

The proposal's future is set in a game of numbers that will be determined by votes lodged by each of FIFA's 211 member nations.

While UEFA has been the most vocal confederation in opposing the FFE, it only represents 55 nations in Europe.

FIFA's Congress operates on a strict one vote principle applied to each member, meaning Mr Infantino's push could still be approved with a majority vote of approval from the remaining 156 nations.

The equation could see smaller nations who have less access to overall FIFA finances compared to some of UEFA's larger European giants swayed by Mr Infantino's funding offer.

Why now, and what could investors gain?

Tim Harcourt, a UTS professor of sports economics and author of the Footynomics website, said while it was "unusual" for a global governing body to seek to sell its sport to private investors, he was not surprised the proposal came less than a fortnight after the end of this year's FIFA World Cup.

"The World Cup surprised people [with] how well it went," he told the ABC.

"Nothing that potentially could have gone wrong in a World Cup happened. So, I think there's a lot of confidence right now in FIFA."

Donald Trump has previously flagged he would like to see the United States host an additional FIFA World Cup during his presidential term. (Reuters: Dylan Martinez)

Mr Harcourt said he expected the FFE could lead to FIFA hosting more large-scale events such as the World Cup more frequently and on a bigger scale.

The FIFA World Cup is currently held every four years. This year's cup was expanded to include 48 nations for the first time, however Mr Infantino has flagged the governing body is considering a 64-team event for the 2030 tournament.

Private investors could also champion more opportunities to cash in on  potential, such as this year's controversial "hydration break" mid-match pauses, Mr Harcourt said.

"You have to be careful about control of the game, you have to be careful of corporate governance and you have to be careful of saturating the game," he said.

"The fact that the World Cup happens every four years … There's quite a nice balance.

"There's sort of natural life cycles in these things you don't want to play around with too much."

World Cup success The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

Mr Harcourt suggested there may be an element of international politics playing into the FFE announcement.

Jared Kushner was one of the chief architects and negotiators of the Abraham Accords that were signed in 2020 between Israel, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates.

The deals were brokered by the Trump administration as part of a broader push to integrate Israel more fully into the Middle East.

In the wake of the US war in Iran and the 2034 FIFA World Cup expected to be hosted by Saudi Arabia, Mr Harcourt said "football diplomacy" could impact how the FFE takes shape.

If that link were to come to fruition, it would mark the latest alignment between Mr Infantino and Mr Trump after he created the FIFA peace prize that was awarded to the US president, and allowed Mr Trump to intervene in a process that led to United States forward Folarin Balogun playing at the World Cup.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Dog euthanised after attacking child in Bunnings
World.content:
A young girl has been taken to hospital after she was attacked by a dog inside a Bunnings outlet in regional Victoria.

Emergency services were called to the Bunnings store in Delacombe, near Ballarat, yesterday at 11.10am.

Advanced life support paramedics treated the child, who was taken to Ballarat Base Hospital in a stable condition.

An Ambulance Victoria spokesperson said the child suffered "a lower body injury".

The City of Ballarat said the dog has since been euthanised.

"The dog was voluntarily surrendered by its owners for euthanasia, which took place on Wednesday afternoon," City of Ballarat director of development and growth Natalie Robertson said.

" The City of Ballarat will conduct a thorough investigation and is unable to comment further while that process is underway. "

A Bunnings spokesperson said their thoughts were with the young girl and her family.

"We understand the child was bitten by a dog and was treated by emergency services before being taken to hospital for further assessment and treatment," the spokesperson said.

"We will support the relevant authorities with their enquiries."

The incident took place inside the Bunnings store.

According to the store's entry information, "well-behaved pets that are on a lead" are permitted inside.

World.title: Renewable rollout prioritised speed over 'social licence', inquiry finds
World.content:
The NSW government has been accused of leaving regional NSW behind in a scathing parliamentary report into renewable energy zones (REZ), with a lack of coherent planning and a failure to listen to impacted communities resulting in "predictable and avoidable harm".

A NSW parliamentary inquiry was charged with investigating the impact of the scheme on impacted communities in 2024, and has since visited each of the five zones before issuing its final report.

The report has made 16 recommendations to the NSW government.

This included a review of all five REZs and the impacts on each regional community.

The inquiry asked that Energy Corporation of NSW, also known as EnergyCo, be subject to formal performance and accountability requirements.

Local councils in each REZ should receive recurrent funding to help with resourcing and a statutory Community Advocate be established to represent landholders.

Inquiry chair and Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MLC Mark Banasiak said the inquiry found the NSW government "railroaded" impacted communities with the scheme's rollout.

Mark Banasiak says impacted communities have been "railroaded" by the state government. (By Sarah Moss)

"It was quite clear that they had no social licence, the social licence had collapsed because they had failed to bring the community along" Mr Banasiak told the ABC.

"Communities just felt what they were saying was just falling on deaf ears."

Mr Banasiak says the report's findings lead him to believe the apparent lack of community consultation was a deliberate choice by the government to ensure the project went ahead smoothly.

" They knew getting community trust was going to be a challenge, so they just didn't bother. "

The report has found a lack of coherent planning and consultation by the government resulted in "predictable and avoidable harm" to impacted communities. (Supplied: Facebook/ Power and Water)

Nobody is Listening

For fourth-generation beef farmer Allison McPhee, the realities of the states' shift towards renewable energy are impossible to ignore.

The transmission line set to snake through NSW from Walcha in the north-west to Bayswater in Sydney will run right through her property on the outskirts of Scone in the Upper Hunter.

She says the impacts on her farm will be profound.

"We will have to re-evaluate the whole way we do things. We would have to reduce our herd because we can't carry as many cattle, which reduces your profitability."

Fourth-generation farmer Allison McPhee is not confident community consultation will improve. (ABC Upper Hunter: Sean Murphy)

The report acknowledged the relationship between Energy Corporation of NSW and impacted communities has been "significantly eroded", failing in it's duty to give those directly affected an avenue to "meaningfully influence outcomes".

It recommends Energy Co be subject to formal performance and accountability requirements, including greater public reporting.

"This is failing because the policy is bad, not because the people are non-compliant," Ms McPhee says.

" Nobody is listening to the local knowledge. "

For grazier Anna Young, whose property near Walcha is at the extreme end of the transmission line, there is caution about what comes next.

Despite being supportive of the report's findings and recommendations, she is less optimistic about how the government will respond.

"My faith in this report leading to change is pretty low," she says.

Upper Hunter residents Anna Young, Libby Crouch and Lucy Haigh oppose EnergyCo's revised transmission line corridor. (ABC Upper Hunter: Sean Murphy)

She says the assessment of the relationship between Energy Co and landowners, which the report found was lacking in "meaningful engagement", has given her some hope.

"I think it's really validating for all communities that have been dealing with Energy Co for years and trying to shout from the rooftops about all the problems, but there doesn't seem to be any accountability."

In its response to the report's findings, the NSW government says the evidence highlights the challenges associated with the "transformation of [NSW's] energy system".

The government says "substantial work" such as financial support for local government, additional compensation and community benefits to impacted areas have taken place in the time since the inquiry tabled its first report in August of last year.

World.title: Cult survivors fearful after inquiry accidentally shares email addresses
World.content:
Abuse survivors who gave evidence to a Victorian parliamentary inquiry into cults and fringe groups say they feel exposed after their email addresses were shared with those they made submissions about.

The Legislative Assembly Legal and Social Issues Committee yesterday released its final report after a year-long inquiry into the recruitment methods and impacts of cults and organised fringe groups.

But the committee inadvertently sent its final recommendations to 330 visible email addresses.

The email list included witnesses who told stories of leaving high-control groups, and those who made submissions from those groups.

"The fact that their email addresses may now be known by their abusers is beyond distressing," said Alex Belle, who is part of Survivors of Coercive Cults and High Control Groups.

"I think if anything, the data breach does reinforce just how damaging cults are, you know, how hard it is for us to leave and leave safely."

Alex got out of the Hebrew Roots movement two-and-a-half years ago and had made an anonymous submission to the inquiry.

They said they had serious concerns for the safety of the respondents.

"And not only may those survivors now be identified, particularly those who had written in anonymously or confidentially, there may be other people who've been mentioned in those reports," they said.

Alex did not want the breach to take away from the landmark report, which recommends outlawing coercive control in group settings as part of 39 recommendations to the Victorian government.

"It's something that's actually, actionable, meaningful, and has finally let us let survivors be heard after years of feeling invisible and has recognised the nuance of cult harm," they said.

"Our advocacy group has had a lot of panicked survivors messaging and calling at the moment and we can't even tell them that their fears aren't founded because they very much are."

Patrick McIvor says the privacy breach is an example of the need for a dedicated commissioner. (Supplied: Patrick McIvor)

Breach highlights need

The inquiry received almost 300 submissions from many who had left groups they believed to have taken control of their lives.

Of the 291 written submissions, 172 were "name withheld" or "confidential".

Patrick McIvor is an advocate survivor and told the ABC while the group applauded the report, the privacy breach was a glaring example of why a commissioner dedicated to addressing group-based coercion was needed.

"It should not overshadow the inquiry's final report, which provides a powerful road map for change and reflects almost every major reform priority survivors called for," Mr McIvor said.

"However, it stopped short of recommending a dedicated commissioner, which we will continue to advocate for.

"This breach shows why a single point of responsibility is so important, a commissioner or similar authority could ensure breaches like this are properly addressed, while identifying and following up other cross-agency failures that the report recognised as an ongoing systemic problem."

Fears for safety

One survivor, who gave evidence anonymously and whose name has been withheld to protect their identity, said they were fearful.

"I just want to know why this has been allowed to happen, who did it and the repercussions for families and individuals who have escaped?" she said.

"Who is going to support us through this?"

She, and many witnesses who made submissions or testified, said they lived with post-traumatic stress disorder.

"We are in these communities and they know where we are," she said.

"I'm worried for a lot of people's safety."

Ryan Carey and his wife Catherine with MP Christine Couzens and Victorian Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny at parliament yesterday after the inquiry's report was tabled. (Supplied: Ryan Carey)

Ryan Carey is a survivor and is part of Stop Religious Coercion Australia.

"I feel physically sick, because I know the real-world impact of the situation," Mr Carey said.

"There's been a lot of bravery for survivors to tell their story and to even get them to trust the government that their anonymity would be kept secret.

"There's a real possibility that there will be retribution to stop people talking in the future."

'Unacceptable privacy breach'

Labor MP Ella George was the chair of the inquiry and said it was an administrative error which will be part of a full review into the secretariat's processes.

"Yesterday, there was an unacceptable privacy breach where email addresses of inquiry stakeholders were made public," Ms George said.

"I want to assure every Victorian who made a submission to our inquiry that we are taking this matter very seriously.

"Many people shared their experiences for the first time, and demonstrated immense courage in speaking out."

The list of stakeholders who were emailed included a large list of people who emailed about the inquiry, including those who made submissions, anyone who asked questions and journalists.

"We note that the stakeholder list is connected with a committee proceeding," Ms George said.

"Therefore, further disclosing, using or sharing that information, including email addresses, may be a breach of parliamentary privilege.

"On behalf of the committee, I offer my sincerest apology for any distress this has caused."

World.title: Beetaloo brings in Halliburton for Top End data centre push
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Beetaloo brings in Halliburton for Top End data centre push Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd July 30, 2026 — 4:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beetaloo Energy has brought global oilfield services giant Halliburton into the fold for its ambitious Beetaloo Digital development in the Northern Territory, signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to advance the integrated gas-to-data centre project. The non-binding agreement represents confirmation in Beetaloo’s plan to assemble a coalition of specialist parties to deliver the project, which is anchored by the company’s vast and untapped Beetaloo Basin gas resource and a recently secured 185-hectare site at Weddell, just outside of Darwin. The proposed location for Beetaloo Energy’s Data Centre initiative in the Northern Territory. The company says that the US$26 billion (A$37 billion) marked capped Halliburton is expected to provide strategic technical expertise and services to support the assessment and development of the upstream gas resource. The US-based giant’s role will likely cover everything from subsurface consulting and field development planning to integrated drilling services and project execution. ‘Following the NT’s decision to grant us exclusivity over the Weddell site, we are committed to building a world-class consortium.’ Beetaloo Energy managing director Alex Underwood



Crucially, Halliburton also delivers the very scalable, modular gas-fired power solutions for hyperscale data centres and Ai infrastructure, making it a natural fit for Beetaloo’s vertically integrated vision. Beetaloo Energy chief executive officer Alex Underwood said: “Following the Northern Territory Government’s decision to grant us exclusivity over the Weddell site, we are committed to building a world-class consortium capable of delivering this opportunity. We are pleased to announce this MOU with Halliburton. The company brings a proven track record in oilfield services, engineering execution, and collaborative solutions, making it a valuable potential participant in the project.” The Beetaloo Digital strategy aims to create a dedicated, new power source for data centres, rather than drawing from the existing Northern Territory grid, by utilising the vast resources trapped within the territories Beetaloo Basin. Management says by intentionally building excess generation capacity, the project could also provide a reliable, large-scale source of baseload electricity for the region while at the same time supporting the rapid growth of data centres in the Asia-Pacific. The plan is designed to tap into the relentless power demand from hyperscale data centres and AI facilities, which operate around the clock.



Beetaloo says that a durable and predictable demand profile supports long-term field development, accelerates upstream investment and could establish a large-scale, cash generator for the company at a much faster uptake. The entire strategy is underpinned by Beetaloo’s commanding 28.9-million-acre tenement position across the Northern Territory. The company is already well on its way to becoming a producer at its Carpentaria pilot project, where construction of a gas plant is underway ahead of planned first gas sales in the fourth quarter of this year. While the Beetaloo is closing in on becoming a gas producer, bringing a major heavyweight like Halliburton on board adds serious credibility to its downstream digital ambitions. The move is a savvy cash generation angle for Beetaloo, as it looks to supply gas to both a hungry domestic market and a rapidly evolving integrated energy and digital infrastructure sector. World.title: Viking maps out US tungsten processing pathway
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Viking maps out US tungsten processing pathway Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 30, 2026 — 4:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Viking Mines has banged a significant technical peg in the ground at its Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA, with an independent concept study confirming a clear and conventional processing pathway just as a drill rig arrives on site to spin the rods at the historic operation for the first time in almost half-a-century. The study, completed by Mineral Technologies, outlines a process for a 300,000-tonne-per-annum (tpa) plant based on established tungsten processing practices. A 3D render of the conceptual 300,000-tonne-per-annum modular processing facility designed for Viking Mines’ Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA. The flowsheet uses scheelite’s high specific gravity to make gravity concentration the natural recovery method, and includes staged crushing, high-pressure grinding, closed-circuit milling, multi-stage gravity concentration using spirals and tables and a flotation stage to recover finer material. The company says the plant design centres on a modular approach, with components made offsite to minimise on-site construction time and risk. The study also highlights the plant’s flexibility, noting that while it has an upper capacity of 300,000 tpa it can run at lower throughputs of 100,000 or 200,000 tpa simply by reducing operating hours.



‘Our near-term focus remains testing the primary tungsten system with the drill bit.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Mineral Technologies has estimated a build time of about 15 months, comprising 12 months for procurement and fabrication and a further three months for on-site assembly. Notably, the processing study was based on a conservative metallurgical recovery of 60 per cent of scheelite, the tungsten-bearing mineral, into a 50 per cent tungsten trioxide concentrate. That figure sits well below the company’s own recent metallurgical test work, which clocked a much bigger 76 per cent recovery to produce a high-quality 56.9 per cent tungsten trioxide concentrate. Importantly, Viking’s reverse circulation drilling program marks a further significant step in its goal to define a maiden mineral resource at the past-producing mine. With earthworks and drill pad preparation already underway, drilling is expected to kick off this week. The company’s maiden campaign is looking to test scheelite-bearing skarn mineralisation across three specific target areas, extending shallow, near-mine high-grade mineralisation and testing for down-dip extensions at the old Linka workings.



The program will also probe for extensions to the south-west under shallow cover and conduct first-pass regional drilling along a broader, seven-kilometre mapped intrusive contact, of which only 10 per cent has been properly tested. Viking has not disclosed indicative capital or operating costs from the study, consistent with ASX guidelines, as a mineral resource or ore reserve has not yet been inked for the project. The maiden drilling campaign represents the critical first step toward establishing the resource. The timing of the program also looks savvy, with European tungsten prices recently hitting multi-year highs of US$3265 (A$4694) per metric tonne unit (MTU) for 88.5 per cent ammonium paratungstate. One MTU equates to 10 kilograms. Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “This study gives us an independent, credible engineering view that Linka mineralisation can be processed through a conventional, well-understood flowsheet – and importantly, through a modular plant designed to keep site works and upfront capital efficient.” Beyond the flagship Linka operations, the company maintains an active footprint across several other asset holdings in Nevada. Viking’s regional land claims include the Alpine, Long, Ragged Top, Terrell and Victory tungsten projects, which are held under various unpatented mineral claim agreements.



The company says it’s actively gathering and evaluating historical exploration data across these peripheral claim blocks to plan future field campaigns. It seems Viking has put its ducks in a row in the best possible way at its Linka project. With the drill rods now ready to spin to check what lies beneath, the company now has a solid technical plan for how to process it. By running the engineering and resource drilling workstreams together, the company is positioning itself to make quick strides once the drill results start rolling in. For Viking, having a clear processing pathway mapped out this early in the game is a solid piece of de-risking that could pay dividends down the track. World.title: Godolphin confirms broad NSW copper-gold porphyry at Goodrich
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Godolphin confirms broad NSW copper-gold porphyry at Goodrich Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Doug Bright July 30, 2026 — 4:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Godolphin Resources has strengthened the case for a potentially sizeable copper-gold porphyry discovery in central New South Wales after drilling at its Goodrich project returned broad mineralised zones starting close to surface. The company’s latest assay results delivered a standout 136.55-metre intercept grading 0.32 per cent copper, 0.16 grams per tonne gold and 43 grams per tonne molybdenum from 81.45m, a classic element signature confirming the presence of an extensive mineralised porphyry system beneath historic workings. Godolphin Resources has identified gossanous outcrop on a low rise in the Goodrich-Yeoval joint venture area. This classic field indicator reinforces the prospectivity of the locality for base and precious metals. A particularly rich contact zone near the top of the mineralised intrusion returned 3.55m at 2.8 per cent copper and 0.18g/t gold from 81.45m. Within the broader interval, the company also highlighted several higher-grade zones, including 26m at 0.52 per cent copper and 0.24g/t gold from 102m, 12m at 0.45 per cent copper and 0.36g/t gold from 131m, and 5m at 0.66 per cent copper and 0.49g/t gold from 158m, the latter including the best molybdenum value of 191.8g/t moly.



‘The broad, near-surface mineralised interval intersected in GGDD004 demonstrates the scale potential of the system.’ Godolphin Resources managing director Ms Jeneta Owens A second diamond drill hole added further support to the emerging exploration model, intersecting 52.97m at 0.20 per cent copper and 0.02g/t gold from 29.15m, including 4.75m at 0.56 per cent copper and an elevated molybdenum response to 404.4g/t moly. Godolphin’s Goodrich project forms part of the company’s larger Yeoval-Goodrich copper-gold joint venture about 70 kilometres northwest of the city of Orange in the renowned Lachlan Fold Belt. Importantly for Godolphin observers, the company retains a 49 per cent interest in the project after its Canadian partner Great Plains Metals completed the initial earn-in stage and secured 51 per cent of the project. Great Plains has now elected to pursue a 70 per cent stake by spending a further $1M on exploration over the next year, importantly allowing Godolphin to maintain exposure without funding the upcoming work programs.



Godolphin Resources managing director Ms Jeneta Owens said: “The confirmation of a copper-gold porphyry mineralisation at Goodrich is an excellent outcome for Godolphin and our partner Great Plains. The broad, near-surface mineralised intercept in GGDD004 validates the exploration model at Goodrich and highlights the potential scale of the system.” Geologically, the results look particularly encouraging. The drilling has intersected chalcopyrite (copper sulphide) bearing monzonite porphyry which has intruded as a stock. Monzonite is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock that contains roughly equal amounts of plagioclase feldspar and alkali feldspar, with less than 5 per cent quartz. It is compositionally intermediate between syenite and diorite. In this context, monzonites - and quartz monzonites - are often well-mineralised because they are associated with volatile-rich, intermediate magmas that often form major porphyry copper and skarn ore systems The intrusion also exhibits mineralised unidirectional solidification textures (UST’s) which are features commonly associated with fertile copper-gold porphyry systems.



UST’s are typically rhythmic, layered bands of comb-like quartz and aplite – very fine-grained “sugary” quartz - that grow inward from the upper margins of cooling magma chambers. They can be major pathfinder indicators for exploration geologists looking for large ore systems suggesting the ground may hold further treasures lurking beneath. Stocks are defined as igneous intrusions from depth which punch upwards across existing rocks layers and may cover a surface area of up to 100 square kilometres. The name separates stocks from larger bodies usually referred to as batholiths and which might otherwise be of the same composition. Management says the results validate the company’s exploration model and point to the potential scale of the emerging system. The partners are also reviewing historic drill core and have submitted 324 previously unassayed samples for laboratory testing, with results expected to help refine targeting across the broader project area. The latest success follows a busy few weeks for Godolphin. In a July investor presentation, the company highlighted the Yeoval-Goodrich joint venture as a key growth opportunity alongside its flagship Lewis Ponds gold-silver-base metals project and the planned Matrix Critical Minerals spin-out of its Narraburra rare earths asset.



Earlier this month, Godolphin outlined plans for the Matrix IPO, which is targeting an $8M-$12M raising and a separate ASX listing in the second half of 2026. With a funded partner advancing drilling at Goodrich and fresh assay results still pending from historical core, Godolphin looks well-placed to maintain its momentum across what is shaping up as one of the company’s key value drivers in its diverse NSW portfolio. World.title: ‘Strange morning’: NT Labor MP charged with assault keeps envoy role for now
World.content:
Updated PoliticsFederalCrime ‘Strange morning’: NT Labor MP charged with assault keeps envoy role for now Rob Harris Updated July 30, 2026 — 4:34pm ,first published 10:19am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling says he will remain focused on serving his electorate after being charged with two counts of assaulting Northern Territory Administrator David Connolly, as pressure mounts on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to strip him of his special envoy role. The member for Solomon, 54, was arrested by Northern Territory police on Thursday morning over an alleged incident involving Connolly at the NT Thailand Grand Festival in Darwin on July 18. Federal Labor MP Luke Gosling. Alex Ellinghausen Police allege Gosling assaulted the administrator, the King’s representative in the Northern Territory, during the community event, where they both attended official proceedings. Gosling later posted photographs from the event on social media. He was taken into custody at Palmerston Police Station on Thursday morning, charged with two counts of assault and granted bail to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 1.



The charges, which Gosling has emphatically denied, carry a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment under the Northern Territory Criminal Code. Breaking his silence after being charged, Gosling said he could not comment on the allegations because the matter was before the courts but described it as “a strange morning”. “I’ve got a job to do, and I’ll be working hard, as always, to serve the people of Darwin and Palmerston,” he said in a statement. He thanked supporters who had contacted him and his office with messages of support for him and his family. “We’re all cracking on with it. I’ll stay focused on doing my job and building a stronger territory and better nation for all of us.”



Opposition figures have seized on the charges, calling on Albanese to immediately stand Gosling aside from his role as special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia. Shadow defence spokesman James Paterson said the allegations were “incredibly serious”. “While everyone is entitled to the presumption of innocence, an arrest for assault requires him to immediately stand down from his duties,” Paterson posted on X. “The PM must act today.” Northern Territory senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price said the investigation should proceed “without fear, favour or political interference” but argued the seriousness of the allegations warranted Gosling standing aside from his additional responsibilities.



Related Article Exclusive

Roberts-Smith case ‘Not appropriate’: Labor MP asks colleagues not to talk about Ben Roberts-Smith But Liberal defence industry and personnel spokesman Phillip Thomson said he was not sure Gosling needed to stand aside. “I’ve kind of questioned the both sides of it,” he said, saying anyone charged “will have their day in court”.

“I do kind of think this …. goes back to the prime minister and he will have to address this at some stage,” adding that the charges were “very serious” and “should be treated as such”. A spokesman for Albanese declined to comment, saying only that there was a legal process underway and it would be inappropriate to comment further. Gosling’s barrister, Marty Aust SC, questioned the handling of the case, warning there was a risk it had become politicised.



“There’s a real concern that there’s a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter’s being handled already,” Aust told reporters outside Palmerston Police Station, according to the NT News. “What I can say is that the charge is completely and utterly denied and will be contested.” Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. Labor holds Solomon on a margin of 7.09 per cent. The Solomon MP, who has represented the Darwin-based electorate since 2016, had earlier dismissed the allegations as “ridiculous”, saying he had no dealings with Connolly beyond congratulating him on his appointment last year.



Gosling reportedly ignored waiting journalists after his release, got into the passenger seat of a Toyota Prado waiting outside the station, and the car then drove away and entered a nearby McDonald’s drive-through. Connolly’s office previously confirmed “an incident occurred” during his attendance at a community event but declined further comment while the police investigation was underway. The former president of NT Cattlemen’s Association’s appointment last year by the Country Liberal government was marked by the emergence of controversial comments he’d previously posted on social media about women’s sport, the prime minister and race. This prompted condemnation from Labor figures, including Gosling, who described the comments at the time as “reprehensible and offensive”. World.title: I’m a medical student. I fear we are selecting future doctors on whether their parents can afford it
World.content:
NationalNSWDoctors at work Opinion I’m a medical student. I fear we are selecting future doctors on whether their parents can afford it Joshua Chan Student doctor July 30, 2026 — 4:27pm

July 30, 2026 — 4:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, the prime minister announced that students in 10 more health professions would be paid while on mandatory placement, physiotherapy, pharmacy and paramedicine among them, at around $338 a week. It is real help, and I am glad for my colleagues who will receive it. Medical students were left out. Again. According to the Australian Medical Students’ Association, we complete between 2000 and 4000 hours of various unpaid placements across our clinical years. I often do not know my timetable for the end of the week or the month. Activities begin at 7am and some fall out of hours or on weekends. Classes are rescheduled repeatedly on short notice. Joshua Chan is in his third year of a medical degree at UNSW. Our placement sites move between suburbs as far-flung as Liverpool and Randwick, and some peers commute two hours each way for a class that runs for one. None of this is anyone’s fault; most medical schools’ timetables look like this, and it is because clinicians cannot tell us on Monday what their Thursday workload will look like – they do not know either. My university is doing its best to educate us inside a health system with no capacity left in it.



But the effect on us is the same, regardless of fault. You cannot choose your class timetable. You cannot pick up day shifts at a casual job on a timetable you receive the night before, or sign a lease when you do not know which part of Sydney you will be sent to next month. And the city we call home boasts a median rent of $824 a week, with renters handing over a record third of their income. I adjudicate debating in public schools, tutor privately, some of it pro bono, and shoot video on weekends. I love all of it, and I am barely holding on to any of it. Paid placements would let me scale that back by choice rather than lose it by attrition. If you are supporting yourself, or a parent, or a sibling, or living three suburbs from a train station and without a car, this schedule does not inconvenience you. It selects you out. That’s even before you apply, when six years as a student does not look survivable. Then, during the degree, come the failed years, the deferred courses, the quiet withdrawals that never reach a workforce statistic. Among First Nations medical students, attrition runs as high as 45 per cent. They are 4.2 per cent of those entering medicine and 2.3 per cent of those graduating. That gap is not a mystery. Related Article Opinion

Medicine As a GP, I’m very worried about changes to how ‘the pill’ will be prescribed Hayley Glasson Medical practitioner Then the crushing costs go to work on the ones who stay. On the first day of medical school, you want nothing more than to be a GP, giving back to the underserved community in which you grew up. Six years of debt and unpaid labour later, the goodwill has drained out of you. Forgoing your regional hometown to fight for a metropolitan specialist training position with double the expected salary now starts to look less like a betrayal and more like simple arithmetic. We are not only filtering who becomes a doctor. We are shaping what kind of doctor they can afford to become.



People will tell you medicine is oversubscribed, and they are right. But subscription is not representation. We are not short of medical students. We are short of the students who would do the work this country most needs. Only 15.6 per cent of us say we are heading for general practice, while emergency medicine and rural generalism are scarcer still, and students entering medicine from the lower socioeconomic deciles are roughly twice as likely to be practising in a disadvantaged area years later. And yet, knowing all this, we persist with a system that structurally excludes the students most likely to become the doctors we need the most, leaving the rest of us to wonder out loud why Mount Druitt and Moree cannot keep a bulk-billing GP. To its credit, this government has done plenty for primary care. Bulk-billing is up almost five percentage points in a year, there are now 137 urgent care clinics, and it is funding the largest GP training program in Australian history: 2000 trainees a year by 2028. But you cannot fix a leaking pipeline by widening the far end. Funded training places do not help if the students who would have filled them left in third year or finished medical school in a financial position prohibiting them from even considering lower-paid regional work. Related Article Opinion

Doctors at work Wonder why emergency doctors are quitting? Spend a day in my shoes Rachael Gill Emergency medical specialist I am not asking for sympathy. When I complain about a commute to someone who has waited 11 months for a specialist appointment, I hear how it sounds, and they would be right to be unimpressed. A lucky few of us, myself included, do not need the payment to survive, and can reassure ourselves that we will, eventually, be well paid. But the chimera of a bright future does not dismiss the costs of today. What we ask for is simpler and cheaper than the alternative: put clinical medical students into the Commonwealth Prac Payment on the same terms as everyone else, and fund the healthcare system such that clinical teaching is not something exhausted senior doctors do in the gaps.



Because the alternative is a profession selected on whether our parents could afford it. And a profession staffed by junior doctors already burnt out on the first day they are handed the pager. Joshua Chan is a third-year medical student at UNSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: First detection of deadly H5N1 bird flu confirmed in Victoria
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBiosecurity First detection of deadly H5N1 bird flu confirmed in Victoria Benjamin Preiss and Mike Foley July 30, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Authorities in Victoria are increasing surveillance of wild animal populations after the detection of the state’s first case of the potentially catastrophic new strain of H5N1 bird flu. A member of the public discovered the ill bird in the coastal town of Portland near the border with South Australia and reported it to authorities. Testing on the greater crested tern subsequently confirmed the bird had contracted the virus. The detection comes after a series of cases in Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland. Bird flu has been detected in greater crested terns in South Australia and Victoria. Neil Bowman Victoria’s chief veterinary officer Graeme Cooke urged anyone who finds a cluster of at least five sick birds of any species to alert authorities. However, he said even a single sick or dead seabird, waterbird, shorebird or bird of prey – or marine mammal, such as seals and dolphins – should be reported to authorities immediately.



“We recognise this can be unsettling news for members of our community,” Cooke said. The virus can devastate poultry and wildlife populations. The latest strain has authorities and farmers on edge amid concerns about an outbreak on poultry farms. The detection of a separate bird flu strain on farms in 2024 resulted in about 1.3 million birds being euthanised, followed by about 600,000 in 2025. Since the detection of the H5N1 virus in Western Australia last month, poultry keepers have been asked to voluntarily house their birds. In Victoria, that period has now been extended to a minimum of 14 days from today. The first confirmed case of H5N1 in Australia was detected in Western Australia. Getty Images H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has been declared ineradicable by authorities, following confirmation on Wednesday that the virus is circulating among local birds.



The national committee on emergency animal diseases, which comprises state and federal chief veterinary officers, as well as scientific experts, said now the virus had spread among local terns it was not feasible to stamp it out of the country. Related Article Lunch with Why this science writer will hole up on a farm in WA if bird flu strain mutates The official declaration triggers national co-ordination for cost sharing in response to the deadly virus. The Albanese government has already committed $113 million to preparations to deal with an H5N1 incursion, with an emphasis on planning to identify an outbreak swiftly and a response to limit its spread. This includes funding to prepare biosecurity officers to respond to an outbreak in farmed poultry, which may involve quarantining farms or districts and restricting transport between locations.



Egg farmer Xavier Prime was forced to consider what it would have been like to euthanise his flock during an avian influenza outbreak in 2024. The detection of the H5N1 strain will now have farmers on edge. Joe Armao Authorities are using aerial surveillance methods, with helicopters and drones monitoring wildlife populations. Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer James Todd said seal and gannet colonies in Portland were among the wildlife vulnerable to the disease. “We’ve been preparing for H5 arrival in Victoria for a few years now,” he said.



Despite the technological response to the virus detection, Todd said co-operation from the community remained the most effective control method at hand. “Our best line of defence at this stage is still the Victorian public.” In a statement, Wildlife Victoria said it received a call from a concerned member of the public earlier this week about the greater crested tern in Portland showing signs of the virus. Seals are among the marine mammals that can be infected with H5N1 Getty Images “Wildlife Victoria monitored the case until Agriculture Victoria responders arrived on scene to contain and test the bird,” it said. “The tern was confirmed positive to H5 bird flu shortly after.”



Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate said farmers should review their biosecurity plans and look out for unusual illness or unexplained bird deaths. “There has been no spread to commercial poultry flocks or any agricultural environment at this stage, and the risk to human health remains very low,” he said. The signs of H5N1 in birds include lack of co-ordination, tremors, swimming in circles, twisted necks, inability to fly or stand, diarrhoea, breathing difficulties, coughing, sneezing, swelling around the head, neck and eyes as well as cloudy eyes and changes in eye colour, as well as sudden death.
