Beetaloo Energy has brought global oilfield services giant Halliburton into the fold for its ambitious Beetaloo Digital development in the Northern Territory, signing a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to advance the integrated gas-to-data centre project. The non-binding agreement represents confirmation in Beetaloo’s plan to assemble a coalition of specialist parties to deliver the project, which is anchored by the company’s vast and untapped Beetaloo Basin gas resource and a recently secured 185-hectare site at Weddell, just outside of Darwin. The proposed location for Beetaloo Energy’s Data Centre initiative in the Northern Territory. The company says that the US$26 billion (A$37 billion) marked capped Halliburton is expected to provide strategic technical expertise and services to support the assessment and development of the upstream gas resource. The US-based giant’s role will likely cover everything from subsurface consulting and field development planning to integrated drilling services and project execution. ‘Following the NT’s decision to grant us exclusivity over the Weddell site, we are committed to building a world-class consortium.’ Beetaloo Energy managing director Alex Underwood



Crucially, Halliburton also delivers the very scalable, modular gas-fired power solutions for hyperscale data centres and Ai infrastructure, making it a natural fit for Beetaloo’s vertically integrated vision. Beetaloo Energy chief executive officer Alex Underwood said: “Following the Northern Territory Government’s decision to grant us exclusivity over the Weddell site, we are committed to building a world-class consortium capable of delivering this opportunity. We are pleased to announce this MOU with Halliburton. The company brings a proven track record in oilfield services, engineering execution, and collaborative solutions, making it a valuable potential participant in the project.” The Beetaloo Digital strategy aims to create a dedicated, new power source for data centres, rather than drawing from the existing Northern Territory grid, by utilising the vast resources trapped within the territories Beetaloo Basin. Management says by intentionally building excess generation capacity, the project could also provide a reliable, large-scale source of baseload electricity for the region while at the same time supporting the rapid growth of data centres in the Asia-Pacific. The plan is designed to tap into the relentless power demand from hyperscale data centres and AI facilities, which operate around the clock.



Beetaloo says that a durable and predictable demand profile supports long-term field development, accelerates upstream investment and could establish a large-scale, cash generator for the company at a much faster uptake. The entire strategy is underpinned by Beetaloo’s commanding 28.9-million-acre tenement position across the Northern Territory. The company is already well on its way to becoming a producer at its Carpentaria pilot project, where construction of a gas plant is underway ahead of planned first gas sales in the fourth quarter of this year. While the Beetaloo is closing in on becoming a gas producer, bringing a major heavyweight like Halliburton on board adds serious credibility to its downstream digital ambitions. The move is a savvy cash generation angle for Beetaloo, as it looks to supply gas to both a hungry domestic market and a rapidly evolving integrated energy and digital infrastructure sector. World.title: Viking maps out US tungsten processing pathway
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Viking maps out US tungsten processing pathway Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward July 30, 2026 — 4:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Viking Mines has banged a significant technical peg in the ground at its Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA, with an independent concept study confirming a clear and conventional processing pathway just as a drill rig arrives on site to spin the rods at the historic operation for the first time in almost half-a-century. The study, completed by Mineral Technologies, outlines a process for a 300,000-tonne-per-annum (tpa) plant based on established tungsten processing practices. A 3D render of the conceptual 300,000-tonne-per-annum modular processing facility designed for Viking Mines’ Linka tungsten project in Nevada, USA. The flowsheet uses scheelite’s high specific gravity to make gravity concentration the natural recovery method, and includes staged crushing, high-pressure grinding, closed-circuit milling, multi-stage gravity concentration using spirals and tables and a flotation stage to recover finer material. The company says the plant design centres on a modular approach, with components made offsite to minimise on-site construction time and risk. The study also highlights the plant’s flexibility, noting that while it has an upper capacity of 300,000 tpa it can run at lower throughputs of 100,000 or 200,000 tpa simply by reducing operating hours.



‘Our near-term focus remains testing the primary tungsten system with the drill bit.’ Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock Mineral Technologies has estimated a build time of about 15 months, comprising 12 months for procurement and fabrication and a further three months for on-site assembly. Notably, the processing study was based on a conservative metallurgical recovery of 60 per cent of scheelite, the tungsten-bearing mineral, into a 50 per cent tungsten trioxide concentrate. That figure sits well below the company’s own recent metallurgical test work, which clocked a much bigger 76 per cent recovery to produce a high-quality 56.9 per cent tungsten trioxide concentrate. Importantly, Viking’s reverse circulation drilling program marks a further significant step in its goal to define a maiden mineral resource at the past-producing mine. With earthworks and drill pad preparation already underway, drilling is expected to kick off this week. The company’s maiden campaign is looking to test scheelite-bearing skarn mineralisation across three specific target areas, extending shallow, near-mine high-grade mineralisation and testing for down-dip extensions at the old Linka workings.



The program will also probe for extensions to the south-west under shallow cover and conduct first-pass regional drilling along a broader, seven-kilometre mapped intrusive contact, of which only 10 per cent has been properly tested. Viking has not disclosed indicative capital or operating costs from the study, consistent with ASX guidelines, as a mineral resource or ore reserve has not yet been inked for the project. The maiden drilling campaign represents the critical first step toward establishing the resource. The timing of the program also looks savvy, with European tungsten prices recently hitting multi-year highs of US$3265 (A$4694) per metric tonne unit (MTU) for 88.5 per cent ammonium paratungstate. One MTU equates to 10 kilograms. Viking Mines managing director and chief executive officer Julian Woodcock said: “This study gives us an independent, credible engineering view that Linka mineralisation can be processed through a conventional, well-understood flowsheet – and importantly, through a modular plant designed to keep site works and upfront capital efficient.” Beyond the flagship Linka operations, the company maintains an active footprint across several other asset holdings in Nevada. Viking’s regional land claims include the Alpine, Long, Ragged Top, Terrell and Victory tungsten projects, which are held under various unpatented mineral claim agreements.



The company says it’s actively gathering and evaluating historical exploration data across these peripheral claim blocks to plan future field campaigns. It seems Viking has put its ducks in a row in the best possible way at its Linka project. With the drill rods now ready to spin to check what lies beneath, the company now has a solid technical plan for how to process it. By running the engineering and resource drilling workstreams together, the company is positioning itself to make quick strides once the drill results start rolling in. For Viking, having a clear processing pathway mapped out this early in the game is a solid piece of de-risking that could pay dividends down the track. He was taken into custody at Palmerston Police Station on Thursday morning, charged with two counts of assault and granted bail to appear in Darwin Local Court on September 1.



The charges, which Gosling has emphatically denied, carry a maximum penalty of 14 years’ imprisonment under the Northern Territory Criminal Code. Breaking his silence after being charged, Gosling said he could not comment on the allegations because the matter was before the courts but described it as “a strange morning”. “I’ve got a job to do, and I’ll be working hard, as always, to serve the people of Darwin and Palmerston,” he said in a statement. He thanked supporters who had contacted him and his office with messages of support for him and his family. “We’re all cracking on with it. I’ll stay focused on doing my job and building a stronger territory and better nation for all of us.”



Opposition figures have seized on the charges, calling on Albanese to immediately stand Gosling aside from his role as special envoy for defence, veterans’ affairs and northern Australia. Shadow defence spokesman James Paterson said the allegations were “incredibly serious”. “While everyone is entitled to the presumption of innocence, an arrest for assault requires him to immediately stand down from his duties,” Paterson posted on X. “The PM must act today.” Northern Territory senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price said the investigation should proceed “without fear, favour or political interference” but argued the seriousness of the allegations warranted Gosling standing aside from his additional responsibilities.



Related Article Exclusive

Roberts-Smith case ‘Not appropriate’: Labor MP asks colleagues not to talk about Ben Roberts-Smith But Liberal defence industry and personnel spokesman Phillip Thomson said he was not sure Gosling needed to stand aside. “I’ve kind of questioned the both sides of it,” he said, saying anyone charged “will have their day in court”.

“I do kind of think this …. goes back to the prime minister and he will have to address this at some stage,” adding that the charges were “very serious” and “should be treated as such”. A spokesman for Albanese declined to comment, saying only that there was a legal process underway and it would be inappropriate to comment further. Gosling’s barrister, Marty Aust SC, questioned the handling of the case, warning there was a risk it had become politicised.



“There’s a real concern that there’s a degree of politicisation in relation to how this matter’s being handled already,” Aust told reporters outside Palmerston Police Station, according to the NT News. “What I can say is that the charge is completely and utterly denied and will be contested.” Under section 44 of the Constitution, a federal MP convicted and sentenced for an offence punishable by at least one year’s imprisonment can be disqualified from parliament, meaning any conviction could trigger a byelection. Labor holds Solomon on a margin of 7.09 per cent. The Solomon MP, who has represented the Darwin-based electorate since 2016, had earlier dismissed the allegations as “ridiculous”, saying he had no dealings with Connolly beyond congratulating him on his appointment last year.



Gosling reportedly ignored waiting journalists after his release, got into the passenger seat of a Toyota Prado waiting outside the station, and the car then drove away and entered a nearby McDonald’s drive-through. Connolly’s office previously confirmed “an incident occurred” during his attendance at a community event but declined further comment while the police investigation was underway. The former president of NT Cattlemen’s Association’s appointment last year by the Country Liberal government was marked by the emergence of controversial comments he’d previously posted on social media about women’s sport, the prime minister and race. This prompted condemnation from Labor figures, including Gosling, who described the comments at the time as “reprehensible and offensive”. World.title: I’m a medical student. I fear we are selecting future doctors on whether their parents can afford it
World.content:
NationalNSWDoctors at work Opinion I’m a medical student. I fear we are selecting future doctors on whether their parents can afford it Joshua Chan Student doctor July 30, 2026 — 4:27pm

July 30, 2026 — 4:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Last week, the prime minister announced that students in 10 more health professions would be paid while on mandatory placement, physiotherapy, pharmacy and paramedicine among them, at around $338 a week. It is real help, and I am glad for my colleagues who will receive it. Medical students were left out. Again. According to the Australian Medical Students’ Association, we complete between 2000 and 4000 hours of various unpaid placements across our clinical years. I often do not know my timetable for the end of the week or the month. Activities begin at 7am and some fall out of hours or on weekends. Classes are rescheduled repeatedly on short notice. Joshua Chan is in his third year of a medical degree at UNSW. Our placement sites move between suburbs as far-flung as Liverpool and Randwick, and some peers commute two hours each way for a class that runs for one. None of this is anyone’s fault; most medical schools’ timetables look like this, and it is because clinicians cannot tell us on Monday what their Thursday workload will look like – they do not know either. My university is doing its best to educate us inside a health system with no capacity left in it.



But the effect on us is the same, regardless of fault. You cannot choose your class timetable. You cannot pick up day shifts at a casual job on a timetable you receive the night before, or sign a lease when you do not know which part of Sydney you will be sent to next month. And the city we call home boasts a median rent of $824 a week, with renters handing over a record third of their income. I adjudicate debating in public schools, tutor privately, some of it pro bono, and shoot video on weekends. I love all of it, and I am barely holding on to any of it. Paid placements would let me scale that back by choice rather than lose it by attrition. If you are supporting yourself, or a parent, or a sibling, or living three suburbs from a train station and without a car, this schedule does not inconvenience you. It selects you out. That’s even before you apply, when six years as a student does not look survivable. Then, during the degree, come the failed years, the deferred courses, the quiet withdrawals that never reach a workforce statistic. Among First Nations medical students, attrition runs as high as 45 per cent. They are 4.2 per cent of those entering medicine and 2.3 per cent of those graduating. That gap is not a mystery. Related Article Opinion

Medicine As a GP, I’m very worried about changes to how ‘the pill’ will be prescribed Hayley Glasson Medical practitioner Then the crushing costs go to work on the ones who stay. On the first day of medical school, you want nothing more than to be a GP, giving back to the underserved community in which you grew up. Six years of debt and unpaid labour later, the goodwill has drained out of you. Forgoing your regional hometown to fight for a metropolitan specialist training position with double the expected salary now starts to look less like a betrayal and more like simple arithmetic. We are not only filtering who becomes a doctor. We are shaping what kind of doctor they can afford to become.



People will tell you medicine is oversubscribed, and they are right. But subscription is not representation. We are not short of medical students. We are short of the students who would do the work this country most needs. Only 15.6 per cent of us say we are heading for general practice, while emergency medicine and rural generalism are scarcer still, and students entering medicine from the lower socioeconomic deciles are roughly twice as likely to be practising in a disadvantaged area years later. And yet, knowing all this, we persist with a system that structurally excludes the students most likely to become the doctors we need the most, leaving the rest of us to wonder out loud why Mount Druitt and Moree cannot keep a bulk-billing GP. To its credit, this government has done plenty for primary care. Bulk-billing is up almost five percentage points in a year, there are now 137 urgent care clinics, and it is funding the largest GP training program in Australian history: 2000 trainees a year by 2028. But you cannot fix a leaking pipeline by widening the far end. Funded training places do not help if the students who would have filled them left in third year or finished medical school in a financial position prohibiting them from even considering lower-paid regional work. Related Article Opinion

Doctors at work Wonder why emergency doctors are quitting? Spend a day in my shoes Rachael Gill Emergency medical specialist I am not asking for sympathy. When I complain about a commute to someone who has waited 11 months for a specialist appointment, I hear how it sounds, and they would be right to be unimpressed. A lucky few of us, myself included, do not need the payment to survive, and can reassure ourselves that we will, eventually, be well paid. But the chimera of a bright future does not dismiss the costs of today. What we ask for is simpler and cheaper than the alternative: put clinical medical students into the Commonwealth Prac Payment on the same terms as everyone else, and fund the healthcare system such that clinical teaching is not something exhausted senior doctors do in the gaps.



Because the alternative is a profession selected on whether our parents could afford it. And a profession staffed by junior doctors already burnt out on the first day they are handed the pager. Joshua Chan is a third-year medical student at UNSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: First detection of deadly H5N1 bird flu confirmed in Victoria
World.content:
NationalVictoriaBiosecurity First detection of deadly H5N1 bird flu confirmed in Victoria Benjamin Preiss and Mike Foley July 30, 2026 — 4:23pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Authorities in Victoria are increasing surveillance of wild animal populations after the detection of the state’s first case of the potentially catastrophic new strain of H5N1 bird flu. A member of the public discovered the ill bird in the coastal town of Portland near the border with South Australia and reported it to authorities. Testing on the greater crested tern subsequently confirmed the bird had contracted the virus. The detection comes after a series of cases in Western Australia, South Australia, New South Wales and Queensland. Bird flu has been detected in greater crested terns in South Australia and Victoria. Neil Bowman Victoria’s chief veterinary officer Graeme Cooke urged anyone who finds a cluster of at least five sick birds of any species to alert authorities. However, he said even a single sick or dead seabird, waterbird, shorebird or bird of prey – or marine mammal, such as seals and dolphins – should be reported to authorities immediately.



“We recognise this can be unsettling news for members of our community,” Cooke said. The virus can devastate poultry and wildlife populations. The latest strain has authorities and farmers on edge amid concerns about an outbreak on poultry farms. The detection of a separate bird flu strain on farms in 2024 resulted in about 1.3 million birds being euthanised, followed by about 600,000 in 2025. Since the detection of the H5N1 virus in Western Australia last month, poultry keepers have been asked to voluntarily house their birds. In Victoria, that period has now been extended to a minimum of 14 days from today. The first confirmed case of H5N1 in Australia was detected in Western Australia. Getty Images H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b has been declared ineradicable by authorities, following confirmation on Wednesday that the virus is circulating among local birds.



The national committee on emergency animal diseases, which comprises state and federal chief veterinary officers, as well as scientific experts, said now the virus had spread among local terns it was not feasible to stamp it out of the country. Related Article Lunch with Why this science writer will hole up on a farm in WA if bird flu strain mutates The official declaration triggers national co-ordination for cost sharing in response to the deadly virus. The Albanese government has already committed $113 million to preparations to deal with an H5N1 incursion, with an emphasis on planning to identify an outbreak swiftly and a response to limit its spread. This includes funding to prepare biosecurity officers to respond to an outbreak in farmed poultry, which may involve quarantining farms or districts and restricting transport between locations.



Egg farmer Xavier Prime was forced to consider what it would have been like to euthanise his flock during an avian influenza outbreak in 2024. The detection of the H5N1 strain will now have farmers on edge. Joe Armao Authorities are using aerial surveillance methods, with helicopters and drones monitoring wildlife populations. Victoria’s chief biodiversity officer James Todd said seal and gannet colonies in Portland were among the wildlife vulnerable to the disease. “We’ve been preparing for H5 arrival in Victoria for a few years now,” he said.



Despite the technological response to the virus detection, Todd said co-operation from the community remained the most effective control method at hand. “Our best line of defence at this stage is still the Victorian public.” In a statement, Wildlife Victoria said it received a call from a concerned member of the public earlier this week about the greater crested tern in Portland showing signs of the virus. Seals are among the marine mammals that can be infected with H5N1 Getty Images “Wildlife Victoria monitored the case until Agriculture Victoria responders arrived on scene to contain and test the bird,” it said. “The tern was confirmed positive to H5 bird flu shortly after.”



Victorian Farmers Federation president Ryan Milgate said farmers should review their biosecurity plans and look out for unusual illness or unexplained bird deaths. “There has been no spread to commercial poultry flocks or any agricultural environment at this stage, and the risk to human health remains very low,” he said. The signs of H5N1 in birds include lack of co-ordination, tremors, swimming in circles, twisted necks, inability to fly or stand, diarrhoea, breathing difficulties, coughing, sneezing, swelling around the head, neck and eyes as well as cloudy eyes and changes in eye colour, as well as sudden death. World.title: Council looks at short-term infrastructure fixes to protect South Dunedin
World.content:
The Dunedin City Council is considering what short-term infrastructure improvements to make in flood-prone South Dunedin.

The council announced it was developing an infrastructure investment package for the area over the next 30 years to protect it from flooding and the effects of climate change.

The plan was expected be put to councillors in December.

The Otago Regional and Dunedin City councils had been considering three possible scenarios for long-term fixes under the South Dunedin Future programme - ranging from raising land and pumping water, creating wetlands and canals, and shifting out of harm's way.

A major managed retreat was not on the table, but between 1100 and 1700 properties might need to be bought to make way for specific public works, land raising or new green spaces.

The Dunedin City Council on Thursday said it would be examining a revised set of long-term futures, including an "engineering focused pipes and pumps option" which would supplement or potentially replace one of the three proposed futures.

This would be presented to both councils in September.

Dunedin Mayor Sophie Barker said the approach provided a clear pathway forward.

"South Dunedin communities have told us they want to see progress on reducing flood risk while also ensuring longer-term adaptation options are thoroughly tested," she said.

"This approach allows both to happen at the same time. Councils can continue progressing work on immediate infrastructure needs while taking the time to carefully assess longer-term options and understand their costs, benefits and implications."

The 30-year infrastructure investment package would build on stormwater work already underway, the Dunedin City Council said.

"This work would involve additional modelling, design and constructability assessments to further develop the list of 10-15 flood protection projects already identified through South Dunedin Future. It would also complement current DCC three waters infrastructure work, which includes the ongoing roll out of the three stormwater projects in the $29.2 million package approved by DCC Council in January 2025," the council said.

"Importantly, the package would be developed so it remains compatible with a range of possible longer-term adaptation approaches."

Otago Regional Council chair Hilary Calvert said councillors needed more information about the options available to reduce flood risk in South Dunedin, the benefits and costs involved, and the trade-offs associated with different approaches.

World.title: How Consumer NZ wants to fix the electricity market
World.content:
Four major changes are needed to fix New Zealand's electricity market, Consumer NZ says.

It has released a new report, which outlines what it says a four main drivers of high power bills, and suggests four solutions.

It said household power bills had risen at nearly twice the rate of wider inflation since the electricity market was reformed 27 years ago, and households were suffering. More than 30,000 had their power disconnected at least once in the past financial year because they could not pay their bills.

"We've been concerned for some time that the electricity sector is not showing up well for consumers … it's doing great things for gentailers, it's doing good things for dividends paid to the government and other shareholders, but increasing numbers of New Zealanders are struggling to pay their power bill," chief executive Jon Duffy said.

"I think there's more than 60 reports that have been written on the electricity sector over the last couple of decades, and none of them was actually written from a consumer's perspective, so we wanted to put something out there that sent the message, particularly in election year, to the government to say something needs to be done to change how the sector's treating consumers."

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

The report said the big power companies were too dominant in the market. "Contact, Genesis, Mercury and Meridian control most of the retail market and own substantial generation assets, giving them advantages that smaller independent retailers and generators do not have."

It said power prices did not reflect real costs, there had not been enough investment in homegrown energy and politics had got in the way of having a long-term plan.

To tackle that, Consumer said the dominance of the gentailers needed to be reduced, power prices should better reflect the cost of generation, there should be more investment in local power sources so that New Zealand was not reliant on coal and gas, and there should be a cross-party energy strategy to put affordability, security and emissions reductions first.

Duffy said he was not suggesting the gentailers had to be broken up, but there needed to be more competition. "It's really difficult for a new entrant to come into the retail part of the market knowing they have to buy power off the very companies they're competing with. Something needs to be done to shift that imbalance of power.

"Secondly, we have a system that prices electricity at the cost of the most expensive fuel.

"So if 95 percent of our generation on a given day is generated by hydro, wind, and solar, which is free fuel, but 5 percent is generated by burning gas and coal, [that drives] the price for all of the electricity generated that day. We don't think that market model, which was actually designed more for European jurisdictions where there's a much lower percentage of renewables, is right for a really highly renewable grid like we have."

He said gentailers were now investing more in generation because of the growing demand from data centres.

"That's cold comfort for the 25 percent of New Zealand households struggling with their power bill."

Duffy said it was a hard issue for politicians to tackle.

"They call it the trilemma in the electricity sector where you've got to balance security of supply, so keeping the lights on, with sustainability, we want to reduce emissions generated by electricity generation, and affordability. You have those three factors, all of which have high importance, but security of supply tends to trump all of them, and I guess if you're a Minister of Energy sitting there, and a gentailer turns up and says, 'well, if you make these changes to the market, we won't be able to supply power, and you're going to have people who vote for you sitting in the dark not able to heat their homes, because we can't get power to them', that scares you into what has actually been over multiple terms of government, basic inaction."

He said it was disappointing that no political parties had released comprehensive policies covering the whole energy system.

"That's why we need a strategy. The challenge for political parties is to go back to the drawing board, do some more thinking, come up with some decent policy to help people out of the situation that politicians have allowed to evolve."

World.title: Greyhound trainers face up to future without racing
World.content:
Greyhound racing industry prepares for shutdown Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

A sense of the inevitable has shrouded the Hatrick Raceway this week as the Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club prepared for its last ever meeting on Friday evening.

The government is shutting down the industry over animal welfare concerns.

In April, Racing Minister Winston Peters announced the Racing Industry Amendment Bill passed its third and final reading with "overwhelming" cross-party support.

"This action wasn't taken lightly, but independent reviews in 2013, 2017 and 2021 provided clear evidence of serious animal welfare concerns."

Peters said while improvements were made, those gains plateaued and injury/death rates remained unacceptably high to the point the sport had lost its social licence.

Owners from around the country gathered at Hatrick Raceway earlier this week for the club's final straight-track meeting.

Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club president, John McArthur, said he'd been in the sport for 50 years.

It was part of his DNA.

Whanganui Greyhound Racing Club president John McArthur has tough decisions ahead about what to do with his dogs. RNZ / Robin Martin

"I just love the fact that the common man - don't forget that the common man - can afford to own a greyhound and take it to the races, look after it and care for it.

"It's not the landed gentry of racehorses. We are the common people and we know that. It's one of the reasons we are in the position we are."

McArthur didn't shy away from the fact dogs sometimes got injured.

He reckoned about nine dogs had been euthanised nationwide this season across hundreds of meetings.

That number climbed to 10 on Tuesday with the death of five-year-old Tiger Jane who fell at Addington Raceway fracturing her left humerus.

McArthur took RNZ through the Hatrick Raceway kennels where the dogs were prepared for racing.

Trainers retrieve their dogs after a race at the Hatrick Raceway in Whanganui. RNZ / Robin Martin

"The dogs come in and they go here where they are identified by the chip in the dog. They are then weighed and they then go up here on to the examination table where the vet examines them.

"He does a full examination of the dogs and if they've come through the veterinary inspection they are then kennelled in their own separate kennel."

When it comes time to race, the dogs were walked out to the straight-track - installed two years ago in the centre of the Whanganui Racecourse at a cost of $3 million - in response to welfare concerns.

The greyhounds are placed in start boxes and then they're off.

The race is over in a matter of seconds ... but Clevedon trainer Peter Heterick loves it nevertheless.

"Aw mate, it's just, yeah, my passion. I love it. You know, dogs they bring something to you that, you know, horses don't.

"They just love being around you, they're kind. They're just beautiful animals."

He was gutted racing was being shut down.

RNZ / Robin Martin

"Aw devastated, yeah, it's just crazy, honestly."

Heterick would be keeping his dogs.

"I'm gonna stay at home and look after them.

"A transition agency take over, but you've still got to look after your dogs, you've got to get up in the morning and take them for a walk, feed them and everything.

"You know, nothings going to change you're just not racing."

Heterick reckons retired greyhounds would make great pets.

"Oh, they will, they will, especially this one here, but she's coming with me."

Greyhounds racing on the Hatrick Raceway straight at Whanganui. RNZ / Robin Martin

In a statement, SPCA chief scientific officer Dr Arnja Dale said the greyhound racing ban was necessary after years of welfare concerns and repeated but unsuccessful attempts to improve safety.

"This is a historic day for animal welfare. It's the beginning of a new chapter where greyhounds can simply be loved as family pets."

Dale said the rehoming challenge for the remaining 1300 greyhounds was significant but achievable.

"The racing is ending, but the work certainly isn't. Our focus now is providing support to the Greyhound Transition Agency to help greyhounds find the loving homes they deserve."

Waikato owner Michael Schneider had come south for the Hatrick Raceway meet.

Waikato trainer Michael Schneider, whose dog, got a second placing on the straight-track this week, says his dogs will be retiring at home with him. RNZ / Robin Martin

He got into racing through adopting a retired greyhound.

"I would go there on Saturday mornings and help them train their dogs and slip them up their straight-track and took our old boy - well he wasn't that old at that time - and just let him run for exercise and just seeing how much they loved it.

"I love the whole idea of animals that have a job to do, but also really love their job."

He had plans for his dogs.

"They're all coming home with us. We've actually bought a property specifically for that. We're setting up a big track for them. Setting up kennels, but they'll probably all end up in the house anyway.

"So, we've got mum and one of the pups at home at the moment and we've got another three coming to retire with us."

Schneider said the prospect of no more racing was 'just gut-wrenching really".

Meanwhile, tough decisions lay ahead for McArthur who had 18 dogs.

"I've got a lot of dogs here that are too old to go into an adoption systems, so I guess I've got virtually no option.

"I'm a superannuitant, I don't have huge pockets loads of cash, so I suppose I will have to make the decision to do something with them, but that's down the track and I'll face that when I have to."

World.title: Minister shuts down mayor's claim of softening stance on local body amalgamation
World.content:
Local Government Minister Simon Watts says policy on amalgamation has not changed, after one mayor indicated a softening of the government's position.

Watts, alongside RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop, announced in May that councils would have three months to come up with plans for reorganising council boundaries, with a focus on abolishing regional councils and creating larger unitary authorities.

"Our message to councils is simple: lead your own reform or we will do it for you. Either way, change is coming," Bishop said at the time.

Tararua wary of amalgamation plans Morning Report Download MP3 5m

That 9 August deadline - pitched as giving councils a "head start" on amalgamation discussions - is fast approaching.

Councils have been consulting and discussing their options but few have come up with firm plans.

Tararua mayor Scott Gilmore spoke to Morning Report on Thursday about how those discussions were going, saying they had great relationships with all their neighbours but "definitely not to a point where there'd be any meaningful proposal being ready to be put forward".

"It's not just amalgamation, and I think that's the problem with the government's head-start proposal is amalgamation is the only option within that process.

"We think that there's other options, like the government first signalled late last year - shared services, other collaboration, other efficiencies."

Discussions had started with Horizons Regional Council, covering Manawatū-Whanganui, but Tararua covered a "massive, massive" area already and regional council areas were based on water catchments, Gilmore said.

As a result, the council was not planning to submit a proposal.

"People are really conscious of their local voice, and I actually think not that we should lose it.

"Our council sees much more risk for us taking part in the head start ... we wouldn't have time to have a good proposal but we might get locked into something that would be really undesirable for our communities, and we're just not willing to do that. And our community told us they don't want us to.

"The way that local government works best is when the people that are close to the action are participating in the decision-making. And you know, when you look at having a huge geographical area, a mass amalgamation, it's going to be really difficult to put that in there."

However, the rhetoric from the government on amalgamation "has changed and has softened", he said.

"I'm really grateful to the minister. I've spoken to him directly a couple of times.

"We've had clarified that the back-stop process will be a collaborative process and it'll be run in a similar way to what they consulted on late last year before all of this head-start bombshell dropped.

"That will give us an opportunity to help us lead our own reforms."

However, Gilmore told RNZ his comments were not based on private conversations "although I have appreciated the opportunity to talk to the minister directly", but based on a letter the minister had sent him.

The letter from Watts, which RNZ has seen, says the backstop "will be broadly based on the original Simplifying Local Government proposal and will be informed by lessons from the Head Start as well as feedback from consultation".

"We are open to innovative approaches from councils as well as current Local Government Act 2002 models. Local voice will continue to be important through design of the backstop."

It also states the final decisions would be made by the government in 2027.

Scott said he did not dispute that the policy had not changed, "rather the language that surrounds it".

He said the government's clarification that it would be based on the original proposal and it expected to work collaboratively with councils and communities was encouraging.

Gilmore criticised the approach taken, saying the "language of 'do it or we'll do it to you' ... was really unhelpful".

Local Government Minister Simon Watts. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Watts rejected the suggestion of a softening.

"There's been no change in government policy," the minister said in a statement.

He indicated that what would happen to councils afterwards - the "back-stop" option - would take council feedback into account but that ultimately the government would decide the way forward.

"Our position is and has always been that we will work with councils - head start was specifically designed to give councils control over their plans.

"Change is coming and the government will progress with the back stop for councils not in the head start. But we've also been clear from the beginning that we want to learn from the councils going through the process before making final decisions on what that back stop looks like."

When asked about mayor Gilmore's comments, RMA Reform Minister Chris Bishop said mayors should refrain from making private conversations public.

"The fastest way to make sure that ministers don't pick up the phone is the knowledge that something that you say to a mayor might end up on the front page of a newspaper - that would be regrettable," he said.

Bishop said he was trying to "stay out of it" because he wanted to see what the regions would come up with.

"There's incessant lobbying going on in Wellington, everyone trying to drag me into the debate in Wellington - obviously because I'm a local MP in Wellington.

"There's incessant efforts to get me to engage. I'm trying to stay out of it because I want the region to come up with a solution," he said.

World.title: Who will pay the price to keep NZ Super affordable?
World.content:
Economists say two new Treasury papers make it clear there's no easy fix to keep New Zealand's pension affordable.

The papers were produced as part of preparing Treasury's long-term fiscal statement and look at how NZ Super is indexed, and how raising the age could affect how affordable it is for the country.

The papers note that New Zealand's ageing population is expected to add to the cost of NZ Super over the coming decades, at the same time as there will be other cost pressures, such as in healthcare. The researchers said addressing the pressure would require policy choices that would affect government revenue, spending and public debt.

The number of working-age people compared to those over 65 is expected to drop from four-to-one now to two-to-one by the end of the century.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

NZ Super already costs more than $20 billion a year.

One of the papers looked at how the pension is indexed. At present, NZ Super is linked to average wages. The paper said that changing that so that it was indexed to price increases, or a mixed indexation, could be a way to reduce the cost.

"These changes not only alleviate the government's tax revenue requirements but also incentivise greater workforce participation and savings, contributing to a stronger economy."

The other looked at the impact of increasing the age of eligibility. But it said the age would need to rise to "very high" levels to keep pension spending at its current level as a proportion of gross domestic product (GDP). It would need to reach 75 by 2100, and 79 if consumption taxes are used to fund increases in health and pension spending.

The researchers calculated that raising the age of eligibility to 70 would reduce gross pension costs by between 1.64 and 1.84 percentage points of GDP by 2065, depending on the assumptions made about workforce participation.

"Net pension costs, which take into consideration tax paid on pensions, would fall between 1.15 and 1.23 percentage points of GDP by the year 2065. This translates into average (gross) cost savings of between 0.33 and 0.37 percentage points of GDP for each additional year that the retirement age is raised. The net-of-tax savings would be 0.23 and 0.25 percentage points of GDP for each year that the age of eligibility is raised."

Simplicity economist Shamubeel Eaqub was part of the review team for Treasury and said the findings were what he would expect.

"If you think about the levers that we need to pull to make superannuation sustainable, indexation and raising the age of eligibility don't do very much ... it creates some benefits, but it's at the margin."

He said a move to the Australian model of some private provision and means-testing of the pension would be the only thing that sufficiently made a difference.

"I think that's what these papers do really well. They really identify that it's not just the cost of the pension you need to think about. It's also those other things that are happening in terms of older people retiring in renting, older people needing more hospital care, those kinds of things. So those costs are still building. It's not like you can look at superannuation isolation.

"I think it's essentially saying there are no easy choices here. There's a big trade-off to be had."

Simplicity economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ

The papers noted that the impact of changes on different parts of society would need to be considered.

People who were more immediately affected would have less time to adapt and could miss out on support, while future generations would benefit from lower tax burdens and improved economic outcomes.

"Within generations, higher-income individuals are less affected by pension reductions and gain more from reduced taxes and a stronger economy, amplifying disparities between low- and high-income households."

They said it would be important to give sufficient warning of any changes.

"Pre-announcing policy changes and spreading changes out over time reduces the burden felt by people from these changes because they have more time to adapt their lifetime behaviour, including consumption, saving, and labour supply."

ANZ senior economist Miles Workman said the papers added to "one of the most significant fiscal challenges facing New Zealand".

"A key message from both is that there is no single policy lever that can fully address the fiscal pressures associated with an ageing population, and every option involves trade-offs between generations, income groups and taxpayers.

"Importantly, maintaining the status quo isn't cost-free either. Without policy changes, the growing cost of superannuation and health spending would ultimately need to be funded through higher taxes, lower spending elsewhere, higher debt, or some combination of all three. The challenge for policymakers is deciding how those costs are shared across current and future generations."

World.title: More school leavers with no qualifications becoming 'new normal': advocates
World.content:
There are fears the high number of school leavers with no qualifications is becoming baked into the education system.

Education Ministry figures show 15 percent of school leavers last year had no NCEA certificates or equivalent qualifications.

It is the third consecutive year the figure has been so high after years sitting at 10-11 percent.

At schools in the poorest neighbourhoods, more than a quarter of last year's leavers had nothing.

Manager of the Whanganui Learning Centre Jen McDonald said the increase had been noticed and felt like it was becoming the new normal.

"We've heard many stories of ones that have just struggled with anxiety at school, the school environment hasn't suited them. Some of them come out of school with enough credits to be passing level 1 or level 2 but they're missing those critical literacy and numeracy credits, so 10 literacy and 10 numeracy, the compulsory credits," she said.

The main way teens achieved the literacy and numeracy credits was through online tests but McDonald said a lot of students who came to the centre failed those simply because they did not cope with exams.

Leaving school or being kicked out without qualifications had a lasting effect on people's self-esteem and on their future opportunities, she said.

"Jobs are few and far between for people with zero qualifications. If they're wanting to have an apprenticeship they need to have at least level 2, so again even if they've got aspirations to be a builder or whatever, they've got a lot of work to do," she said.

Often the young people the centre worked with were very capable but they had not received the support or the environment they needed to succeed, McDonald said.

The Kākano Youth Arts Collective in West Auckland also worked with young people who had left school with nothing.

Director Mandy Patmore said the teens it saw had not coped with school or with alternative education.

"A lot of those young people, they just don't fit, so they're kind of being cast aside and it doesn't look like from our perspective there's a whole lot of nets to catch them. It just seems like they go into an abyss," she said.

"They're expected to go into employment but they've got no skills or support networks to make that happen."

The collective's youth support coordinator Sarah Candler said many schools were too quick to kick teens out.

"The number one thing is that it is way, way too easy for schools to exclude kids," she said.

"Often the reasons for the kid losing their entire education is one mix-up, one fight in the playground, one incident of something going wrong and they're a really at-risk kid already and they go," she said.

Excluding students was disastrous because they were under huge pressure to get jobs and get on in life but had none of the qualifications they needed to help them get there, Candler said.

More leaving with level 2

Meanwhile, the school leaver figures did have some good news - 78 percent of last year's leavers had at least NCEA level 2 and 59 percent had level 3, both improvements on the previous year.

Papakura High School principal Simon Craggs said it was good to see an increase in level 2 attainment because that was the baseline for employment and further study.

"It's disappointing not to see the number of students leaving without qualifications reduce but unsurprising I guess given schools have been grappling with a lot of change over the last few years," he said.

World.title: Samoa on the brink of international rugby ban, local media reports
World.content:
Samoa is on the brink of being suspended by rugby's world governing body, local media is reporting.

It comes after the Samoan government announced on Wednesday it was withdrawing support of Lakapi Samoa due to "unresolved internal issues and division" at the union.

According to Samoa Observer, World Rugby has given the Samoan government until Friday "to accept a proposed review of its decision to withdraw recognition and financial support from Lakapi Samoa".

"Failure to accept the review or respond by the deadline could result in Samoa being suspended from international rugby for four years," the news outlet reported.

It added the development follows a meeting between Samoa Rugby Union and World Rugby representatives on Thursday.

RNZ Pacific has contacted World Rugby and Lakapi Samoa for comment.

Samoa's Prime Minister La'aulialemalietoa (La'auli) Leuatea Schmidt revealed in March his government would set up a rival union to govern the sport in the country if the entire Lakapi Samoa board did not resign.

In February, La'auli expressed dissatisfaction at the status of the game in Samoa, saying at the time the sport had been "politicised".

"We're coming in to clear out all the politicians inside our rugby union," he said at the time.

"At this stage, our rugby is very impoverished ... we are in the level that Samoa had never been before, because of what? Because of management."

In June, World Rugby formally appointed Lakapi Samoa chairman Afioga Namulauuli Papali'i as Samoa's representative on the World Rugby Council.

World.title: Defence Force training infrastructure in 'World War II era', new documents reveal
World.content:
The Defence Force is on its biggest push ever to get more combat ready and lethal at the same time its training infrastructure is in "World War II era", according to newly released documents.

Proactively released Cabinet papers from April and May outline the big deficit.

"The infrastructure to support training of recruits, in particular, is not in a position to meet existing ... demand in an effective way," said one 12-page paper that asked for, and got, a start to planning for an upgrade to how recruits are trained.

"Much of the infrastructure required to train NZDF personnel, like classrooms or rifle ranges, is World War II era, and is increasingly ineffective, and creating a potential for unsafe training environments.

"Investment is needed to avoid future failure."

The paper asked Cabinet to back a business case for fixing this, and Budget 2026 put in $23m.

However, this only funds a design phase out to 2029-30.

That means an actual fix of systems and infrastructure together appears at least three years away.

RNZ asked Defence Minister Chris Penk what immediate measures he is taking and is awaiting a response.

The paper said one upgraded rifle range would be added meantime, but one or two other short-term moves "to add resilience to a significantly degraded capability" were blanked out.

'Failing condition makes it difficult to train'

The deficiencies are a big hurdle to Defence's must-have in its new workforce strategy "to grow more soldiers, sailors and aviators, with urgency" and more tech-savvy ones as drone, cyber and electronic warfare take over.

Instead, "poor infrastructure in failing condition makes it difficult to train and retain people."

An example is old manual target practice ranges not suitable for modern weapons. Two other examples were blanked out.

The wider context is grim:

The state of bases and facilities was a key reason given at scrutiny week in June for the land combat readiness falling to 45 percent at the end of 2025.

Defence has admitted its training systems are degraded too much to rapidly boost battlefield adaptability and agility.

NZDF's ways of managing its existing assets do not meet Treasury standards, and it is slow to get contracts for projects signed up.

Eroded by old gear and slow take-up of new tech, 60 percent of the army's land training system had got to the end of its life, said the May Cabinet paper.

Recruits 'most pressing'

The whole system relied in the first place on recruit training but this was significantly degraded and the "most pressing" thing needing fixing.

That fix would focus on Waiouru camp and line up with Australia, which was putting almost a billion dollars into recruit training, as well as looking to the US, UK and Singapore.

The paper that Penk lodged with Cabinet showed the ministers - Judith Collins was Defence Minister at the time - walking a line between "capability and affordability", even after Defence got a $9 billion fillip in new spending over four years from 2025.

So they narrowed in on a new recruit training system and curriculum which was the "minimum viable capability needed in the short term", and would need to integrate with Australia, other partners and other government services.

"Australian designs will be used where possible" in the detailed business case that is now being worked on.

'Future growth' option not chosen

A third more ambitious option that catered for "future growth and the introduction of new and emerging ... capabilities" did not make the cut.

Budget 2026 also had funding for an undisclosed amount for a new 'virtual training' facility at Linton camp near Palmerston North.

Defence has a huge estate, huge budgets and a chequered track record running it all.

The latest available Treasury report on how NZDF was doing with its big capital investments said it was no longer reporting a significant underspend (which can indicate projects hitting delays). Its actual spend on projects at $406m, and its spending on repairs and maintenance at $193m, at that stage were only a bit behind forecast.

However, Defence spending on specialist equipment and on data/digital was running well behind forecast.

The report for the September-December 2025 quarter showed it took about a year for procurement processes to get to the point of signing contracts, among the slower on the major public agencies covered by the Treasury investment reports.

Its asset registers and asset management plans were not up to scratch according to the latest gauge in June 2025. An update for 2026 won't be publicly available for months.

Labour's defence spokesperson Damien O'Connor said it supported the direction of the Defence Capability Plan.

"Personnel is the most acute issue facing NZDF. Labour sees this as a priority and will get advice on ensuring training capacity is built when in government," he said.

World.title: Final frontiers drive Hazlewood in twilight years
World.content:
Josh Hazlewood has more boxes to tick in a stellar career after returning to peak fitness following several injury impacted years.

The 35-year-old Australia paceman, veteran of 76 Tests, has never won a series in India or England, two classic confrontations that loom large in the 20 Tests at least the team are set to play in the next 12 months.

Australia have not won an away Ashes series since 2001, while 2004 was the last triumph in India — well before any of the current squad were playing Tests.

Australian men's Tests in 2026/27 August 12-26: Two Tests vs Bangladesh

Two Tests vs Bangladesh October 9-31: Three Tests in South Africa

Three Tests in South Africa December 9-January 7: Four Tests vs New Zealand

Four Tests vs New Zealand January 21-February 23, 2027: Five Tests in India

Five Tests in India March 11-15, 2027: One Test vs England

One Test vs England June, 2027: World Test Championship final (potential)

World Test Championship final (potential) June-July, 2027: Five Tests in England

"The big series are obviously England and India. I haven't won in South Africa either, so there are a few boxes to tick off there, not just me, but this whole playing group," Hazlewood said.

"That's been a driving factor during this prep, it is in the back of your head, and in the months leading into it. They're real big Test series, all away against tough competition. Hopefully we get the job done."

Hazlewood's most recent setback in the Test sphere came when Achilles tendon and hamstring injuries cruelled any involvement in last summer's Ashes series.

Since then he has returned to the bowling crease with a bang, helping Royal Challengers Bengaluru win back-to-back IPL titles.

Hazlewood has been preparing with other members of the Australia squad at the National Cricket Centre in Brisbane ahead of two Tests against Bangladesh in Darwin and Mackay next month.

He said the "big days" of training in one location and without other playing commitments had been ideal.

Can't get enough cricket from Grandstand? Tune in for the latest cricket news, interviews and analysis from the ABC team in the Grandstand Cricket Podcast.

"Leading into other Test series and Test matches, you're playing T20, you're playing one-dayers, you're travelling, so it's tough to fit those bowling sessions in," he said.

"It's just trying to replicate a day in the field of Test cricket. It's bowling multiple spells in a day. It's bowling back-to-back days."

"This has been tailor-made for a Test match, which I think should work out well."

Hazlewood said it would be "tough" for any of the quicks in the squad to play every Test in the next year.

"Maybe a spinner," he quipped.

Hazlewood, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Scott Boland, Brendan Doggett and Michael Neser will all be vying for games.

Boland, who has been in sensational Test form, has been mostly overlooked when Hazlewood was previously available, but it need not be an either/or proposition.

"I think we've only played one game together … in England at Edgbaston, which was nice. I'd love to play more with Scotty," Hazlewood said.

"We're obviously a little bit similar, but there are still a lot of differences in our bowling. Every time he's come in, he's done unbelievably well. His career just keeps getting better and better the older he gets.

"I think there are enough opportunities in the next 12 to 18 months for us to play a lot of cricket, hopefully, together. We've got Ness (Neser) and Doggy (Doggett) there as well, so I think we'll have to lean on all six at some point in the next 18 months."

Hazlewood's most recent injuries have coincided with home Tests, but he is not sweating over what transpired in the past.

"We've got a nice lead-in this time. We've got Test matches abroad, so hopefully we hit the ground running again in Australia," he said.

"I've been lucky enough to play 70-odd Test matches now, which is quite a lot in terms of Aussie quicks. Hopefully I can tick a few more off."

AAP

World.title: People across Ireland wake up at all hours to watch AFLW
World.content:
In the middle of the night in a house in Ballinamore, in the North West of Ireland, Sharon O'Dowd wakes up to put on an Australian broadcast.

Two years ago, her young sister Eilish, who she helped raise with 12 years between them, moved from County Leitrim to Sydney to play AFLW for GWS.

Sharon and Eilish ODowd at a Gaelic game. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

When one of two of Eilish's matches haven't been available to stream across the ocean, the mother of two — her kids three and six — has put the commentary on and sat and listened instead while the rest of her house sleeps.

"I don't mind getting up this early as I love to watch her and the Giants play," Sharon told ABC Sport.

"If it's a particularly early game I usually go back to bed after it."

Sharon is one of many families across Ireland who wake up at all hours to watch GAA-turned-AFLW stars.

There are 47 Irish players in the AFL women's competition, many of whom will be on show in this weekend's inaugural AFLW Australia v Ireland clash in Sydney.

Their feats regularly make headlines back home.

Eilish with the first touch of her ball for GWS scored the fastest opening goal in AFLW history. The clip — in which she won the tap in the ruck and bolted straight through the corridor to score within 15 seconds — made the national news.

Sharon and EIlish O'Dowd. (Supplied: Sharon O'Dowd)

As it was her first game, Sharon was still getting familiar with the stream and watched, stunned, from her phone.

"I was in shock when she scored because I just couldn't believe what had happened," Sharon said.

"Everyone else in my house was asleep so I couldn't even celebrate with them. I knew my parents were watching the game in their house so I texted them.

"But it had happened so quickly they didn't even see it because they hadn't got logged into their streaming account fast enough."

Luckily, they have since watched the video of the replay multiple times.

Vikki Wall is a two-time premiership player with North Melbourne. (Getty: Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos)

Over in Dunboyne, a town of less than 10,000 people in County Meath, the Wall family regularly pack their house for North Melbourne games.

Tom and Caroline Wall's daughter, Vikki Wall, is a star sportswoman from the Eastern Coast.

She twice led County Meath to historic All-Ireland Senior Championship titles in 2021 and 2022 before being signed as an international rookie by North Melbourne and playing all 13 games of her 2022 debut season.

Vikki Wall is a star player in Ireland. (Supplied: Caroline Wall)

She missed the 2023 AFLW season to play rugby sevens for Ireland ahead of the Paris Olympics and returned to Arden Street to win premierships in 2024 and 2025.

"We've had events in our house where 30-plus people come and have breakfast and cheer on the teams," Tom told ABC Sport.

"We try to watch all of Vikki's matches but it can be difficult to access the games online sometimes, so we listen to the match commentaries on the radio, if necessary."

Like Sharon, this means getting up before the sun. "But it's worth it," said Tom.

Dublin, Ireland, August 15, 2021: Vikki Wall of Meath is congratulated by family following the TG4 All-Ireland Senior Ladies Football Championship Semi-Final match between Cork and Meath at Croke Park. (Getty: Stephen McCarthy/Sportsfile)

Vikki's younger sister Sarah was drafted to the Kangaroos last year. Thankfully for Tom and Caroline, this means still just the one early alarm.

Similarly, Collingwood's Sarah Rowe is a cross-code athlete, whose dad has followed her career across the globe.

Sarah represented County Mayo across all age groups from under-12 to the senior team before she moved to Australia.

There, she became a fan favourite for the Magpies after debuting in 2019 and won an A-League Women's championship with the Central Coast Mariners in 2025.

Her father Alan hasn't missed a game.

"My passion for the AFLW is total," Rowe told ABC Sport.

Sarah Rowe with her dad Alan after winning the A-League Women championship. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

"I originally had not a clue about the rules, regulations or how to play the game but over a period of time, I've got to understand everything about it, I've seen the great players grow and understood the game passionately and very deeply, to now [to be able to] say that's it's one of the great games that I love watching."

Rowe has made the trip over to Sydney for the first AFLW Australia v Ireland representative game, as he does for all her big games: her 50th, 75th and Collingwood's 2022 semi-final against Adelaide.

"It's a great honour to represent the country at the highest level and I will be there with great pride and for the family and for the town of Ballina," Rowe said.

Alan Rowe hasn't missed a single game of his daughter's, Collingwood star Sarah Rowe. (Supplied: Alan Rowe)

Back in Ballina, Sarah's mother Grainne will be watching the match with "everybody within our family," Rowe said, including aunties, uncles and cousins.

"It's one of the big days of sporting life within the Irish calendar.

" And it'll be one that everyone will be so much looking forward to watching and very proud to be a part of. "

Sharon said it gets hard being away from Eilish, but she's happy players like her sister can give their all to the game overseas.

"When she has had a great game I would just love to be there to be able to tell her how amazing she is, and also when she is having a hard time or she gets injured I would love to be able to make sure she is ok. We do video calls all the time though so that helps," Sharon said.

The AFLW Australia v Ireland Cup and Best on Ground medal ahead of the inaugural clash. (Getty: Matt King/AFL Photos)

She's hoping it'll be a very happy FaceTime after Saturday's game against Australia at North Sydney Oval.

"It is an incredibly proud moment for all our family to see Eilish wear an Irish jersey and represent her country. There is no higher honour in sport in my opinion," she said.

"I'd imagine for this game the whole family will get up early to see her. We will have our Irish flags out and cheer the whole team on."

World.title: Storm coach responds to Munster's PNG ultimatum
World.content:
A part of Craig Bellamy would love it if he and Cameron Munster could bow out of Melbourne together.

But as the pair consider their NRL futures, Bellamy remains committed to supporting Munster whether or not he signs with expansion franchise PNG.

Storm veteran Munster turned the heat on Bellamy on Wednesday by claiming he would reject interest from the Chiefs for 2028 if Bellamy remained Melbourne's coach for that season.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Bellamy re-signed with the Storm through 2028 in February, but the master mentor's diagnosis with a neurodegenerative condition has since cast doubt over his future.

On Thursday, Bellamy reiterated "the next year or two I'll be finishing up" but did not say whether his health would permit coaching on as late as 2028.

Bellamy handed Munster his NRL debut in 2014 and coached him in two premiership triumphs, with the 31-year-old now the Storm's longest-serving active player.

For Bellamy, the chance to bow out together would be fitting, but Munster indicated on Wednesday he may not be able to wait for the coach to make his own decision.

"I'd love to go right through my coaching career with him, ending about the same time," Bellamy said.

"[But] he's got a decision to make. He'll make the right decision for what's right for his family. He's got the right to do that.

"I'll back 'Mun' up, whatever he wants to do."

Munster remains sidelined with a knee injury for Friday's clash with resurgent Canterbury and is now joined on the pine by captain and hooker Harry Grant.

In a season of injury carnage, Bellamy said Grant's hamstring problem was another big blow for the 12th-placed Storm.

"Any team losing their captain, that's a big loss, but Harry especially," Bellamy said.

"He's always in the middle of the play whether it be with the ball or without the ball."

Injuries, roster turnover and a seven-game losing streak early in the season have all left the Storm's finals hopes hanging by a thread ahead of round 22.

A loss to the Bulldogs would ensure they miss the top eight for only the second time under Bellamy, and first since mass salary cap breaches consigned them to the wooden spoon in 2010.

It would also mark a 12th loss of the year — the most the Storm would have suffered in any of their 24 seasons under Bellamy.

"We know it's going to be a tough ask tomorrow night, but we've had a good week's preparation with the guys we've had," Bellamy said.

AAP

World.title: Cricketer dubbed 'Clicky Ponting' suspended as stats show unusual trend
World.content:
The club at the centre of the "Clicky Ponting" scandal in English amateur cricket has suspended its player over the matter.

Saltburn Cricket Club said Brian Devine had been suspended for the rest of the season after several videos were posted online with claims Devine was clicking his fingers as the ball passed the bat to mimic the sound of an edge.

The club has forfeited its next match in the North Yorkshire and South Durham Cricket League.

"We are treating this allegation with the utmost seriousness and, as a family-centric club, we are fully cooperating with the league's investigation," a statement read.

"We believe that the club acted decisively as soon as the complaint and investigation were made known to us.

"The player at the centre of the complaint has been suspended and will not play again for the club this season or in the foreseeable future, pending the outcome of this investigation."

Devine is yet to comment on the matter and an investigation into the claims has yet to be completed, with the allegations so far unproven.

However, an amateur data analyst on social media platform X said they had trawled all scorecards from Saltburn games and found wicketkeeper catches dramatically increased when Devine was playing.

"Been requested to split it by the matches where Devine (the slip clicker) played, and it's even more stark," X account @maxtempers, which usually posts about British politics, wrote.

"39 keeper catches in 13 matches with Devine. 5 keeper catches in 7 without."

The post followed an original analysis that found wicketkeeper catches increased four-fold when the particular keeper standing alongside Devine in the alleged clicking footage was playing, including eight catches in one innings.

The record at Test level is seven catches in one innings, shared by five players.

"The league has received a formal complaint regarding alleged incidents in a Division Two game on Saturday 25 July, 2026," a league statement read when the controversy came to light.

"A full investigation has been initiated and until such time as the formal processes are complete no further comment will be made."

Australian cricket podcasters The Grade Cricketer have offered to provide financial support to Devine and Saltburn.

World.title: Broncos premiership prop announces medical retirement due to blood clots
World.content:
Brisbane Broncos premiership prop Corey Jensen has announced his medical retirement from the NRL after ongoing problems.

Jensen, who played 95 games for Brisbane including last year's grand final win over Melbourne Storm, also played 58 games in five seasons for North Queensland.

After becoming unwell during round seven, Jensen was diagnosed with a pulmonary embolism (blood clots in the lungs).

"After receiving medical advice and speaking to specialists, it's clear that it's no longer safe for me to play rugby league," he told reporters.

Jensen said he had been told he would have to take blood thinners for the rest of his life.

Big Ben heading to NFL The Brisbane Broncos are releasing forward Ben Te Kura from the rest of his NRL contract to allow him to pursue his dream of playing in the NFL.

"Since [the diagnosis] I've been able to train properly again, it's been like a mini pre-season, and I can do everything other than the contact, which is the frustrating part.

"Overall, my health's pretty good, I can continue training in the future and it's not going to affect me in any way."

The Broncos had confirmed he had another incident with deep vein thrombosis in his calf a year earlier, with both incidents considered unprovoked, meaning there was no obvious trigger such as a long-haul flight or injury.

"I leave with absolutely no regrets," he said, thanking his teammates for being part of the premiership win with them.

"I never chased individual recognition, but being part of a team, seeing people grow and knowing that in some way I may have contributed."

Corey Jensen played 95 games for the Broncos after joining the Brisbane side for the 2022 season. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Jensen teared up, thanking his wife Shannen for all her support and the sacrifices she had made.

"People see the player, but they don't always see what partners give up behind the scenes," he said.

Jensen is a qualified sports scientist, having completed a Bachelor of Sport and Exercise Science at James Cook University, and will have a bright future in that space if he chooses to pursue it.

Jensen was not a star as a youth but, through hard work, turned himself into a weapon after debuting for the Cowboys in 2017 and playing in the grand final.

"The late Paul Green gave me my debut back then.

"I was a bit of a late bloomer, so I'm grateful they took a punt on me, and I have to acknowledge how much the Cowboys did for my career," Jensen said.

"Coming down here was kind of a kind of a new lease on life. The Broncos gave me the opportunity, and I'm eternally grateful for what this club's done for me both on and off the field."

ABC/AAP

World.title: Quick hits: Swimmer spurns Love Island offer, dictator's grandson's vow
World.content:
A Scottish swimmer rejects an approach to appear on a dating reality show, Idi Amin's grandson reveals his royal plans and an Australian weightlifter adds to his family's medal history.

Here are the quick hits from day six of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Swimmer gives up Love Island opportunity

Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan turned down an offer to appear on Love Island. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

Last year, Scottish swimmer Katie Shanahan had a choice to make.

Should she keep training with an eye on earning Commonwealth Games selection?

Or appear on reality dating program Love Island?

Shanahan spurned the chance to enter the villa and chose to focus on her swimming career and the decision is paying off.

The 22-year-old won silver in the women's 200m backstroke at the Glasgow Games.

"I'm the biggest Love Island fan ever. I've watched every season", Shanahan told BBC Scotland News.

"Last year the producers asked me and [English swimmer] Abbie Wood if we would be interested in doing it.

"I couldn't go on, though, because [I was] focusing on the swimming, but who knows in the future?

"I was a bit tempted but the swimming had to come first."

2. Idi Amin's grandson's vow

Aziz Abdul is disqualified during his bout on day six. (Reuters: Matthew Childs)

Carrying a family legacy into a sporting occasion can be a good thing.

In this instance, we're not sure it is.

Ugandan 90+kg boxer Aziz Abdul is the grandson of former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin.

Amin took charge in a coup in 1971 and ruled the country for eight years, during which an estimated half a million people were killed and the country's entire Asian population was expelled.

The Butcher of Uganda, as he was also known, had a bizarre fascination with Scotland, which was the subject of a film starring Forest Whitaker as Amin, The Last King Of Scotland.

It appears his grandson shares a similar love for the nation.

"In everything we do, God knows tomorrow," he told BBC Sport Scotland.

"It's God's plan. I might be the new king of Scotland. It's possible.

"When I arrived, I put up the flag, 'cause I like Scotland so much."

He fought England's Damar Thomas on day six in Glasgow but was disqualified for a headbutt during their quarterfinal.

3. Ollie's fall

Oliver Hoare falls during the mile heats. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

Ollie Hoare suffered a major scare in the mile heats, falling half way through the race after appearing to be tripped.

"There was no-one in front of me and I fell down," Hoare later said in the mix zone.

"Tough to have that happen because obviously I wanted to compete on my own merit, and having something like that happen sucks.

"I got up and kept competing because that's what we do."

The Australian team immediately appealed to get Hoare into Saturday's final and were successful, meaning the worst of things for Hoare was a bit of track rash.

"I'm a bit scabbed up and feeling crap about it but we move on," he said.

He joins fellow Australians Adam Spencer and Cam Myer in the final.

4. Like father, like son

Oliver Saxton secured Commonwealth Games bronze in Scotland 40 years after his dad did the same. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

At the 1986 Edinburgh Commonwealth Games, English weightlifter Andrew Saxton claimed his first Commonwealth Games medal, a bronze in the 100kg sub-heavyweight division.

Forty years later, his son, Australian Ollie Saxton, achieved the same result in the 94kg division in Glasgow.

Saxton senior went on to win three golds in Auckland — back then you got a medal for the snatch, clean and jerk, and overall — something that would only earn him one medal today.

He represented England in those two Games, but four years after that, in Victoria, British Colombia, he won a silver for Australia.

Something for Ollie to aspire to in four years in Ahmedabad.

5. Bobsleigh 'bootcamp' for Welsh shot putter

Keeping busy during the athletics off-season is not a problem for Adele Nicoll.

The Welsh shot putter has one of the more unusual sporting crossover stories, mixing shot putt with bobsleigh.

And she's pretty good at both. In February she was flying down on the Pista Olimpica Eugenio Monti in Cortina d'Ampezzo at the 2026 Winter Olympics, where she finished 18th in the monobob and 15th in the two-woman.

She thinks the rigours and unglamorous life of a bobsled athlete places her in good stead for athletics.

"In athletics, we just get our kit bag and we turn up to the track, but with the bobsleigh we're driving the vans around the world," Nicoll told the BBC.
